takeHome: First-pass success 78% direct, 83% video Macintosh, 88% video hyperangulated in 2,423 elective intubations.
Fewer rescue mask ventilations and operator switches with video; no more trauma to teeth or lips.
Hyperangulated video blade is the logical default under in-line stabilization.
posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters.** Video laryngoscopy has won in the ED and ICU, but routine OR intubation still largely runs on direct laryngoscopy. COVALENT is the largest OR trial, and it separates standard-blade from hyperangulated video devices.

**What they did.** Three-arm RCT at six centres in Germany and Austria (March 2022 to February 2025). Adults needing intubation for elective surgery were randomized 1:1:1 to direct laryngoscopy, video laryngoscopy with a Macintosh blade, or video laryngoscopy with a hyperangulated blade, stratified by site and Mallampati class. 2,532 randomized; 2,423 analyzed. Several device brands were used.

**What they found.**
- First-pass success: 78.2% direct, 82.9% video Macintosh, 87.6% video hyperangulated; every pairwise comparison P<.001.
- Cormack-Lehane grade 1 views: 58.8%, 74.7%, 87.6%.
- Intermittent mask ventilation needed in 11.8% with direct vs about 4% with either video device; fewer operator switches with video.
- Time to glottic view shortest with hyperangulated (14.1 s vs 16.7 vs 20.5), yet time to capnography was about 72 s in all arms.
- No difference in desaturation, regurgitation or dental injury overall; after a failed first attempt, lip or dental injury or blood on the blade was lower with the hyperangulated blade (10.9% vs about 23-24%).

**Caveats.** Operators unblinded; elective patients; the outcome is first-pass success, not patient harm; JAMA Network Open rather than a flagship journal.

**For the anesthesiologist.** The authors call video laryngoscopy the new standard for routine airway management. For trauma it strengthens the case for a hyperangulated video blade as first choice under manual in-line stabilization, where the view, not the time, is the limiting factor.

posts.headline: Four doses of dapagliflozin around cardiac surgery nearly halve postoperative AKI
posts.summary: A Dutch double-blind trial in 7 hospitals randomized 784 elective cardiac surgery patients to dapagliflozin 10 mg or placebo from the day before surgery through postoperative day 2.
takeHome: AKI within 7 days: 28% vs 52%; RR 0.54 (95% CI 0.45-0.65).
No excess atrial fibrillation (45% both) or reoperation (11% vs 10%).
Cheap, short, and already on formulary; watch for ketoacidosis and confirm in other cohorts.
posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters.** Cardiac surgery-associated AKI affects roughly a third of patients and nothing pharmacological has reliably prevented it. SGLT2 inhibitors protect kidneys in chronic disease, and this trial (Oosterom-Eijmael and colleagues, JAMA online 30 July 2026) is the first adequately powered perioperative test.

**What they did.** 784 adults undergoing elective cardiac surgery at 2 academic and 5 non-academic Dutch hospitals were randomized, double-blind, to dapagliflozin 10 mg or placebo once daily, starting the day before surgery and continuing through postoperative day 2 (four doses). The primary outcome was AKI by KDIGO criteria within 7 postoperative days.

**What they found.** AKI occurred in 28% of the dapagliflozin group vs 52% of the placebo group (RR 0.54, 95% CI 0.45-0.65; P less than .001). Postoperative atrial fibrillation was 45% in both arms and reoperation 11% vs 10%. The published abstract does not report dialysis, mortality or ketoacidosis rates in detail, so those need the full paper.

**Caveats.** The placebo-arm AKI rate of 52% is high, which suggests sensitive creatinine-based ascertainment and amplifies the absolute difference. Most of the benefit will be stage 1 AKI unless the full results show otherwise. Euglycemic ketoacidosis with perioperative SGLT2 inhibitors is a known concern and the usual advice is to stop them 3-4 days before surgery, which this trial deliberately contradicted; safety data on ketoacidosis will decide uptake.

**For anesthesiologists.** This is the most promising renoprotective drug result in cardiac surgery in years and it is actionable at the preoperative visit. Expect protocol discussions with surgeons and nephrologists; the sensible position is to await the full safety data and confirmatory trials before routine adoption, while no longer reflexively stopping SGLT2 inhibitors in patients already taking them.

posts.headline: FDA licenses Ezplaz, the first US freeze-dried plasma: room-temperature storage, reconstituted in minutes
posts.summary: On July 29, 2026 the FDA granted a biologics license to Vascular Solutions (Teleflex) for Ezplaz, a single-donor freeze-dried plasma for adults who need plasma when other plasma products are unavailable.
takeHome: First FDA-licensed freeze-dried plasma: stored 2-25 C for 12 months, reconstituted in about 1-2.5 minutes.
Label: adults needing plasma when other plasma products are unavailable, including massive transfusion and warfarin bleeding.
A logistics win; no trial shows Ezplaz itself improves survival.
posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters.** The US has run military dried plasma on emergency use authorizations for a decade while France, Germany and others used it routinely. On July 29, 2026 the FDA issued a biologics license for Ezplaz (Vascular Solutions LLC, a Teleflex subsidiary), the first freeze-dried plasma approved for US use.

**What it is.** A single unit of fresh frozen plasma, freeze-dried into a plastic bag rather than glass, from male-only donors to limit TRALI, supplied as group AB or group A with low-titer anti-B. Stored at 2-25 C for up to 12 months, reconstituted with the supplied sterile water in about 1-2.5 minutes, and given IV or IO. The kit includes the transfer and transfusion sets.

**Label.** Adults who need plasma when other plasma products are not available: bleeding or pre-procedure patients with multiple factor deficiencies, massive transfusion with clinically significant coagulopathy, and bleeding warfarin patients. Contraindications are plasma hypersensitivity and IgA deficiency. Labeling notes limited effect on minimally elevated INR (about 1.5-1.7). A postmarketing safety study focused on thrombotic events has been reported as a condition of approval.

**Caveats.** This is a logistics approval, not an outcome claim. Prehospital plasma RCTs were mixed (PAMPer positive in air transport, COMBAT and the French lyophilized-plasma trial neutral), and no trial has shown Ezplaz itself changes mortality. The Defense Health Agency has prioritized a licensed domestic source, so military demand will shape early supply.

**For the anesthesiologist.** Expect dried plasma in rural EDs, helicopters, hybrid ORs and mass-casualty caches, and in the first bags that arrive with transferred patients. The Joint Trauma System issued a companion CPG on June 9, 2026 covering dried plasma use across roles of care, including as a 1:1 partner for red cells when whole blood is unavailable.

posts.headline: PROSPECT hip arthroplasty update backs supra-inguinal fascia iliaca and PENG blocks; QL and ESP not recommended
posts.summary: PROSPECT updated its 2021 total hip arthroplasty guideline from 103 studies published 2020 to 2024, focusing on motor-sparing regional techniques.
takeHome: Core: scheduled paracetamol, NSAID, single-dose IV dexamethasone (10 mg or less); low-dose intrathecal morphine (0.1 mg) optional with spinal.
Supra-inguinal fascia iliaca block and pre-operative PENG block gave the most consistent analgesia.
Quadratus lumborum and erector spinae blocks: inconsistent efficacy and more motor weakness, so not recommended.
posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters.** Hip arthroplasty is among the highest-volume operations in any hospital and the block menu has exploded: fascia iliaca, PENG, quadratus lumborum, erector spinae, local infiltration. PROSPECT's update tells you which ones earned their place.

**What they did.** Systematic review of randomised trials and reviews published January 2020 to June 2024 (103 studies included), assessing pain within 24 hours, opioid consumption, functional recovery and adverse effects, with recommendations graded by expert consensus. Non-randomised studies without validated pain outcomes were excluded.

**Recommendations.**
- Unchanged core: scheduled paracetamol and NSAIDs, plus a single IV dose of dexamethasone (10 mg or less).
- Low-dose intrathecal morphine (0.1 mg) may be considered for hospitalised patients having spinal anaesthesia.
- Supra-inguinal fascia iliaca compartment block and pre-operative PENG block gave the most consistent analgesia and are the preferred motor-sparing regional options when feasible.
- Quadratus lumborum and erector spinae plane blocks: inconsistent efficacy and higher risk of motor weakness; not recommended.
- Single-shot local infiltration analgesia remains an alternative where advanced techniques are unavailable.

**Caveats.** Recommendations are consensus-graded, and head-to-head trials of PENG versus supra-inguinal fascia iliaca remain few. The supra-inguinal fascia iliaca recommendation goes beyond the 2021 guidance.

**What it means.** If you cover arthroplasty lists, the default pairing is now paracetamol, NSAID and dexamethasone plus a PENG or supra-inguinal fascia iliaca block, with low-dose intrathecal morphine for inpatients having a spinal. Drop the QL and ESP from the hip pathway.

posts.headline: Remimazolam anaesthesia causes more delirium than propofol in older lung resection patients
posts.summary: 455 patients aged 65 or older having lung resection were randomised to remimazolam or propofol anaesthesia. Delirium in the first 3 days occurred in 48% vs 31%, failing non-inferiority and driven by emergence delirium.
takeHome: Delirium 48% vs 31% (RR 1.53, 95% CI 1.21-1.94); risk difference 16.5% exceeded the 10% non-inferiority margin.
Excess was emergence delirium (46% vs 28%); delirium after PACU discharge was similar (4% vs 5%).
Think twice before routine remimazolam maintenance in older thoracic patients.
posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters.** Remimazolam is being adopted for maintenance anaesthesia because of its haemodynamic stability and reversibility, exactly the properties that appeal in older thoracic patients. Whether a benzodiazepine anaesthetic increases delirium was the obvious unanswered question.

**What they did.** Randomised non-inferiority trial at Shanghai Chest Hospital. Patients aged 65 or older having lung resection received remimazolam or propofol anaesthesia. Trained assessors blinded to allocation screened for delirium with the Confusion Assessment Method twice daily in the PACU and for 3 days. Non-inferiority margin: 10 percentage points absolute.

**What they found (455 analysed).**
- Delirium within 3 days: 108/227 (48%) with remimazolam vs 71/228 (31%) with propofol; RR 1.53, 95% CI 1.21-1.94.
- Absolute difference 16.5 points (95% CI 7.7-25.3), crossing the margin; non-inferiority not established.
- Emergence delirium 46% vs 28% (RR 1.65, 95% CI 1.28-2.12); delirium after PACU discharge 4% vs 5%.
- Delirium-positive assessments 9% vs 7% of all assessments.

**Caveats.** Single centre. The excess is almost entirely emergence delirium, which is transient; 30-day MMSE, PACU and hospital stay were secondary outcomes worth reading in the full paper before judging the clinical weight.

**What it means.** Remimazolam is not a free lunch in the elderly. If you use it for maintenance in older lung resection patients, expect more agitation and confusion on waking and plan for it, or stay with propofol.

posts.headline: NBE will certify Interventional Echocardiography with a new IEeXAM; Advanced PTE applicants lose one paperwork hurdle
posts.summary: On July 1, 2026 the National Board of Echocardiography announced an Examination and Certification of Special Competence in Interventional Echocardiography; on October 8 it dropped the 'studied but not performed' case log from the Advanced PTE supervised-training application.
takeHome: IEeXAM prerequisites, pathways and first exam date are not yet published; NBE has an interest form for updates.
Advanced PTE certification via supervised training now needs Testamur status, a letter of service and licensure only.
Registration for the 2027 Advanced PTEeXAM and ASCeXAM opened August 28, 2026.
posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters.** Structural heart imaging is the fastest-growing part of perioperative echo, and until now there was no board credential for it; cardiac anesthesiologists who image TEER, TAVR and appendage closures have relied on the 2023 ASE competency statement and local privileging. A National Board of Echocardiography certification changes the credentialing conversation with hospitals and with cardiology.

**What was announced.** On July 1, 2026, NBE announced a new Examination and Certification of Special Competence in Interventional Echocardiography, the IEeXAM, for physicians who specialize in imaging for structural heart interventions. Prerequisites, eligibility pathways and the first exam date were not published; NBE says details will follow and opened an interest form for email updates.

**The Advanced PTE change.** On October 8, 2026, NBE removed the requirement that Supervised Training Pathway applicants for Advanced Perioperative TEE certification submit a log of 'Studied, but not performed' cases. The upload field is gone from the portal and the handbook has been updated. The change applies immediately to new and pending applications; a passing Advanced PTEeXAM (Testamur status), a letter of service and licensure are still required.

**Also in the window.** Registration for the 2027 ASCeXAM and Advanced PTEeXAM opened August 28, 2026, and in March NBE said it is developing an integrated maintenance-of-certification pathway with Inteleos for clinicians certified in more than one imaging modality.

**Caveats.** Who qualifies for the IEeXAM, and whether a perioperative TEE background will count toward it, is the open question; ASE and SCA leadership both describe ongoing engagement with NBE on its roadmap.

**For us.** If you image structural cases, get on the IEeXAM list now. If you are finishing fellowship, the Advanced PTE application just got shorter.

posts.journal: Am J Respir Crit Care Med
posts.headline: ATS 2026: high-flow strongly recommended for de novo hypoxemic failure, NIV for hypercapnia and risky extubations
posts.summary: The American Thoracic Society published its official clinical practice guideline on noninvasive respiratory support for adults with acute respiratory failure, covering high-flow nasal cannula, facemask and helmet NIV, and CPAP.
takeHome: De novo hypoxemic failure: high-flow over standard oxygen (strong, moderate certainty); NIV or CPAP conditional.
Hypercapnic failure: facemask NIV (strong); high-flow only as a monitored alternative if pH above 7.25.
After ICU extubation: high-flow or NIV; prefer NIV when extubation-failure risk is high.
posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters.** Noninvasive support choices (high-flow, NIV, helmet, CPAP) have multiplied since the 2017 ERS/ATS NIV guideline, and COVID-19 produced a flood of trials. This official ATS guideline (Goel, Ferreyro, Pitre and colleagues; online 29 June 2026, print September 2026) is the first comprehensive US statement to integrate them.

**What it recommends.** For de novo acute hypoxemic respiratory failure: high-flow nasal cannula over standard oxygen (strong recommendation, moderate certainty), with NIV by facemask or helmet and CPAP by facemask or helmet each suggested conditionally over standard oxygen, and no recommendation between high-flow and NIV or CPAP. For acute hypercapnic respiratory failure, including COPD exacerbations: facemask NIV (strong, moderate), with high-flow suggested only as an alternative in mild acidemia (pH above 7.25) when monitoring and prompt escalation to NIV are available. After extubation from critical illness: high-flow or facemask NIV suggested over standard oxygen (conditional, moderate), and in patients at high risk of extubation failure, NIV preferred over both standard oxygen and high-flow (conditional, moderate). Immune status did not credibly modify the hypoxemic-failure effect.

**Caveats.** Most recommendations are conditional with low or moderate certainty. The guideline predates SOHO (NEJM, March 2026), which found high-flow lowered intubation but not mortality in hypoxemic failure; SOHO is consistent with, not contrary to, the strong high-flow recommendation.

**For anesthesiologists.** This is the reference for post-extubation planning in the cardiothoracic ICU: a high-risk extubation (obesity, COPD, heart failure, prolonged ventilation) should go to NIV, not high-flow alone. Note that NOTACS (JAMA Netw Open, April 2026) found no benefit from routine prophylactic high-flow after cardiac surgery, so target the high-risk patient rather than everyone.

posts.headline: EARLY TAVR at 5 years: treating asymptomatic severe AS still beats watching; death and stroke diverge after year 2
posts.summary: Five-year update of the EARLY TAVR trial (901 patients aged 65 or older with asymptomatic severe aortic stenosis randomized to transfemoral TAVR or clinical surveillance), presented by Philippe Genereux at New York Valves 2026.
takeHome: Death, stroke or heart failure hospitalization: 15.2% early TAVR vs 24.2% surveillance, HR 0.58.
Death or stroke similar for 2 years, then lower with early TAVR (landmark HR 0.61 from year 2).
Roughly three quarters of surveillance patients had crossed to TAVR; waiting delays, it does not avoid, the valve.
posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters.** The 2024 primary EARLY TAVR result pushed guidelines toward early intervention in asymptomatic severe aortic stenosis, but critics pointed out the benefit was mostly fewer heart failure admissions. The 5-year data answer part of that.

**What they did.** 901 patients aged 65 or older with asymptomatic severe AS were randomized to transfemoral SAPIEN 3 TAVR or clinical surveillance. Philippe Genereux presented median 5-year follow-up at New York Valves on 24 June 2026.

**What they found.**
- Death, stroke or unplanned heart failure hospitalization: 15.2% vs 24.2%, HR 0.58 (95% CI 0.43-0.78).
- All-cause death 10.3% vs 12.3% (HR 0.84, not significant); stroke 4.8% vs 7.6% (HR 0.63, not significant).
- Heart failure hospitalization 3.5% vs 10.3% (HR 0.32), concentrated in the first two years.
- Landmark analysis from year 2: death or stroke HR 0.61 (0.40-0.94) favoring early TAVR.
- Nearly three quarters of the surveillance arm eventually underwent TAVR.

**Caveats.** Presented, not yet published; death and stroke were not significant on their own; everyone was transfemoral-TAVR eligible, so this says little about surgical candidates or those under 65; the mechanism of late harm with waiting (valve degeneration, AF, acute decompensation) is speculative.

**For the anesthesiologist.** Asymptomatic severe AS is becoming a treat-now diagnosis, so expect more structural volume in patients who feel well and more SAVR referrals in the younger, surgically preferable subset. The EVOLVED trial (early AVR in patients with myocardial fibrosis) was negative, so the debate is not fully over.

posts.headline: In US DCD liver transplants, both NRP and normothermic machine perfusion beat cold storage; neither beats the other
posts.summary: Propensity-matched analysis of 4,632 US DCD liver transplants (UNOS 2022-2024) found normothermic regional perfusion and super-rapid recovery plus normothermic machine perfusion each improved one-year graft survival versus super-rapid recovery with static cold storage, with no difference between the two strategies.
takeHome: NRP plus cold storage: graft survival HR 0.42 vs cold-stored super-rapid recovery grafts.
Super-rapid recovery plus NMP: graft survival HR 0.54; NRP vs NMP not different.
Adding NMP after NRP did not add benefit; cold storage alone for DCD livers is becoming hard to defend.
posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters.** DCD now accounts for a growing share of US liver transplants, and programs are choosing between donor-side normothermic regional perfusion (NRP) and recipient-side normothermic machine perfusion (NMP). No randomized comparison exists. This national analysis is the largest look at the question so far and the authors frame it as supporting both as standard of care.

**What they did.** Using UNOS/OPTN data for 4,632 adult DCD liver transplants from 2022 to 2024, the group inferred procurement and preservation strategy from death-to-cross-clamp and preservation times, then compared propensity-matched cohorts for one-year graft and patient survival. Strategy mix: super-rapid recovery plus NMP 56.9%, super-rapid recovery plus cold storage 20.2%, NRP plus cold storage 12.1%, NRP plus NMP 10.8%.

**What they found.** Compared with super-rapid recovery and cold storage, graft survival was better with NRP plus cold storage (HR 0.42, 95% CI 0.29-0.61) and with super-rapid recovery plus NMP (HR 0.54, 95% CI 0.32-0.92). NRP versus NMP showed no difference (graft survival HR 0.81, 95% CI 0.47-1.40). Adding NMP after NRP did not improve outcomes.

**Caveats.** Retrospective, with strategy inferred rather than recorded; back-to-base NMP is likely misclassified; only one year of follow-up; no biliary complication data.

**For the anesthesiologist.** Expect fewer cold-stored DCD livers. NRP cases also bring anesthesiologists into donor-side perfusion logistics and ethics discussions at many centers. Grafts arriving on NMP come with viability data (lactate clearance, bile production) that should inform your expectations for reperfusion and early graft function.

posts.headline: SODa-BIC: short-course bicarbonate fixes the numbers but not kidney outcomes or death in vasopressor-dependent acidosis
posts.summary: A double-blind trial in 55 ICUs across seven countries randomized 500 adults on vasopressors with pH under 7.30 and base excess of -4 or less to up to 5 hours of protocolized 8.4% sodium bicarbonate or dextrose placebo.
takeHome: MAKE30: 40.2% vs 39.4%; no benefit.
RRT within 30 days 16.8% vs 20.9%, not significant; recurrence of acidosis halved.
Routine bicarbonate for moderate acidemia in shock is not supported; BICARICU-2 covers the severe group.
posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters.** Bicarbonate for lactic and mixed acidosis in shock is given on physiological faith. SODa-BIC, the ANZICS Clinical Trials Group trial published in NEJM online 12 June 2026, is the first blinded, placebo-controlled test in a broad vasopressor-dependent population.

**What they did.** 500 adults (498 analyzed) on a continuous vasopressor with metabolic acidosis (pH under 7.30, base excess -4 mmol/L or less) within 2 hours were randomized to 8.4% sodium bicarbonate diluted to 600 mmol/L, titrated to pH 7.30 or above and base excess 0 or above over a maximum of 5 hours, or an indistinguishable 5% dextrose placebo delivered by the same algorithm. The primary outcome was major adverse kidney events at 30 days (MAKE30).

**What they found.** MAKE30 occurred in 40.2% (98/244) with bicarbonate vs 39.4% (100/254) with placebo; adjusted difference 1.2 points (95% CI -7.1 to 9.4). In-hospital death by day 30 was 25.4% vs 24.0%. RRT within 30 days was 16.8% vs 20.9% (difference -3.9, 95% CI -10.6 to 2.7), and RRT dependence at day 30 was 5.7% vs 9.1%, both non-significant. Recurrence of metabolic acidosis within 7 days fell from 55.7% to 32.0%, so the drug did what it was supposed to biochemically. Hypokalemia requiring correction was the main adverse effect (1.6% vs 0).

**Caveats.** Moderate acidemia, a 5-hour course, and a composite endpoint. Severe acidemia (pH 7.20 or below) with AKI was BICARICU-2's territory, where bicarbonate reduced dialysis.

**For anesthesiologists.** In the cardiac ICU, bicarbonate for a pH of 7.25 on norepinephrine will make the gas look better and nothing else. Reserve it for severe acidemia with AKI, hyperkalemia, or specific indications such as tricyclic toxicity.

posts.headline: ARISE FLUIDS: after 1-2 L, early pressors and fluids-first give the same 90-day outcome in septic shock
posts.summary: A 1,000-patient trial in 51 EDs and ICUs in Australia, New Zealand and Ireland randomized early septic shock, after 1-2 L of fluid, to restricted fluids with immediate vasopressors or further fluid to 30 mL/kg with later vasopressors.
takeHome: Days alive and out of hospital to day 90: 76 in both groups.
Early pressors gave about 1.1 L less fluid in 24 h and less reported pulmonary edema (0.6% vs 5.0%).
Day-90 mortality 16.4% vs 14.4%, not significant. Individualize; neither dogma wins.
posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters.** CLOVERS and CLASSIC left the fluids-versus-pressors question open. ARISE FLUIDS, the ANZICS and ACEM trial presented at the Critical Care Reviews Meeting and published in NEJM online 11 June 2026, is the third large trial and uses a patient-centered endpoint.

**What they did.** 1,000 adults with early septic shock in the emergency department, already given 1,000-2,000 mL of IV fluid, were randomized to a vasopressor-first strategy (stop fluid resuscitation, start vasopressors immediately, peripheral administration allowed, 250 mL boluses only for specified triggers) or a fluids-first strategy (further boluses toward 30 mL/kg within 3 hours, vasopressors later). The primary outcome was days alive and out of hospital through day 90.

**What they found.** Median 76 days in both groups (difference 0.0, 95% CI -2.7 to 2.7). Day-90 mortality was 16.4% vs 14.4% (RR 1.14, 95% CI 0.85-1.54) and day-28 mortality 12.9% vs 10.0% (RR 1.29, 95% CI 0.91-1.85), neither significant but both pointing the wrong way for early pressors. Median 24-hour fluid was 1,140 vs 2,248 mL. Vasopressors were started within 24 hours in 86.5% vs 67.6%. Reported pulmonary edema was 0.6% vs 5.0%, and ICU admission 76.5% vs 67.8%.

**Caveats.** Open label, so the pulmonary-edema difference is vulnerable to ascertainment bias. The vasopressor-first group needed more ICU beds. Mortality was low, so the trial cannot rule out a small harm from early pressors.

**For anesthesiologists.** After an initial 1-2 L, there is no evidence-based reason to force either more fluid to 30 mL/kg or immediate pressors. Reassess, use dynamic indices or echo, and choose per patient. Peripheral norepinephrine in the ED or OR holding area was safe here.

posts.headline: Bicarbonate during in-hospital cardiac arrest does not improve return of circulation in a 913-patient blinded trial
posts.summary: Twenty-one Danish hospitals randomized adults with in-hospital cardiac arrest to up to 100 mmol IV sodium bicarbonate or placebo during CPR.
takeHome: Sustained ROSC 39% vs 37%; RR 1.05 (95% CI 0.88-1.24).
First placebo-controlled trial of intra-arrest bicarbonate; no signal of benefit.
Keep bicarbonate for hyperkalemia or sodium-channel toxicity, not routine arrests.
posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters.** Sodium bicarbonate is still pushed during many in-hospital arrests on the assumption that correcting acidosis helps defibrillation and vasopressor response, despite guidelines advising against routine use since 2010. The Danish trial by Granfeldt and colleagues, published in JAMA online 11 June 2026 (print 25 August), is the first adequately sized blinded test.

**What they did.** 913 adults with in-hospital cardiac arrest at 21 Danish hospitals were randomized, double-blind, to IV sodium bicarbonate (up to 100 mmol) or placebo during resuscitation; 779 were included in the primary analyses (372 bicarbonate, 407 placebo). The primary outcome was sustained return of spontaneous circulation.

**What they found.** Sustained ROSC occurred in 39% (146/372) with bicarbonate vs 37% (150/407) with placebo; RR 1.05 (95% CI 0.88-1.24; P = .62). The authors conclude the result does not support routine bicarbonate in in-hospital cardiac arrest.

**Caveats.** A ROSC endpoint rather than survival with good neurological outcome; the trial was not large enough to detect a small survival effect, and the dose was fixed rather than guided by blood gases. Patients with known hyperkalemia or drug toxicity as the cause were not the target population.

**For anesthesiologists.** This group, with the same Danish network behind the VAM-IHCA steroid-vasopressin trial, keeps supplying the blinded in-hospital arrest trials that nobody else runs. The practical point for OR and cardiac ICU arrests is that reaching for an amp of bicarb because the pH is 7.1 during CPR has no evidence behind it; fix the cause, keep compressions going, and reserve bicarbonate for hyperkalemia and tricyclic or sodium-channel blocker toxicity.

posts.headline: LOGICAL: conservative oxygen after cardiac arrest does not improve neurological survival in 1,840 patients
posts.summary: A 53-ICU trial nested in the Mega-ROX program randomized unresponsive ventilated adults after cardiac arrest to conservative oxygen (SpO2 90-95%, FiO2 down to 0.21) or liberal oxygen (no upper limit, minimum FiO2 0.3).
takeHome: Favorable GOS-E at 180 days: 38.2% vs 39.7%; RR 0.97.
Survival 48.0% vs 49.7%; no difference in cognition, quality of life or ventilation duration.
Avoid hypoxemia and extreme hyperoxia; chasing SpO2 90-95% adds nothing.
posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters.** Hyperoxia after cardiac arrest has been blamed for worse neurological outcome since the early observational data, and the BOX and EXACT trials gave conflicting signals. LOGICAL, published in NEJM online 10 June 2026 (Hodgson, Mackle, Young and the ANZICS Clinical Trials Group), is the largest dedicated test.

**What they did.** 1,840 unresponsive adults receiving mechanical ventilation after cardiac arrest in 39 Australian, 13 New Zealand and 1 Irish ICU were randomized, nested inside the Mega-ROX registry trial, to conservative oxygen (SpO2 alarm limits 90-95%, FiO2 reduced to 0.21 whenever SpO2 exceeded the lower limit) or liberal oxygen (lower alarm 90%, no upper limit, minimum FiO2 0.3). The primary outcome was survival with a favorable functional outcome (GOS-E 5-8) at 180 days.

**What they found.** 38.2% (313/819) with conservative oxygen vs 39.7% (353/890) with liberal oxygen; adjusted risk difference -0.9 points (95% CI -5.5 to 3.7), RR 0.97 (0.87-1.09). Survival at 180 days was 48.0% vs 49.7%. Quality of life, MoCA cognition, discharge home, ventilation duration and length of stay did not differ, and no subgroup benefited, including by timing of enrollment after ROSC.

**Caveats.** Open label, and the separation in actual oxygen exposure between arms was modest, which is a limitation of pragmatic SpO2-targeted designs. It does not address the first minutes after ROSC in the field.

**For anesthesiologists.** Together with UK-ROX (JAMA 2025) in general ICU patients, LOGICAL closes the question for routine conservative oxygen targeting after arrest: keep SpO2 above 90% and avoid gross hyperoxia, but do not run FiO2 0.21 at the expense of hypoxemic dips in a post-arrest brain.

posts.headline: MARCH: carbocisteine and nebulized hypertonic saline do not shorten ventilation and both cause harm
posts.summary: A 2x2 factorial trial in 71 UK ICUs randomized 1,956 ventilated adults with difficult-to-clear secretions to enteral carbocisteine, nebulized 6-7% saline, both, or usual airway care.
takeHome: Duration of ventilation unchanged with either drug (HR 0.96 and 1.00).
Carbocisteine raised upper GI bleeding (1.4% vs 0.2%); hypertonic saline caused bronchospasm and desaturation.
Stop routine mucoactive prescribing in ventilated patients.
posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters.** Mucolytics and nebulized hypertonic saline are prescribed to a large share of ventilated ICU patients with thick secretions, on almost no randomized evidence. MARCH, published in NEJM online 10 June 2026, is the definitive UK test.

**What they did.** Connolly and colleagues randomized 1,956 adults receiving invasive ventilation for acute respiratory failure, expected to need it for at least 48 hours, with difficult-to-clear secretions as judged by the bedside team, in a 2x2 factorial design: enteral carbocisteine 750 mg three times daily, nebulized hypertonic saline (6% or 7%, 4 mL four times daily), both, or usual airway clearance alone, for up to 28 days. The primary outcome was duration of mechanical ventilation.

**What they found.** Median ventilation was 186.1 vs 172.7 hours with and without carbocisteine (adjusted HR 0.96, 95% CI 0.87-1.05) and 184.5 vs 174.3 hours with and without hypertonic saline (HR 1.00, 0.91-1.10), with no interaction. Reintubation, ICU and hospital stay, and day-28 and day-60 mortality did not differ. Carbocisteine increased clinically important upper GI bleeding (1.4% vs 0.2%; RR 6.51). Hypertonic saline increased bronchoconstriction needing bronchodilators (2.4% vs 0.4%) and hypoxemia during nebulization (4.1% vs 0.3%).

**Caveats.** Open label and pragmatic, so the secretion phenotype was clinician-defined; a narrower population (for example tracheostomized patients with chronic lung disease) was not tested separately.

**For anesthesiologists.** In the cardiothoracic ICU, where post-bypass patients with COPD often get hypertonic saline or a mucolytic by habit, this trial says the habit buys nothing and carries small but real risks. Suction, humidification and physiotherapy remain the standard.

posts.headline: SNaPP: sugammadex modestly cuts pulmonary complications vs neostigmine in 3,498 abdominal and thoracic patients
posts.summary: Pragmatic international phase 4 RCT at 44 hospitals in Australia, New Zealand and Hong Kong randomized adults 40 and older having at least two hours of abdominal or thoracic surgery to sugammadex or neostigmine. Postoperative pulmonary complications or death by day 7 occurred in 19.0% versus 21.5% (RR 0.88, 95% CI 0.77-1.00; P=0.049).
takeHome: Absolute risk reduction about 2.5 points; the difference was driven by atelectasis (18.4% vs 21.1%), not pneumonia or aspiration.
Deaths were 1 vs 2; no treatment-related adverse events.
Authors conclude sugammadex can be considered first-line for aminosteroid reversal; the accompanying editorial urges caution.
posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters.** Whether sugammadex improves patient-centered pulmonary outcomes, rather than just train-of-four ratios, has been debated since the large retrospective cohorts (Kheterpal 2020) suggested benefit. SNaPP is the first adequately powered randomized test.

**What they did.** The ANZCA Clinical Trials Network group (Leslie, Darvall, Chan, Peyton, Myles and colleagues) randomized 3,498 adults aged 40 or older undergoing abdominal or thoracic surgery under general anesthesia lasting at least two hours, at 44 hospitals in Australia, Aotearoa New Zealand and Hong Kong, to sugammadex or neostigmine at the end of surgery (July 2023 to July 2025). Patients were blinded; the primary outcome was a composite of postoperative pulmonary complications or death up to hospital discharge or postoperative day 7.

**What they found.** The primary outcome occurred in 19.0% of the sugammadex group and 21.5% of the neostigmine group (RR 0.88, 95% CI 0.77-1.00; P=0.049). Atelectasis, the most common component, was 18.4% versus 21.1% (RR 0.86). Pneumonia (2.1% vs 2.2%), aspiration (0.2% vs 0.4%) and death (0.1% in each arm) did not differ. No adverse events were judged treatment-related.

**Caveats.** The confidence interval touches 1.0 and the P value is borderline. The effect is almost entirely atelectasis, which is often a radiologic rather than a clinical diagnosis. Dosing and the use of quantitative monitoring in each arm will matter when the full paper is scrutinized. Fernandez-Bustamante and Eikermann's linked editorial, "a word of caution," makes those points.

**For the anesthesiologist.** SNaPP supports sugammadex as a reasonable default for aminosteroid reversal in longer abdominal and thoracic cases, but the benefit is modest and cost-sensitive systems can still defend neostigmine with quantitative monitoring. Quantitative neuromuscular monitoring remains the non-negotiable part regardless of drug.

posts.headline: FDA clears EchoNext, the first AI that reads a 12-lead ECG to flag six kinds of structural heart disease
posts.summary: Pathwai's EchoNext, developed at Columbia and NewYork-Presbyterian, received 510(k) clearance on June 8, 2026 to identify adults who should get an echocardiogram based on a routine ECG.
takeHome: Validated on 102,219 patients from four health systems: composite sensitivity 73.7%, specificity 75.2%, NPV 84.6%.
Flags moderate-plus AS or regurgitation, severe LVH, LVEF under 45%, RV dysfunction and pulmonary hypertension; not for paced patients.
A referral trigger, not a rule-out; expect it to generate preop echo requests.
posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters.** Every surgical patient gets an ECG; very few get an echo. An ECG-based flag for structural disease is the kind of screen that will land in preop clinics whether anesthesiologists ask for it or not.

**What was cleared.** EchoNext (Pathwai, Inc.; K260332; clearance letter June 8, 2026) analyzes 12-lead ECGs in patients 18 and older without implanted pacemakers and, when it detects structural heart disease, flags up to six sub-labels: aortic stenosis (moderate or greater), valvular regurgitation (moderate or greater), severe LV hypertrophy, LVEF below 45%, RV dysfunction (moderate or greater) and pulmonary hypertension (PASP 45 mmHg or higher, or TR Vmax 3.2 m/s or higher). It is explicitly labeled as identifying patients for further follow-up, not as a rule-out tool.

**Performance.** In the FDA validation set of 102,219 patients from four US and Canadian health systems (structural disease prevalence 34.8%), composite sensitivity was 73.7%, specificity 75.2%, PPV 61.6% and NPV 84.6%. Sub-label PPVs were low, 11.8% for aortic stenosis for example. The underlying model, published in Nature in July 2025 by the Columbia group, was trained on more than 700,000 ECG-echo pairs from about 230,000 patients; in a prospective deployment of nearly 85,000 patients, about 9% were flagged and, among flagged patients who went on to echo, nearly three quarters had structural disease.

**Caveats.** Modest sensitivity and specificity; low sub-label PPV means many flagged echos will be normal; the 510(k) summary describes the validation design inconsistently; it is distributed through a clinical reference app, so uptake may outpace local governance.

**For us.** A positive flag in an elective surgical patient is a reasonable trigger for an echo before anesthesia. A negative flag changes nothing about your exam.

posts.headline: Pooled RCTs: higher intraoperative BP targets do not reduce AKI, myocardial injury or death in noncardiac surgery
posts.summary: Systematic review and meta-analysis with trial sequential analysis of 15 randomized trials (15,603 patients) comparing higher with routine intraoperative blood pressure targets during elective noncardiac surgery under general anesthesia found no reduction in acute kidney injury, acute myocardial injury or mortality; a possible delirium signal did not survive trial sequential analysis.
takeHome: No benefit of higher BP targets for AKI, myocardial injury or mortality across 15,603 randomized patients.
Delirium RR 0.73 (95% CI 0.54-0.98) but trial sequential analysis says the evidence is insufficient.
Avoiding hypotension still matters; chasing supranormal MAP targets does not, on current trial evidence.
posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters.** Large observational datasets tie intraoperative hypotension to kidney and myocardial injury, which pushed many departments toward tighter, higher MAP targets. The randomized evidence (INPRESS, POISE-3, GUARDIAN and others) has been mixed, and this synthesis asks whether the trials, taken together, show benefit.

**What they did.** Chiou and colleagues pooled 15 randomized trials enrolling 15,603 adults undergoing elective noncardiac surgery under general anesthesia that compared higher intraoperative blood pressure targets with routine management. Outcomes were acute kidney injury, acute myocardial injury, postoperative delirium and mortality, with trial sequential analysis to judge whether the accumulated information was sufficient.

**What they found.** Higher targets did not reduce acute kidney injury or acute myocardial injury, and mortality was unchanged. Postoperative delirium was less frequent with higher targets (RR 0.73, 95% CI 0.54-0.98), but trial sequential analysis judged the evidence insufficient to confirm it. The authors conclude that targeting higher intraoperative blood pressure does not improve major postoperative outcomes compared with routine management and call for adequately powered trials on delirium.

**Caveats.** Trials differ in targets, comparators, duration of hypotension avoidance and how pressors were used; several large recent trials dominate the pooled estimates; heterogeneous outcome definitions. Null pooled effects do not prove that profound or prolonged hypotension is harmless.

**For the anesthesiologist.** Treat hypotension promptly, but a MAP target of 80 or higher for everyone is not supported. This gives anesthesiologists a citable counterweight when surgeons or ICU colleagues demand supranormal pressures, and it reframes the next question as how low is too low rather than how high is better.

posts.headline: ASE's first M-TEER imaging guideline: standard views, standard steps, and 3D MPR preferred for puncture and grasp
posts.summary: ASE published its first guideline dedicated to intraprocedural imaging for mitral transcatheter edge-to-edge repair, laying out the views, procedural steps and the information the imager must communicate at each stage.
takeHome: Favors live 3D multiplanar reconstruction over 2D TEE for transseptal puncture site and leaflet grasp; 2D remains acceptable.
Defines what the imager must call out to the operator at each step, in 2D, biplane, 3D volume and MPR formats.
Cardiac anesthesiology represented on the writing group; endorsed by SCAI. Expect it to shape training and credentialing.
posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters.** M-TEER volumes keep climbing and the imager is half the procedure, yet until now there was no society algorithm for what to show and say at each step. Many of us in cardiac anesthesia run the probe for these cases, so this is our document as much as the cardiologists'.

**What it is.** A 12-author ASE writing group chaired by Stephen Little (Houston Methodist) with Nishath Quader as co-chair, and with cardiac anesthesiology on the panel (G. Burkhard Mackensen among the authors), published the guideline in the June 2026 JASE (39:529-550; DOI 10.1016/j.echo.2026.03.003). SCAI endorsed it. ASE posted it June 3 and issued a press release June 8, 2026.

**What it says.** The document states plainly that no standard algorithm existed to guide the interventional echocardiographer, then specifies the imaging views, the standard procedural steps, and the imaging information that must be communicated to the operator using 2D, biplane, 3D volume and multiplanar reconstruction formats. Its clear preference is live 3D MPR for precision: to optimize the transseptal puncture location that sets catheter geometry for grasping, and to guide the clip into proper alignment with the mitral leaflets for an effective grasp. 2D TEE can still be used. It also spells out what the imager must bring: detailed mitral anatomy, fast real-time 2D and 3D manipulation, and enough procedural experience to anticipate problems.

**Caveats.** Expert consensus, not outcome data, and the specific recommendation language lives in a 28 MB full text with many video loops.

**For us.** If you image TEER, expect this to become the reference for training, privileging and the shared vocabulary with your interventionalist.

posts.headline: Ninth STS-Pedimacs report: 1,465 pediatric VADs, 73% one-year survival, CHD now 28% of implants
posts.summary: Annual STS-Pedimacs registry report on durable pediatric ventricular assist devices implanted September 2012 to December 2024, with a focused analysis of biventricular support.
takeHome: Survival on device 77% at 6 months and 73% at 1 year, improving across eras; best in adolescents and cardiomyopathy.
CHD is 28% of implants and 61% of those are single-ventricle, the group with the worst transplant and survival rates.
Biventricular support means sicker children and significantly lower survival than LVAD alone.
posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters.** STS-Pedimacs is the North American registry for durable pediatric ventricular assist devices, and the annual report is the benchmark against which programs, payers and regulators judge outcomes.

**What they did.** The ninth report analyses 1,465 patients implanted between 19 September 2012 and 31 December 2024, with a focused analysis of children who received biventricular support.

**What they found.**
- Congenital heart disease is a growing share of implants, now 28%; 61% of those CHD patients had single-ventricle physiology. Among cardiomyopathy patients, 93% had dilated cardiomyopathy.
- Implantable continuous-flow pumps were the most common device type (508 patients, 35%).
- Survival on device was 77% at 6 months and 73% at 1 year, best in 11- to 19-year-olds, in cardiomyopathy and with implantable continuous-flow devices, and improving across the 2012-2015, 2016-2020 and 2021-2024 eras.
- Single-ventricle CHD patients had lower transplant rates and lower survival than cardiomyopathy patients.
- Children needing biventricular support were sicker at implant and had significantly lower survival than LVAD-only patients.

A companion UNOS analysis in the same journal (Bilgili et al.) of 254 US children bridged with the HeartMate 3 found 90.6% reached transplant, with 96.6% one-year and 85.8% five-year post-transplant survival, equivalent for CHD and acquired disease.

**Caveats.** Registry data with evolving case mix; adverse-event rates are in the full report rather than the abstract, and survival is reported on device, not intention-to-treat from listing.

**For the anesthesiologist.** Expect more VAD-supported children with single-ventricle anatomy and more BiVAD configurations coming for implant, revision and transplant; these are the groups with the worst numbers and the hardest inductions. The HM3 data support the trend toward implantable continuous-flow pumps in adolescents, which simplifies life out of hospital and the anesthetic for non-cardiac procedures.

posts.headline: Early neurodevelopment after infant heart surgery: genetic diagnosis costs >1 SD; d-TGA fares best, TOF and AVSD worse
posts.summary: Cross-sectional analysis of the Cardiac Neurodevelopmental Outcome Collaborative registry linked to PC4: 942 Bayley assessments in 868 children under 30 months who had bypass surgery, across 25 sites.
takeHome: A genetic diagnosis lowered cognitive, language and motor scores by 16-21 points, more than any cardiac factor.
After adjustment, d-TGA scored highest; tetralogy and AVSD among the lower-scoring diagnoses.
Longer stays, more catheterizations and lower caregiver education tracked with worse scores; anesthesia was not isolated.
posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters.** Neurodevelopmental impairment is the most common long-term morbidity after infant heart surgery, and anesthetic exposure is one of the modifiable factors families ask about. The Cardiac Neurodevelopmental Outcome Collaborative (CNOC) registry is now large enough to compare diagnoses on a common scale.

**What they did.** Cross-sectional analysis of CNOC follow-up data linked to the Pediatric Cardiac Critical Care Consortium registry, from 25 sites (May 2019 to June 2022). Children under 30 months who had surgical repair or palliation requiring cardiopulmonary bypass and completed Bayley-III/4 testing were included: 942 assessments in 868 children, median age at index operation 20 days, 11.8% with a genetic diagnosis.

**What they found.** A genetic diagnosis was the dominant factor: those children scored more than one standard deviation lower on all three indexes (cognitive 18.8, language 16.1, motor 20.9 points lower; P<0.001 for each). After adjustment, cardiac diagnosis still mattered: children with d-transposition had the highest cognitive scores, while tetralogy of Fallot and atrioventricular septal defect were among the diagnoses scoring lower. Lower birth weight, male sex, older age at first surgery, longer hospital stay, more catheterizations and lower caregiver education were each independently associated with poorer performance.

**Caveats.** Cross-sectional and limited to children who returned for follow-up, which may bias toward sicker or better-resourced families; it cannot attribute causation to any perioperative variable, and anesthetic exposure was not modelled separately.

**For the anesthesiologist.** The strongest signals are non-anesthetic: genetics, prematurity and cumulative hospital burden. That is reassuring when counselling about anesthesia, but the longer stays and repeated catheterizations that track with worse scores are exactly where sedation minimisation, early extubation and delirium prevention programs operate. The authors argue for routine developmental surveillance after any first-year cardiac surgery, which anesthesia departments can help trigger.

posts.headline: Sham-controlled trial: continuous parasternal (SPIP) blocks cut opioid use by ~21 MME over 72 h after sternotomy
posts.summary: 318 adults having median sternotomy at Canadian centres received bilateral superficial parasternal intercostal plane catheters with 0.2% ropivacaine or saline for 48 hours. Cumulative 72-hour opioid use fell by 20.7 morphine milligram equivalents; pain scores were similar.
takeHome: 72-h opioid consumption 20.7 MME lower than placebo (95% CI -39.0 to -2.3; p=0.027).
Pain scores, delirium, QoR-15 and discharge opioid use were not different; no serious block-related complications.
A modest but real opioid-sparing effect; whether catheters beat single shots remains open.
posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters.** Parasternal plane blocks have spread rapidly in cardiac ERAS without a large sham-controlled trial, which is why the 2026 ASA guideline could only give a conditional recommendation for cardiothoracic blocks. EPOCH CardioLink-10 is the trial that was missing.

**What they did.** Pan-Canadian, multicentre, double-blind, placebo-controlled RCT (NCT06028126), enrolling August 2023 to December 2025. Adults having median sternotomy received bilateral superficial parasternal intercostal plane catheters with 0.2% ropivacaine (20 mL bolus, basal infusion plus 5 mL boluses every 3-4 hours for 48 hours, maximum 592 mg) or identical saline. Primary outcome: cumulative opioid consumption over 72 hours in morphine milligram equivalents.

**What they found (modified intention to treat n=318; 164 ropivacaine, 154 placebo; median age 67; 23% women).**
- 72-hour opioid use lower with ropivacaine by 20.7 MME (least-squares mean difference; 95% CI -39.0 to -2.3; p=0.027).
- Pain scores, delirium, Quality of Recovery-15 and opioid use at discharge were similar.
- No serious block-related complications; prespecified adverse events did not differ.

**Caveats.** The effect is modest (about 7 MME per day) and the confidence interval approaches zero. Catheters add nursing workload and cost; a correspondence in the same journal asked whether a single injection should come first.

**What it means.** This is the best evidence yet that parasternal blockade does something real after sternotomy, and it supports putting SPIP blocks in the cardiac ERAS bundle. Whether a single shot, liposomal bupivacaine or a catheter is the right format is the next question.

posts.headline: End-ischemic HOPE cuts early allograft dysfunction nearly in half in extended-criteria liver grafts
posts.summary: US multicenter RCT (Bridge to HOPE) randomized 219 recipients of extended-criteria DBD or DCD livers to static cold storage plus portal-venous hypothermic oxygenated perfusion versus cold storage alone. HOPE reduced early allograft dysfunction from 37% to 20%.
takeHome: Portal-venous HOPE after cold storage: EAD 20.2% vs 37.3%, absolute reduction 17 points.
Works for both extended-criteria DBD and DCD grafts; this is the trial behind the FDA VitaSmart clearance.
Expect more marginal grafts arriving on a pump; plan for post-reperfusion physiology that may be calmer.
posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters.** Machine perfusion has moved from European trials to US practice, but the US had no randomized data and no FDA-cleared cold perfusion device. Bridge to HOPE fills both gaps.

**What they did.** Fifteen US liver transplant centers randomized 219 adult recipients of extended-criteria donor livers (DBD and DCD) 1:1 to static cold storage followed by end-ischemic portal-venous HOPE (n=109) or cold storage alone (n=110), with one year of follow-up. The primary outcome was early allograft dysfunction (Olthoff criteria).

**What they found.** EAD occurred in 20.2% of HOPE grafts versus 37.3% of controls, a rate difference of -17.1% (95% CI -27.2 to -7.0). The trial met both its noninferiority (P<0.001) and superiority (P=0.005) thresholds. The data package supported the January 2026 FDA De Novo clearance of the VitaSmart HOPE system, the first US-cleared hypothermic oxygenated perfusion device for livers.

**Caveats.** Open-label, EAD is a surrogate, and the study was powered for noninferiority with superiority as a secondary test. One-year graft and patient survival were not the primary endpoints. Portal-venous-only HOPE (not dual arterial plus portal) was studied.

**For the anesthesiologist.** HOPE is cheap and simple compared with normothermic perfusion, so it is likely to spread fast to marginal grafts. Mechanistically it is supposed to blunt ischemia-reperfusion injury, so watch for less severe post-reperfusion syndrome and lower vasopressor requirements after unclamping, although this trial did not report intraoperative hemodynamics. Expect your surgeons to accept older and DCD grafts more often.

posts.headline: OFACAR: opioid-free anaesthesia for on-pump cardiac surgery lowers 30-day complications, but the result is fragile
posts.summary: 320 adults having elective cardiac surgery with cardiopulmonary bypass at two French hospitals were randomised to opioid-free anaesthesia (ketamine, dexamethasone, lidocaine, magnesium) or sufentanil-based anaesthesia. The 30-day composite of complications or death was 75.4% vs 84.5%.
takeHome: Composite complications/death 75.4% vs 84.5% (RR 0.90, 95% CI 0.80-0.99, p=0.049); fragility index 1.
Fewer cardiovascular (64% vs 75%) and digestive (2.5% vs 11%) complications; 0 vs 6 deaths.
Hypothesis-generating: do not abandon sufentanil yet, but OFA in cardiac surgery is now worth a large trial.
posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters.** Opioid-free anaesthesia has mostly been studied in bariatric and laparoscopic surgery with pain and nausea endpoints. OFACAR asks a harder question: in on-pump cardiac surgery, does removing opioids change major complications?

**What they did.** Blinded, multicentre superiority RCT at two French university hospitals (August 2021 to December 2023). 320 adults having elective cardiac surgery with cardiopulmonary bypass were randomised to opioid-free anaesthesia (IV ketamine, dexamethasone, lidocaine and magnesium sulfate) or sufentanil-based anaesthesia. Primary outcome: composite of neurological, respiratory, cardiovascular or renal complications and/or death within 30 days.

**What they found (mean age 66; 77% men).**
- Composite: 120/159 (75.4%) OFA vs 136/161 (84.5%) control; RR 0.90, 95% CI 0.80-0.99, p=0.049. Fragility index 1.
- Cardiovascular complications 64.2% vs 75.2% (RR 0.86), driven mainly by myocardial damage (61.6% vs 72.1%).
- Digestive complications 2.5% vs 11.2% (RR 0.22, 95% CI 0.08-0.65).
- Deaths 0 vs 6 (p=0.014).

**Caveats.** The primary result hangs on a single patient; the composite is very broad (three quarters of patients met it) and 'myocardial damage' is a biomarker-driven component. Two centres, 320 patients. An Anesthesiology editorial in August 2026 asks whether this is 'a signal worth pursuing', which is about right.

**What it means.** A ketamine-lidocaine-magnesium-dexamethasone recipe is feasible for bypass cases and did not harm anyone here. It is not yet a reason to abandon sufentanil, but it moves opioid-free cardiac anaesthesia from fringe to trial-worthy.

posts.headline: TOWAR: no mortality advantage for prehospital whole blood over components; 21-day-old units perform the same
posts.summary: Cluster-randomized phase 3 trial across 44 US air-medical bases (1,020 patients) comparing up to 2 units of low-titer group O whole blood with component transfusion, with a nested storage-age substudy.
takeHome: 30-day mortality 25.9% whole blood vs 20.5% components; adjusted OR 1.24, not significant.
Units stored 15-21 days did as well as fresher units; use the full shelf life.
Exploratory harm signal in SBP <=70 mm Hg patients deserves caution before defaulting to whole blood.
posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters.** TOWAR is the US counterpart to SWiFT, run by the PAMPer group, and it also tested whether whole blood stored out to 21 days performs as well as fresher units.

**What they did.** Pragmatic cluster-randomized phase 3 trial across 44 air-medical bases (May 2022 to June 2025). Bases were randomized 2:1 in monthly blocks to up to 2 units of low-titer group O whole blood or to components (red cells and/or plasma) for injured adults at risk of hemorrhagic shock. 1,020 patients were enrolled (715 whole blood, 305 components); the primary analysis included 695 and 298.

**What they found.**
- 30-day mortality 25.9% with whole blood vs 20.5% with components; adjusted OR 1.24 (95% CI 0.87-1.76; P=0.24).
- No reduction in deaths at 3, 6 or 24 h, in hemorrhagic death or in TBI death; 24-h red cell and plasma use not meaningfully lower.
- Exploratory signal the wrong way: in patients with SBP <=70 mm Hg, mortality 34.5% vs 24.1% (OR 1.59, 95% CI 1.02-2.47), not multiplicity-adjusted.
- Storage age: 30-day mortality 27.1% for units aged 15-21 days vs 26.4% for 1-14 days (adjusted OR 0.99).

**Caveats.** Open label, cluster allocation, crossover and pre-randomization transfusion, a two-unit cap, and power only for a 10-point difference. It does not test prehospital blood versus none; everyone got blood. Presented at ATS and published the same day.

**For the anesthesiologist.** Two neutral NEJM trials in one spring. Whole blood is not harmful and the full 21-day shelf life looks usable, which helps inventory. But a survival advantage over balanced components is not supported, and the shocked subgroup deserves a close look before whole blood is treated as the default product.

posts.headline: PATCH-Trauma at 24 months: prehospital TXA still shows no functional or survival benefit
posts.summary: Subgroup analysis of the PATCH-Trauma RCT with 24-month Glasgow Outcome Scale-Extended follow-up in 516 severely injured patients randomized to prehospital tranexamic acid or placebo.
takeHome: Favorable GOS-E at 24 months: 64.0% TXA vs 58.4% placebo, P=0.20.
No change in GOS-E trajectory between 6 and 24 months; mortality unchanged.
Early TXA does not trade survival for disability, but do not expect a functional benefit.
posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters.** PATCH-Trauma (NEJM 2023) found that prehospital TXA in severely injured patients reduced early deaths but did not improve 6-month functional outcome, which left everyone asking whether survivors were simply left disabled or would recover later. This follow-up answers that with 24-month data.

**What they did.** A subgroup analysis of the PATCH-Trauma trial (1 g TXA prehospital plus 1 g infusion over 8 h versus placebo) at sites that collected 24-month Glasgow Outcome Scale-Extended data. Of 584 eligible patients, 516 had 24-month outcomes. Published online May 15, 2026 in JACEP Open (first author Biswadev Mitra).

**What they found.**
- Favorable functional outcome at 24 months: 64.0% with TXA vs 58.4% with placebo (P=0.20).
- Change in GOS-E between 6 and 24 months: no difference (coefficient -0.06, 95% CI -0.30 to 0.19; P=0.64).
- Mortality did not differ at any time point in this subgroup.

**Caveats.** A subgroup, not the full trial, so underpowered for a 5-6 point absolute difference; functional outcome after trauma is dominated by brain and orthopedic injury rather than bleeding; loss to follow-up; a secondary emergency-medicine journal rather than the parent trial's venue.

**For the anesthesiologist.** Late recovery did not rescue the functional endpoint, but there is also no signal that TXA trades early survival for long-term disability. This lands six months after EAST's conditional recommendation for routine TXA and is consistent with it: give it early, do not expect it to change what the patient looks like at two years.

posts.headline: Berlin Heart EXCOR Active driver: zero device malfunctions and 98% 90-day survival across 158 children
posts.summary: Prospective multicenter US evaluation of the new mobile EXCOR Active driving system: 40 children under an FDA investigational device exemption plus 118 under continued access, with independent event adjudication.
takeHome: No major device malfunctions in either cohort; 90-day mortality 0% (IDE) and 90-day survival 98.1% (continued access).
Stroke 12.5% in the IDE cohort; 15-23% were converted to another support modality.
Registry-based evaluation of a Class III pediatric device is proposed as a template for future approvals.
posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters.** The Berlin Heart EXCOR is the only durable VAD approved for infants and small children, and its original IKUS driver is a large console that keeps the child in hospital and tethered. The EXCOR Active driver was designed to make these children mobile, with longer battery life and more physiologic pump control.

**What they did.** A prospective, multicenter US evaluation. Forty children were enrolled under an FDA investigational device exemption and a further 118 under a continued-access protocol, with adverse events adjudicated by an independent clinical events committee and a data safety monitoring board, using existing pediatric VAD registry infrastructure. Primary endpoints were major device malfunction, adverse events, and success (alive on support, transplanted or recovered at 90 days).

**What they found.** In the IDE cohort (mean age 38 months, 55% congenital heart disease) there were no major device malfunctions; at 90 days 65% remained supported, 17.5% had been transplanted, 15% had been converted to another support modality and one child was explanted for recovery. Stroke occurred in 12.5%, and 90-day mortality was 0%. In the 118 continued-access patients there were again no major device malfunctions; 37% were transplanted, 31% were alive on device, 6% explanted for recovery, 23% converted, and 90-day survival was 98.1%.

**Caveats.** Single-arm with no concurrent IKUS comparator, and the stroke rate is a reminder that EXCOR remains a paracorporeal pulsatile pump with its anticoagulation burden. Conversion to other support in 15-23% is not trivial.

**For the anesthesiologist.** When you anesthetize EXCOR patients for cannula revisions, non-cardiac procedures or transplant, the driver change alters logistics (transport, battery, alarms) more than physiology. The bigger story is methodological: a Class III pediatric device evaluated through a registry rather than a bespoke trial, proposed as a template for future pediatric device approvals.

posts.headline: AATS 2026 consensus sets 34 rules for antithrombotic care in neonates and infants having cardiac procedures
posts.summary: AATS-commissioned multidisciplinary panel used a modified Delphi process to standardise periprocedural antithrombotic testing and therapy for neonates and infants undergoing congenital cardiac surgery and catheter interventions.
takeHome: Neonatal hemostasis is developmentally different; testing and therapy are framed around that.
Covers heparin, direct thrombin inhibitors and antiplatelet agents, their monitoring, and device-specific regimens.
Pre-, intra- and post-procedural guidance in one place: align your bypass and shunt protocols to it.
posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters.** Neonates and infants undergoing cardiac surgery or catheter interventions have an immature, rapidly changing hemostatic system, and thrombosis of shunts, conduits and central lines remains a leading cause of death after stage 1 palliation. Practice has varied from center to center with little to anchor it.

**What they did.** The AATS commissioned a panel of congenital cardiac surgeons, cardiologists, interventionalists, hematologists, intensivists and pharmacologists who used a modified Delphi process to build a framework for periprocedural antithrombotic testing and therapy. The result is 34 consensus statements with supporting figures and tables, published in JTCVS (172:618-662.e7).

**What it covers.**
- How neonatal and infant coagulation differs from older children and adults, and why that changes dosing and monitoring.
- Testing for congenital, acquired and therapy-related hemostatic abnormalities before and after procedures.
- The anticoagulants and antiplatelet agents in common use and how to monitor them.
- Pre-, intra- and post-procedural management, including device- and procedure-specific recommendations for the short and long term.

**Caveats.** Delphi consensus, not trial evidence: the underlying literature is thin, and the statements will need revision as prospective data (for example on bivalirudin in circuits) accrue. Dosing details should be read in the full tables rather than the abstract.

**For the anesthesiologist.** This is the document to reconcile your heparin management on bypass, your post-shunt heparin-to-aspirin transition and your line-thrombosis prophylaxis against. For those running ECMO or VAD programs it also sets a shared vocabulary with hematology and surgery. Expect CCAS and institutional protocols to cite it.

posts.headline: ASE publishes its first guideline on cardiac ultrasound artifacts: how each one looks, why it happens, how to beat it
posts.summary: A global ASE writing group produced a structured catalog of 2D, Doppler and 3D artifacts, giving mechanism, clinical impact, case examples and mitigation for each, in the May 2026 JASE.
takeHome: Artifacts persist on modern platforms; the fix is operator recognition, not newer hardware.
Classic traps called out: artifacts that mimic aortic dissection and ventricular thrombus.
A teaching reference for the OR, where device shadowing and reverberation are part of every TEE.
posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters.** Every one of us has been fooled by a linear echo in the ascending aorta or a bright blob at the LV apex. Until now there was no imaging-society document devoted to artifacts; ASE says this is the first.

**What it is.** 'Recommendations for the Identification and Mitigation of Cardiac Ultrasound Artifacts: A Guideline from the American Society of Echocardiography', chaired by Muhamed Saric (NYU Langone) with Anita Sadeghpour as co-chair, published in the May 2026 JASE (39:435-475; DOI 10.1016/j.echo.2026.01.007), with an ASE press release on May 4, 2026. It was written by a global author group and ships with a large library of figures and video loops.

**What it does.** For each artifact across 2D, spectral Doppler, color Doppler and 3D, it follows one structure: what it looks like on the image, the ultrasound physics or external-device interference that creates it, how it can change diagnosis and management, real case examples, and how to avoid or reduce it. It also covers artifact-like phenomena that are not true artifacts. The press release singles out misdiagnosis of aortic dissection and ventricular thrombus as the kind of consequential error the document is aimed at.

**Caveats.** An educational guideline, not a trial, and much of the value is in the multimedia rather than the text.

**For us.** Intraoperative TEE is artifact-rich: cannulas, prosthetic valves, pacing wires, electrocautery, and a probe sitting millimetres from the structure of interest. The authors' point is that operator education remains essential even as hardware improves. Worth putting in front of fellows before their first week in the OR.

posts.headline: PRoMPT BOLUS: balanced crystalloid no better than saline for kidney outcomes in 9,041 children with septic shock
posts.summary: Pragmatic RCT across 47 emergency departments in five countries randomised children (2 months to under 18 years) with suspected septic shock to balanced fluid or 0.9% saline for up to 48 hours.
takeHome: Major adverse kidney events at 30 days: 3.4% balanced vs 3.0% saline (RR 1.10, 0.88-1.40).
Hospital-free days identical; less hyperchloraemia and hypernatraemia but more hyperlactataemia with balanced fluid.
Either fluid is defensible for paediatric resuscitation; choose by availability and electrolytes.
posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters.** Adult trials (SMART, BaSICS, PLUS) pushed many of us toward balanced crystalloids, and paediatric sepsis guidance leaned the same way on thin evidence. PRoMPT BOLUS is the definitive paediatric answer.

**What they did.** Pragmatic, multinational RCT in 47 emergency departments across five countries. Children aged 2 months to under 18 years with suspected septic shock and abnormal perfusion were randomised to balanced crystalloid or 0.9% saline for resuscitation and maintenance fluid for up to 48 hours. 9,041 children were enrolled; after withdrawals 4,235 (balanced) and 4,247 (saline) were analysed. The primary outcome was major adverse kidney events within 30 days (death, new renal replacement therapy, or persistent kidney dysfunction).

**What they found.** The primary outcome occurred in 3.4% with balanced fluid and 3.0% with saline (difference 0.4 percentage points, 95% CI -0.5 to 1.3; RR 1.10, 0.88-1.40). Hospital-free days were identical (median 23). Balanced fluid produced less hyperchloraemia (31.4% vs 49.0%) and hypernatraemia (1.8% vs 3.1%) but more hyperlactataemia (19.8% vs 16.7%). Other safety outcomes did not differ.

**Caveats.** Event rates were low, so the trial cannot exclude small differences in rare outcomes; most children received modest fluid volumes, and effects in massive-volume resuscitation or in cardiac surgical patients were not studied.

**For the anesthesiologist.** For paediatric resuscitation, saline is not the villain it has been painted as. Choose by what is hanging, by sodium and chloride, and by what your pharmacy stocks, and stop agonising over the bag. For trauma and perioperative paediatric fluid choice, this is the largest dataset you will get for years.

posts.headline: STS 2026 POAF guideline: amiodarone prophylaxis is Class I, beta-blockers and posterior pericardiotomy IIa
posts.summary: First STS clinical practice guideline on prevention and treatment of new-onset postoperative atrial fibrillation after cardiac surgery, presented at STS 2026 and published in Annals of Thoracic Surgery (co-led by Subhasis Chatterjee and Stefano Schena).
takeHome: Class I: perioperative oral amiodarone prophylaxis (about 3-6 g cumulative) and cardioversion for unstable POAF.
Class IIa: perioperative beta-blockers and posterior pericardiotomy (NNT about 7).
Anticoagulation for POAF is IIb and individualized; routine anticoagulation of everyone is discouraged.
posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters.** POAF hits a quarter to a third of cardiac surgical patients and the prophylaxis menu has been a matter of local habit. This is the first STS clinical practice guideline on the topic, complementing the 2019 SCA/EACTA practice advisory many of us still cite.

**What it says.** Fifteen recommendations in a phase-based framework: eight preventive, three intraoperative adjuncts, four postoperative. Two are Class I, two IIa, eight IIb and three Class III.
- Class I: perioperative oral amiodarone for prevention, with a cumulative dose around 3-6 g (bradycardia about 2-4%, heart block 1-2%, comparable to beta-blockers), and cardioversion for hemodynamically unstable POAF. Postoperative initiation of amiodarone is considered effective.
- Class IIa: perioperative beta-blockers, and posterior pericardiotomy, a five-minute addition with a number needed to treat near 7.
- Class IIb: anticoagulation decisions, individualized to stroke risk and other indications; routine anticoagulation of every POAF patient is discouraged.
- Three Class III recommendations label interventions as ineffective (the full text lists them).

**Caveats.** Many recommendations rest on IIb-level evidence; optimal timing and duration of anticoagulation remain uncertain, as does the role of arrhythmia burden; the document frames POAF as a marker of perioperative vulnerability warranting follow-up rather than reflexive escalation. Presented 30 January 2026 at STS; epub 18 April 2026.

**For the anesthesiologist.** Expect protocols to add oral amiodarone loading preoperatively or on arrival in the ICU, expect surgeons to ask for posterior pericardiotomy, and plan beta-blocker continuation. Have the pacing and conduction conversation before you load amiodarone in a patient with marginal AV conduction.

posts.headline: Six anaesthesia societies: sterile gowns need not be mandatory for uncomplicated single-shot spinals
posts.summary: A literature review and three-round Delphi involving the Association of Anaesthetists, Royal College of Anaesthetists, OAA, Regional Anaesthesia UK, College of Anaesthesiologists of Ireland and ANZCA produced 10 statements and 11 recommendations on asepsis for adult single-shot spinal anaesthesia.
takeHome: Routine sterile gown use for uncomplicated adult single-shot spinal anaesthesia should not be mandatory.
Hand hygiene and facemask use remain essential core aseptic measures; the statement defines the rest.
Framed as proportionate and sustainable infection prevention; expect debate where gowning is routine.
posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters.** International guidance on gowning for spinal anaesthesia differs and practice varies by country. This is the first multisociety statement to say explicitly that routine gowning for a single-shot spinal is not required, and it comes from the societies whose members gown most consistently.

**What they did.** The Association of Anaesthetists, Royal College of Anaesthetists, Obstetric Anaesthetists' Association, Regional Anaesthesia UK, College of Anaesthesiologists of Ireland and ANZCA reviewed the literature (239 articles identified, 39 full texts) on infective sequelae, time to establish anaesthesia, infection-prevention measures, the roles of clinician and assistant, and attitudes to infection prevention. Statements and recommendations were refined through a three-round modified Delphi completed by 32 professional experts and one patient representative.

**What they found.**
- 10 statements and 11 recommendations; consensus on 8 statements and all 11 recommendations.
- Routine sterile gown use for uncomplicated adult single-shot spinal anaesthesia should not be mandatory.
- Effective hand hygiene and facemask use remain essential; the statement defines the core aseptic measures for these patients.
- The approach is framed as proportionate, evidence-aligned and environmentally sustainable.

**Caveats.** It applies to uncomplicated single-shot spinals in adults, not to catheters or complex cases. Two statements did not reach consensus. The infection evidence is sparse because events are rare, so this is a judgement about proportionality, not proof of equivalence.

**What it means.** Expect UK, Irish and Australasian departments to revise policies this year and some pushback from infection-control teams. For North American readers it is confirmation that gown-free single-shot spinals are defensible, provided the rest of the aseptic technique is rigorous.

posts.headline: TRISCEND II at 2 years: TR stays gone in 95%, but a mortality benefit only appears after adjusting for crossover
posts.summary: Two-year results of the randomized EVOQUE transcatheter tricuspid valve replacement trial, presented at ACC.26, showed durable TR elimination and quality-of-life gains; intention-to-treat mortality and heart failure hospitalization were not significantly different.
takeHome: ITT: death 19.1% vs 25.3% (p=0.19); death or HF hospitalization 36.0% vs 43.7% (p=0.16).
Crossover-adjusted and Bayesian analyses favored TTVR but were post hoc; pacemakers 19.7% vs 9.0%.
Severe bleeding in year two was lower with TTVR, 5.5% vs 14.9%; these TEE-guided implants are now routine hybrid-room work.
posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters.** EVOQUE is the only transcatheter tricuspid replacement with a randomized trial and FDA approval; these are the first data beyond the one-year primary endpoint and the first look at whether eliminating TR saves lives.

**What they did.** TRISCEND II randomized 400 patients with symptomatic severe TR 2:1 to EVOQUE TTVR plus medical therapy or medical therapy alone (median age 79, 76% women). Controls could cross over after one year. Vinod Thourani presented two-year outcomes at ACC.26 in New Orleans on March 30, 2026; no simultaneous publication was found.

**What they found.**
- Intention to treat: all-cause mortality 19.1% vs 25.3% (p=0.192); HF hospitalization 26.8% vs 32.3% (p=0.312); death or HF hospitalization 36.0% vs 43.7% (p=0.161).
- Crossover-stratified landmark analysis: mortality 19.1% vs 44.9% among controls who never crossed over (p<0.001); death or HF hospitalization 36.0% vs 57.4% (p=0.004). A non-prespecified Bayesian sensitivity analysis estimated mortality of 19.1% vs 29.4% (p=0.03).
- About 95% of TTVR patients had mild or less TR at two years versus 15.4% on medical therapy; crossover patients achieved the same.
- KCCQ overall score rose 17.8 points with TTVR vs 14.1 with medical therapy.
- Cumulative pacemaker rate 19.7% vs 9.0% (p=0.006); severe bleeding between years one and two 5.5% vs 14.9% (p=0.008); nonelective tricuspid reintervention 0.8% vs 3.8% (p=0.047). No difference in stroke.

**Caveats.** Powered for a one-year composite, not for mortality; only 28 non-crossover controls had complete two-year data; crossover patients were sicker at baseline; discussant Paul Sorajja called the results 'incredibly provocative' and the presenters called the mortality analyses hypothesis-generating.

**For us.** EVOQUE implants under general anesthesia with continuous TEE guidance are becoming routine. The one-in-five pacemaker rate and RV behavior after abrupt elimination of TR are the problems we manage in the room and the ICU.

posts.headline: Neither fluid balance nor vasopressor dose during liver transplant predicted early allograft dysfunction in 852 patients
posts.summary: Eight-center Canadian and French cohort of consecutive liver transplant recipients found 7-day early allograft dysfunction or primary nonfunction in 28%, with no association with intraoperative fluid balance or norepinephrine-equivalent vasopressor dose after adjustment for hypotension.
takeHome: Adjusted RR 1.02 per liter of positive fluid balance; RR 1.03 per 25 mcg/kg norepinephrine equivalent. Both null.
Restrictive-versus-liberal and pressor-heavy-versus-light arguments lack outcome data; this is the best cohort yet.
Accompanying Anesthesiology editorial (Douville, July 2026) calls it a signal-in-the-noise problem awaiting an RCT.
posts.deepDive:
