**Why it matters.** Liver transplant anesthesiologists argue endlessly about restrictive fluids with high vasopressor doses versus more liberal volume. Guidance rests on physiology and small single-center series. This is the first multicenter cohort designed specifically to test whether either exposure tracks with graft outcome.

**What they did.** Consecutive adult recipients at eight centers in Canada and France (January 2021 to May 2023; n=852, 836 with complete data; median MELD 3.0 of 20) had intraoperative fluid balance (blood products, cell saver, colloids, crystalloids divided by 1.5, minus estimated blood loss) and total vasopressor dose (25 mcg/kg norepinephrine-equivalent increments) modeled against 7-day early allograft dysfunction or primary nonfunction, adjusting for confounders including intraoperative hypotension.

**What they found.** The primary outcome occurred in 28% (236 patients). Neither fluid balance (adjusted RR 1.02 per liter, 95% CI 0.97-1.06) nor vasopressor dose (adjusted RR 1.03 per 25 mcg/kg, 95% CI 0.99-1.06) was associated with it. The accompanying editorial, "Hemodynamic Management in Liver Transplantation: Searching for Signal in the Noise" (Anesthesiology, 14 July 2026), frames the result as a mandate for randomized trials rather than a license for any strategy.

**Caveats.** Observational; exposures are summary totals that cannot capture timing (for example, pressor dose during the anhepatic phase versus after reperfusion); residual confounding by indication is unavoidable; other secondary outcomes such as AKI were not the focus of the abstract.

**For the anesthesiologist.** Dogmatic positions on either side of the fluid-pressor debate are not supported. Treat hypotension, keep the graft perfused, and hold off on judging colleagues who run their cases differently until a trial reports.

posts.headline: SURVIV: mitral valve-in-valve beat redo surgery at 1 year, driven by 12.5% in-hospital surgical mortality
posts.summary: Investigator-initiated randomized trial at seven Brazilian centers comparing transcatheter mitral valve-in-valve with redo surgical mitral valve replacement in 150 patients with failed bioprostheses, presented as a late-breaker at ACC.26.
takeHome: Death or disabling stroke at 1 year: 5.3% valve-in-valve vs 20.8% redo surgery (HR 0.23).
Surgery arm had 12.5% in-hospital mortality, 15.3% AKI, 11.1% major bleeding; stay 14 vs 4 days.
Valve-in-valve had more cardiac rehospitalization (16% vs 2.8%) and higher gradients; durability unknown.
posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters.** Failed mitral bioprostheses are common, and valve-in-valve has spread on registry data alone. SURVIV is the first randomized comparison with redo surgery.

**What they did.** Dimytri Siqueira presented the trial at ACC.26 in New Orleans on 29 March 2026. 150 patients with symptomatic bioprosthetic mitral dysfunction (mean age 58, 72% women, about a quarter with more than one prior mitral operation, likely many with rheumatic disease) were randomized 1:1 to transcatheter valve-in-valve with SAPIEN 3 or redo surgical replacement, with blinded event adjudication.

**What they found.**
- Primary endpoint, all-cause death or disabling stroke at 1 year: 5.3% vs 20.8% (HR 0.23, 95% CI 0.07-0.68, P=0.005), almost entirely from the first 30 days.
- In-hospital death 0% vs 12.5%; disabling stroke 0% vs 8.3%; AKI 0% vs 15.3%; major bleeding 1.3% vs 11.1%; median stay 4 vs 14 days.
- Against valve-in-valve: cardiac rehospitalization 16% vs 2.8% at 1 year, including leaflet thrombosis, and a higher mean gradient (6.7 vs 5.4 mmHg).

**Caveats.** Surgical mortality was more than double what STS data predict for redo mitral surgery, with concomitant procedures in the surgical arm and pandemic-era care; the discussants were blunt about this. Only 1-year follow-up, and no simultaneous publication was identified. A two-center US retrospective series in Annals of Thoracic Surgery (April 2026) found the opposite at 5 years: mortality 40.9% after valve-in-valve vs 20.3% after redo surgery.

**For the anesthesiologist.** Expect heart teams to lean further toward valve-in-valve for older or frail patients. For younger patients, durability, gradients and anticoagulation after mitral valve-in-valve remain unsettled, and you should expect to keep doing redo sternotomies.

posts.headline: STEMI-DTU: Impella unloading before PCI in anterior STEMI without shock fails to shrink infarcts, 30% major bleeding
posts.summary: In 527 patients with anterior STEMI and no shock, 30 minutes of Impella CP unloading before PCI did not reduce infarct size on cardiac MRI and exceeded the prespecified bleeding and vascular safety goal.
takeHome: Infarct size about 1% smaller with unloading, not significant; no difference in heart-failure events.
BARC 3 to 5 bleeding 30.4%, all access-site; door-to-PCI 40 minutes longer, ischemic time 47 minutes longer.
Impella remains a shock device; shock patients were excluded, so DanGer Shock still stands.
posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters.** The 'door-to-unload' idea is that 30 minutes of Impella CP unloading before reperfusion shrinks anterior infarcts and prevents later heart failure. It had animal data and a feasibility trial behind it, and a positive result would have put a large-bore pump into every anterior STEMI. STEMI-DTU (Kapur, with Stone and O'Neill as co-principal investigators; late-breaker at ACC.26 on 28 March 2026 with simultaneous JACC publication) tested it properly.

**What they did.** 527 patients with anterior STEMI and no cardiogenic shock at 55 sites were randomized to Impella CP placement with a 30-minute delay before PCI, or immediate PCI. Primary endpoint: infarct size as a fraction of LV mass on cardiac MRI at 3 to 5 days.

**What they found.**
- No difference in infarct size: about 1% smaller with Impella by intention-to-treat and 1.9% by per-protocol, neither significant, consistent across subgroups.
- No differences in heart-failure events or other secondary outcomes.
- Door-to-PCI was 40 minutes longer and total ischemic time 47 minutes longer with unloading. Median support lasted 10.4 hours.
- Treatment-related BARC 3 to 5 bleeding or major vascular complications exceeded the preset 26.5% performance goal: major bleeding 30.4%, all access-site, and major vascular complications 4.2%.

**Caveats.** Blood pressure in the Impella arm was high (around 140 mmHg), which the investigators think limited unloading; a follow-up trial with nitroglycerin and beta-blockade is planned. Shock patients were excluded, so DanGer Shock is unaffected.

**For us.** Large-bore access for unloading in a hemodynamically stable STEMI buys bleeding and delay, not myocardium. Impella stays a shock device. If a lab tries to extend it to non-shock STEMI, this is the trial to cite.

posts.headline: Ex-preterm hernia repair: apnea risk drops below 1% around 65 weeks PMA after GA but 45 weeks after spinal
posts.summary: Individual-participant-data meta-analysis of 12 prospective studies (751 former preterm infants having open inguinal herniorrhaphy) redrawing postanesthesia apnea risk by postmenstrual age and technique.
takeHome: 17.6% had postanesthesia apnea; general anesthesia carried roughly six-fold higher odds than neuraxial.
Risk falls below 1% at about 65 weeks PMA after GA but about 45 weeks after neuraxial.
Anemia mattered only above 48 weeks PMA. Technique, not just age, should set the admission plan.
posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters.** The admit-for-apnea-monitoring rule for infants under 60 weeks postmenstrual age rests on Cote's 1995 combined analysis of infants anaesthetised decades ago. Anesthesia has changed; the thresholds had not.

**What they did.** Individual-participant-data meta-analysis of 12 prospective studies of former preterm infants undergoing open inguinal herniorrhaphy (n=751). The goal was to identify the PMA above which postanesthesia apnea risk falls below 1%, by anaesthetic technique.

**What they found.** Postanesthesia apnea occurred in 132 infants (17.6%). After general anaesthesia the estimated risk was about 10% at 53 weeks PMA, 5% at 57 weeks and under 1% at roughly 65 weeks. After neuraxial anaesthesia the same thresholds fell to about 38, 40 and 45 weeks. Compared with neuraxial, general anaesthesia had six-fold higher odds of apnea (P=0.008) and apnea started earlier. Anaemia increased risk only in infants above 48 weeks PMA.

**Caveats.** Studies spanned different eras, monitoring definitions and anaesthetic drugs; the 1% line is a modelled estimate with widening uncertainty at the tails. Only open herniorrhaphy was studied.

**For the anesthesiologist.** Two practice points. First, the technique you choose changes the monitoring plan: an awake spinal lets a 46-50-week ex-preterm go home from a day unit in many settings, while GA pushes the safe line past 60 weeks. Second, screen and treat anaemia in older ex-preterms. Departments should rewrite PMA admission policies by technique rather than a single cutoff; an accompanying Anesthesiology editorial (Matava) proposes exactly such a framework.

posts.headline: FDA clears two AI tools that flag moderate-to-severe aortic stenosis from plain 2D echo views, no Doppler needed
posts.summary: GE HealthCare's AutoAS (March 2026) and iCardio.ai's CardioVision (November 2025) received 510(k) clearance to suggest moderate or severe aortic stenosis from B-mode transthoracic images alone.
takeHome: AutoAS: AUC 93%, sensitivity 75%, specificity 92% on 401 studies; readers' sensitivity rose 5.5 points when aided.
CardioVision works from a single PLAX loop in primary care: AUROC 0.945, NPV 0.955 on 650 studies from 12 sites.
Both are triage aids for adults with native valves, not a substitute for a Doppler exam before anesthesia.
posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters.** Undiagnosed severe AS is one of the few things on a preop POCUS that changes the anesthetic on the spot. Both of these tools work from B-mode images with no Doppler, which is exactly what a non-expert captures on a handheld.

**What was cleared.** GE HealthCare's Automated Aortic Stenosis Software, AutoAS (K254161, decision March 27, 2026), analyzes previously acquired 2D TTE clips in PLAX, PSAX-AV and AP5 views and returns 'suggestive' or 'not suggestive' of moderate-to-severe AS with a confidence score. In a standalone test of 401 studies from four US institutions, against a majority of three level-III echocardiographers using ASE valve-area criteria, AUC was 93.2% (95% CI 90.5-95.6), sensitivity 75.2% and specificity 92.4%. In a multi-reader study of 220 studies, five echocardiographers' sensitivity improved by 5.5 points (95% CI 1.5-9.5) with specificity unchanged (0.897 vs 0.900). iCardio.ai's CardioVision (K251293, November 21, 2025) needs a single PLAX cine loop and is indicated for adults over 21 in outpatient settings such as primary care; on 650 studies from 608 subjects at 12 US sites, AUROC was 0.945, sensitivity 0.896, specificity 0.872, PPV 0.734 and NPV 0.955.

**Caveats.** Retrospective validation; neither tool is for prosthetic valves or prior valve repair; both are labeled as aids that must be reviewed by a qualified physician and never used alone for management. AutoAS's 75% sensitivity means roughly one in four significant AS cases is missed.

**For us.** A useful safety net in preop clinics and on handhelds, but a flagged patient still needs a Doppler gradient and valve area before the induction plan is set, and a negative result does not clear a murmur.

posts.journal: Intensive Care Med / Crit Care Med
posts.headline: Surviving Sepsis 2026: peripheral pressors, MAP 60-65 if over 65, prolonged beta-lactams, no beta-blockers
posts.summary: SCCM and ESICM published the 2026 international sepsis and septic shock guideline on 23 March 2026 with 129 statements, 46 of them new, replacing the 2021 edition.
takeHome: Start vasopressors peripherally rather than waiting for a central line; add vasopressin when norepinephrine is escalating.
Initial MAP 65 remains strong; 60-65 suggested for patients 65 and older.
Strong: prolonged beta-lactam infusion after a loading dose. Suggest against beta-blockers and IV vitamin C.
posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters.** The Surviving Sepsis Campaign guideline is the reference document for sepsis bundles, quality metrics and payer expectations worldwide. The 2026 edition, co-published in Intensive Care Medicine and Critical Care Medicine on 23 March 2026 (Prescott, Antonelli, Alhazzani and a 69-member panel from 23 countries), has 129 statements with 46 new ones.

**Hemodynamics.** Crystalloids remain first-line (strong), balanced solutions suggested over saline except in traumatic brain injury, with starches recommended against and routine albumin not suggested. At least 30 mL/kg within 3 hours stays as a conditional suggestion, now with remarks on adjusted body weight above BMI 30 and frequent reassessment. New: give a fluid bolus first, then vasopressors if hypotension persists, with concurrent pressors case by case. Start vasopressors peripherally instead of waiting for central access. Norepinephrine first; add vasopressin when norepinephrine is escalating (no numeric threshold); add epinephrine if MAP stays inadequate; suggest against terlipressin. Initial MAP 65 mm Hg is a strong recommendation; 60-65 is suggested for adults 65 and older. Either invasive or noninvasive pressure monitoring is acceptable; invasive is advised on high or escalating pressor doses.

**Antimicrobials.** Immediate antibiotics, ideally within 1 hour, for septic shock and probable or definite sepsis (strong); a time-limited rapid assessment and 3-hour window for possible sepsis without shock. Prolonged or continuous beta-lactam infusion after a loading dose is a strong, high-certainty recommendation (BLING III). New conditional suggestions: prehospital antibiotics when in-hospital evaluation will take over 60 minutes, against empiric anaerobic cover without risk factors, procalcitonin to shorten courses, and selective digestive decontamination in low-resistance units.

**Adjuncts.** Suggest IV corticosteroids in septic shock, against beta-blockers (esmolol, landiolol) to treat shock, against IV vitamin C, and against polymyxin B hemoperfusion.

**For anesthesiologists.** The peripheral-pressor and lower-MAP-in-the-elderly changes will reach the OR and PACU quickly.

posts.headline: Prehospital whole blood did not beat red cells plus plasma in UK air-ambulance trauma (SWiFT, NEJM)
posts.summary: Pragmatic open-label RCT across 10 English air ambulance services: up to 2 units of leukodepleted whole blood versus up to 2 units of red cells plus 2 of plasma in bleeding trauma patients. 942 randomized, 616 in the primary analysis.
takeHome: Up to 2 units prehospital whole blood: death or massive transfusion 48.7% vs 47.7% with red cells plus plasma.
Mortality identical at 24 h, 30 and 90 days; no safety penalty either way.
Justify whole blood programs on logistics, not on a survival claim.
posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters.** Whole blood has swept through US prehospital and trauma-centre practice on the back of observational data. SWiFT is the first large randomized test of the prehospital question.

**What they did.** Pragmatic, open-label, phase 3 superiority RCT across 10 English air ambulance services (physician-paramedic HEMS). Injured patients needing prehospital transfusion got up to 2 units of leukodepleted whole blood or up to 2 units of red cells plus 2 units of plasma. 942 were randomized; after prespecified exclusions (mostly traumatic cardiac arrest and non-traumatic bleeding) 616 had primary-outcome data.

**What they found.**
- Death or massive transfusion within 24 h: 48.7% whole blood vs 47.7% standard care (RR 1.02, 95% CI 0.80-1.31; P=0.84).
- Mortality at 24 h, 30 days and 90 days: all similar (10.1 vs 10.0%, 27.5 vs 26.0%, 30.4 vs 27.2%).
- Serious adverse events 31 vs 37; thrombotic events similar. Abnormal prothrombin time was more common after whole blood (40.7 vs 30.5%).

**Caveats.** Two units is a small dose next to what follows in the resuscitation bay. The trial was powered for a 12-point absolute difference, protocol deviations ran about 7% in each arm, and results come from a mature HEMS system with short transport times, not rural ground EMS.

**For the anesthesiologist.** Whole blood is feasible and safe prehospital, but it did not reduce death or massive transfusion. Read together with TOWAR two months later, the burden of proof has shifted back onto whole blood programs, which should be justified on logistics rather than on a survival claim.

posts.headline: SOHO: high-flow nasal oxygen does not reduce mortality in acute hypoxemic respiratory failure, but intubations fall
posts.summary: A French multicenter trial randomized 1,116 adults with PaO2/FiO2 of 200 or less, respiratory rate above 25 and infiltrates to high-flow nasal cannula or standard oxygen.
takeHome: 28-day mortality 14.6% in both arms.
Intubation by day 28: 42.4% vs 48.4% with high-flow (difference -5.9 points).
High-flow remains first-line for comfort and avoiding intubation; it is not a survival drug.
posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters.** FLORALI (2015) made high-flow nasal cannula the default for de novo hypoxemic respiratory failure on the strength of a secondary mortality signal in a 310-patient trial. SOHO, from the same group (Frat, REVA Network), is the adequately powered test, published in NEJM online 17 March 2026 (print 4 June 2026).

**What they did.** 1,116 adults with acute hypoxemic respiratory failure (PaO2/FiO2 of 200 or less, respiratory rate above 25, pulmonary infiltrates) were randomized to high-flow nasal oxygen or standard oxygen therapy. The primary outcome was 28-day mortality.

**What they found.** Death by day 28 occurred in 14.6% of each group (81/556 vs 81/554; difference -0.05 points, 95% CI -4.21 to 4.10). Intubation by day 28 was lower with high-flow: 42.4% vs 48.4% (difference -5.93 points, 95% CI -11.78 to -0.08). Serious adverse events during spontaneous breathing (cardiac arrest or pneumothorax) were 2.3% vs 1.1%.

**Caveats.** Open label, and the intubation difference is a secondary outcome with a confidence interval that just clears zero. Mortality was lower than the FLORALI era, which limits power for a survival effect.

**For anesthesiologists.** The 2026 ATS guideline (AJRCCM, June 2026) still gives a strong recommendation for high-flow over standard oxygen in de novo hypoxemic failure, and SOHO supports that for intubation avoidance and comfort. What SOHO removes is the expectation that high-flow lowers mortality, which matters when deciding how long to persist before intubating a patient who is not improving.

posts.headline: The 2025 ASE diastolic algorithm grades most catheter-proven HFpEF as normal or grade 1, JACC study finds
posts.summary: Mayo-led investigators ran the updated ASE diastolic grading against invasively confirmed HFpEF in ambulatory, hospitalized and external cohorts and found it misses the majority of cases.
takeHome: In 756 ambulatory HFpEF patients, two-thirds graded normal or grade 1; over 60% of those had resting wedge 15 mmHg or higher.
Only 9.5% of grade 1 patients with invasive exercise testing met the ASE stress criteria; AUC versus noncardiac dyspnea was 0.61.
Do not let a normal diastolic grade on preop echo or intraop TEE rule out HFpEF; weigh pretest probability.
posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters.** The July 2025 ASE diastolic update was meant to cut 'indeterminate' calls and reduce the need for catheterization. This JACC paper from Barry Borlaug's group tests it against the invasive gold standard and the result is uncomfortable.

**What they did.** Three groups: ambulatory, compensated HFpEF patients with invasive exercise hemodynamics (n = 756) plus an external validation cohort; hospitalized patients studied while decompensated and again after recompensation (n = 88); and noncardiac dyspnea controls. First author Tomonari Harada; JACC March 17, 2026 (87:1261-1275; DOI 10.1016/j.jacc.2025.11.024).

**What they found.**
- Ambulatory HFpEF: 32.8% graded normal, 34.8% grade 1, 30.0% grade 2-3, 3.4% indeterminate. More than 60% of those graded normal or grade 1 had resting PAWP of 15 mmHg or higher.
- Decompensated inpatients: 25.0% graded normal or grade 1, rising to 51.1% once recompensated.
- Among 116 grade 1 patients with simultaneous exercise hemodynamics and stress imaging, 11 (9.5%) met the ASE stress criteria, a 90.5% false-negative rate; the external cohort looked similar.
- The algorithm separated HFpEF from noncardiac dyspnea with an AUC of 0.61.
- HFpEF patients graded normal or grade 1 still carried about fivefold the risk of death or HF hospitalization versus controls (HR 5.37, 95% CI 1.27-22.6).

**Caveats.** Referral populations with high pretest probability; observational; the algorithm was not built as a stand-alone HFpEF test, and the authors' conclusion is to interpret grades alongside pretest probability and HFpEF-specific frameworks rather than to abandon them.

**For us.** The diastolic grade on the preop echo, or on your intraop TEE, is not a rule-out. The obese, hypertensive, dyspneic 75-year-old with a 'normal' grade should still be managed as HFpEF when you plan fluids, vasopressors and the post-bypass strategy.

posts.headline: ISHLT renames PGD 'early graft dysfunction', drops the inotrope score, grades severity by need for MCS
posts.summary: The 10-year update of the ISHLT consensus on graft dysfunction in the first 72 hours after heart transplant replaces the 2014 PGD definitions with a two-tier early graft dysfunction scheme and separates vasoplegia and secondary causes.
takeHome: PGD becomes EGD (under 24 h) and sEGD (24 to 72 h); known causes are secondary graft dysfunction.
Severe means MCS was needed: VA-ECMO, LVAD/BiVAD or new IABP; inotrope score is gone.
Severe EGD-LV is split by failure to wean from CPB versus failure after weaning; vasoplegia is defined separately.
posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters.** Since 2014, 'primary graft dysfunction' with its mild/moderate/severe grades and inotrope score has defined early failure after heart transplant and framed every conversation about coming off bypass. The 10-year update (Kobashigawa and colleagues, from a 2024 Prague consensus conference; J Heart Lung Transplant, 13 March 2026) rewrites the definitions.

**What changed.**
- PGD is renamed early graft dysfunction (EGD) for dysfunction within 24 hours; 24 to 72 hours is subsequent early graft dysfunction (sEGD). Dysfunction with an identifiable cause is secondary graft dysfunction (SGD): surgical, pulmonary hypertension, immunologic, respiratory or iatrogenic.
- Grading is two-tier, non-severe or severe, decided by whether MCS is needed. The inotrope score is gone.
- Non-severe EGD-LV: LVEF 40% or less with RAP over 15, PCWP over 20 or CI under 2.0, needing inotropes. Severe: the same plus VA-ECMO, surgical or percutaneous LVAD/BiVAD or a newly placed IABP. ECMO continued by institutional policy alone does not count.
- EGD-RV: RVEF 35% or less and/or TAPSE under 1.6 cm with inotrope-dependent hemodynamics; severe if VA-ECMO or RVAD is required.
- Severe EGD-LV is split into immediate presentation (failure to wean from CPB) and delayed (failure after successful weaning), because timing appears to carry prognosis.
- Vasoplegia (refractory hypotension, preserved CI, SVR under 800) is kept separate, either complicating EGD or contributing to SGD.

**Risk and prevention.** Ischemic time, donor age and hyperoxia, undersizing of 30% or more by predicted heart mass, DCD donors, recipient LVAD, pre-transplant ECMO or dialysis, amiodarone and RAAS inhibitors. Stop amiodarone before listing and hold RAAS inhibitors before surgery. Peripheral VA-ECMO cannulation was associated with better 1-year survival in one meta-analysis.

**For us.** The grade is assigned in our OR from our TEE and hemodynamics. Learn the new names before the next M&M.

posts.headline: EIT-guided individualised PEEP improves OLV mechanics but not pulmonary complications after lung cancer surgery
posts.summary: 400 patients aged 60 or older having lung cancer surgery were randomised to electrical impedance tomography-guided PEEP or fixed PEEP 5 cmH2O. Driving pressure fell and oxygenation improved, but postoperative pulmonary complications were 28% vs 25%.
takeHome: Individualised PEEP (median 11 cmH2O during OLV) cut driving pressure 15 to 12 cmH2O and raised PaO2/FiO2.
Pulmonary complications 28% vs 25% (RR 1.09, 95% CI 0.79-1.52): no benefit, consistent with PROTHOR.
Better intraoperative numbers do not translate into fewer complications; do not chase driving pressure alone.
posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters.** After PROTHOR showed that fixed high PEEP does not help, the obvious rebuttal was 'you should have individualised it'. This trial did exactly that, with electrical impedance tomography, in the patients most likely to benefit.

**What they did.** Single thoracic centre (Shanghai Chest Hospital). 400 patients aged 60 or older having lung cancer surgery were randomised to EIT-guided individualised PEEP or fixed PEEP 5 cmH2O. Primary outcome: postoperative pulmonary complications. Secondary outcomes included driving pressure, oxygenation index, extrapulmonary complications, 30-day complications and length of stay.

**What they found.**
- Individualised PEEP was median 11 cmH2O during one-lung ventilation and 9 cmH2O during two-lung ventilation.
- Driving pressure during OLV 12 vs 15 cmH2O, and during two-lung ventilation 9 vs 12 cmH2O (both p<0.001).
- Oxygenation index during OLV 26.7 vs 22.7 kPa (p<0.001).
- Pulmonary complications 54/195 (28%) vs 50/197 (25%); RR 1.09, 95% CI 0.79-1.52, p=0.60.

**Caveats.** Single centre, and the PPC definition and baseline risk differ from PROTHOR, so the absolute numbers are not directly comparable. EIT is not widely available, and whether cheaper compliance-based titration behaves the same is untested here.

**What it means.** Together with PROTHOR and the JAMA DESIGNATION trial in abdominal surgery, this is the third 2025-2026 trial in which better intraoperative mechanics did not reduce complications. Driving pressure is a useful dial but not a surrogate endpoint you can bank on. Set PEEP for oxygenation and haemodynamics and stop expecting it to prevent pneumonia.

posts.headline: ESAIC/ESPA publish the first European guideline on neuromuscular block in children: indications, monitoring and reversal
posts.summary: The 2025 ESAIC and ESPA Guidelines on neuromuscular block in anaesthetised children (Veyckemans et al., Eur J Anaesthesiol 2026;43:295-323, online March 4, 2026) address when to use neuromuscular blockers in children, how to monitor them quantitatively, and how to reverse them, prompted by APRICOT data showing only 16% of children receiving a blocker were monitored.
takeHome: First dedicated pediatric NMB guideline from ESAIC/ESPA; 29-page document with an infographic for the OR.
APRICOT: 60.8% of pediatric intubations used an NMBA but only 16% had neuromuscular monitoring; the guideline aims to close that gap.
Pediatric EMG-based quantitative monitors are now available; expect them to become the expected standard in children as in adults.
posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters.** Adult guidelines (ASA 2023, ESAIC 2023) made quantitative neuromuscular monitoring and sugammadex-based reversal the standard, but children were left out of both. The European APRICOT study showed that 60.8% of pediatric tracheal intubations involved a neuromuscular blocker yet only 16% of those children were monitored, and residual block in children is linked to postoperative respiratory complications.

**What it is.** The European Society of Anaesthesiology and Intensive Care and the European Society for Paediatric Anaesthesiology convened a guideline group (Veyckemans, Debouche, Kaufmann, Disma, Amigoni and colleagues) that published the 2025 ESAIC and ESPA Guidelines on neuromuscular block in anaesthetised children: indications, monitoring and reversal in the European Journal of Anaesthesiology (published online March 4, 2026; print April 2026, volume 43, pages 295-323), with an erratum in June 2026 and correspondence already published. ESAIC lists it as a March 2026 guideline with an accompanying infographic and podcast.

**Scope.** Indications for neuromuscular blockers at induction and during maintenance in children, quantitative monitoring (including the newly available pediatric electromyography-based monitors), and reversal strategies including sugammadex. Read the open-access document for the individual recommendation grades.

**Caveats.** Pediatric evidence is thin and many recommendations will rest on extrapolation from adults and expert consensus; US practice is governed by the ASA 2023 guideline, which is not pediatric-specific.

**For the anesthesiologist.** If you anesthetize children, even occasionally, the expectation is moving to quantitative monitoring whenever a blocker is given, the same standard adults now have. Equipment procurement (pediatric EMG sensors) is the practical first step.

posts.headline: Sibling-matched data put the epidural-autism scare to rest: adjusted HR 1.06, confidence interval crossing 1
posts.summary: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 19 studies (searched to September 2025) on neuraxial labour analgesia and offspring neurodevelopmental disorders, prioritising family-based designs.
takeHome: Sibling comparisons: no association with autism (aHR 1.06, 0.98-1.14) or with ADHD.
Population analyses show aHR 1.10 that shrinks as familial confounding is controlled.
Counsel families plainly: no convincing evidence that labour epidurals harm neurodevelopment.
posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters.** Since the 2020 JAMA Pediatrics report linking labour epidurals to autism, several large cohorts have produced small positive associations and SOAP, ASA and others have had to issue reassurance. The open question has been whether residual family-level confounding explains the signal.

**What they did.** Systematic review and meta-analysis of 19 studies (search to September 2025) of epidural, caudal or combined spinal-epidural labour analgesia and offspring neurodevelopmental disorders, with pre-specified emphasis on family-based (sibling-matched) designs, which control for shared genetic and environmental factors that population models cannot.

**What they found.** In sibling-matched analyses, neuraxial analgesia was not associated with autism spectrum disorder (adjusted HR 1.06, 95% CI 0.98-1.14) or with ADHD. Conventional population-based analyses gave a small positive estimate (adjusted HR 1.10, 95% CI 1.08-1.13), but the effect shrank progressively as more familial confounding was addressed. No clinically meaningful associations emerged for other neurodevelopmental disorders.

**Caveats.** Observational data only; sibling designs have their own limitations (carryover of exposure between pregnancies, smaller samples), and heterogeneity in exposure definitions and outcome ascertainment remains.

**For the anesthesiologist.** This is the clearest synthesis to date that the epidural-autism association behaves like confounding, not causation. Use the sibling-matched hazard ratio when a patient raises the question, and keep the message simple: no convincing evidence of harm to the child's neurodevelopment from labour neuraxial analgesia.

posts.headline: Keep maternal SBP at 90% of baseline, not 80%: fewer acidotic babies and less nausea in 1,183-patient RCT
posts.summary: Multicentre RCT of term cesareans under spinal: noradrenaline titrated to keep systolic pressure at 90% versus 80% of baseline until delivery; primary outcome umbilical artery pH.
takeHome: Mean umbilical artery pH identical (7.33), but pH below 7.2 fell from 2.2% to 0.5% with the 90% target.
Hypotension halved (36% vs 71%); nausea or vomiting 10% vs 18%; the cost was one extra bolus.
Supports early, tight vasopressor titration to near-baseline pressure from the moment the spinal is in.
posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters.** Everyone treats spinal hypotension at cesarean, but the target has been a matter of taste: keep it near baseline versus avoid overshooting with vasopressors. This trial tested the two most common numbers head to head with a neonatal primary outcome.

**What they did.** A multicentre randomised controlled trial enrolled 1,183 women with term pregnancies having cesarean delivery under spinal anaesthesia. From intrathecal injection until delivery, noradrenaline was titrated to keep systolic blood pressure at 90% of baseline (n=590) or 80% of baseline (n=593). The primary outcome was umbilical artery pH.

**What they found.** Mean umbilical artery pH was the same in both arms (7.33 vs 7.33, p=0.11). But fetal acidaemia (pH below 7.2) was rarer with the tighter target: 0.5% vs 2.2% (p=0.020). Mothers did better too: hypotension below 80% of baseline occurred in 36.1% vs 70.5%, severe hypotension (below 60%) in 3.9% vs 7.8%, and nausea or vomiting in 9.8% vs 18.4%. The price was a median of two noradrenaline boluses instead of one, with no excess harm reported.

**Caveats.** The primary outcome was neutral; the pH below 7.2 result is a secondary endpoint with few events (3 vs 13). Bolus-based titration was used rather than a prophylactic infusion, and generalisability to high-risk or pre-eclamptic patients is untested.

**For the anesthesiologist.** This backs the 2018 international consensus target of keeping maternal systolic pressure at or above 90% of baseline, using noradrenaline early rather than waiting for a number to fall. If you are still titrating to about 80%, this is a reason to tighten up.

posts.headline: ISHLT publishes first clinical cardiac xenotransplant standards since 2000, including anesthesia and blood product rules
posts.summary: The 2026 ISHLT Consensus Statement on Clinical Cardiac Xenotransplantation sets patient selection, pig gene-edit, immunosuppression, infection-surveillance and perioperative standards for pig-to-human heart transplants, with explicit pathways to trials.
takeHome: First candidates: patients ineligible for durable MCS and allotransplant, with low anti-pig antibody and negative cytotoxic crossmatch.
Perioperative: TEE plus transpulmonary thermodilution, avoid unscreened blood products, use cell salvage, start antiarrhythmics early.
Before an IND trial: 5 to 10 primate cases across centers surviving at least 6 months.
posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters.** Two patients have received gene-edited pig hearts (January 2022 and September 2023, surviving 60 and 40 days), and several groups are heading toward FDA-regulated trials. The ISHLT's first xenotransplant statement since 2000 (Mehra, Reichart, Mohiuddin and a 23-member international panel; J Heart Lung Transplant, 20 February 2026) defines what a center must have in place.

**Key positions.**
- First adult candidates: patients who cannot receive durable MCS or an allograft, with the xenograft as destination therapy; low-level anti-pig antibody on flow crossmatch and a negative cytotoxic crossmatch.
- Source pigs: knockout of the three carbohydrate antigens (alpha-Gal, Neu5Gc, Sda) plus human complement- and coagulation-regulatory transgenes.
- Immunosuppression: induction with antithymocyte globulin, anti-CD20 and a complement inhibitor; anti-CD40 or anti-CD154 costimulation blockade with steroids, calcineurin inhibitor and mycophenolate; mTOR inhibitor and tight blood pressure control if the graft hypertrophies.
- Infection: herds screened for porcine CMV/roseolovirus (found in the first recipient), PERV-C-negative donors preferred, validated recipient monitoring.
- Before an IND-qualifying trial: 5 to 10 primate cases across centers surviving at least 6 months with normal graft function.

**Perioperative statements written for us.** General anesthesia to allotransplant standards with TEE and transpulmonary thermodilution, because PA catheters can be hard to place in the pig heart; avoid inotropes and vasopressors where possible and start antiarrhythmics early; avoid blood products because they may carry anti-pig antibodies, screen any that are needed, and use cell salvage; replete calcium, magnesium, potassium and phosphate carefully; size by stroke volume; expect caval orientation that can kink.

**Caveats.** Evidence-informed but untested beyond two human cases.

**For us.** If your center is an early site, this is the protocol the transplant anesthesia group will be asked to implement.

posts.headline: Evolut Low Risk at 6 years: death or disabling stroke even, but reintervention rising after TAVR by year 7
posts.summary: Six-year outcomes of 1,414 low-risk patients randomized to self-expanding TAVR or surgery, published in JACC in February 2026, with a prespecified look at reintervention.
takeHome: Death or disabling stroke 23.3% TAVR vs 20.4% SAVR (P=0.43); curves crossed around year 5.
Reintervention 5.5% vs 3.3% at 6 years and 9.8% vs 6.0% at 7 years (P=0.02), mostly for aortic regurgitation.
Low-risk 65-year-olds choosing TAVR should hear that reintervention, not death, is the emerging difference.
posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters.** Together with PARTNER 3, this trial underpins the low-risk TAVR indication. Durability beyond five years is the unanswered question for younger patients, and this report is the first look past that line for a self-expanding valve.

**What they did.** John Forrest and colleagues reported 6-year follow-up of 1,414 patients (730 TAVR, 684 surgery) randomized at 87 sites between 2016 and 2019 with predicted surgical mortality of 3% or less. Reintervention was analyzed by valve actually implanted.

**What they found.**
- All-cause death or disabling stroke: 23.3% TAVR vs 20.4% surgery (P=0.43). The curves, which favored TAVR early, crossed near year 5 and now numerically favor surgery. Noncardiovascular death 11.0% vs 8.7%; cardiovascular death nearly identical.
- Reintervention: 5.5% vs 3.3% at 6 years (P=0.07) and 9.8% vs 6.0% at 7 years in the subset with follow-up (P=0.02). The excess was for aortic regurgitation, not stenosis.
- A post hoc signal linked off-guidance postdilation to AR-related reintervention.

**Caveats.** Earlier-generation self-expanding devices and techniques; incomplete 7-year data; surgical prostheses were heterogeneous; 10-year follow-up is planned.

**For the anesthesiologist.** Low-risk patients will keep coming to the TAVR suite, but a growing number will come back for valve-in-valve or explant. Plan for more redo structural work, TEE assessment of paravalvular and central regurgitation, and surgical TAVR explants, for which the STS released a dedicated risk model this year.

posts.headline: PROSPECT 2026: intrathecal morphine, paracetamol, NSAID and dexamethasone are the post-cesarean analgesia standard
posts.summary: ESRA's PROSPECT working group updated its procedure-specific recommendations for elective cesarean under neuraxial anaesthesia from 61 randomised trials.
takeHome: Give intrathecal morphine 50-100 µg (or diamorphine 300 µg) plus scheduled paracetamol and an NSAID.
Dexamethasone at delivery; a fascial plane block or wound infiltration when no neuraxial opioid is given.
Systemic opioids are rescue only; Joel-Cohen incision and unclosed peritoneum are part of the bundle.
posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters.** Post-cesarean analgesia protocols vary widely, and the previous PROSPECT recommendation predated much of the fascial plane block and dexamethasone literature. PROSPECT is ESRA's procedure-specific, evidence-graded series and is widely used to build enhanced recovery pathways.

**What they did.** The PROSPECT Working Group updated its systematic review of randomised trials and meta-analyses of analgesic, anaesthetic and surgical interventions for elective cesarean under neuraxial anaesthesia. Trials of emergency cesarean or general anaesthesia were excluded. Sixty-one RCTs informed the recommendations.

**What they recommend.**
- A preoperative intrathecal long-acting opioid: morphine 50-100 µg or diamorphine 300 µg.
- Paracetamol, an NSAID and dexamethasone at delivery, then regular paracetamol and NSAIDs postoperatively.
- Systemic opioids for rescue only.
- When a neuraxial opioid is not given, one of the recommended fascial plane blocks, or local anaesthetic wound infiltration as the alternative.
- Surgical technique matters: Joel-Cohen incision and leaving the peritoneum unclosed.

**Caveats.** Recommendations are for elective neuraxial cases; the optimal dose of long-acting epidural opioid and the best regional technique when opioids are avoided remain open questions the authors flag for research. Standardised outcome sets are still lacking.

**For the anesthesiologist.** If your pathway already uses low-dose intrathecal morphine plus scheduled paracetamol and NSAID, you are compliant; the practical additions are dexamethasone at delivery for everyone and a clear default block when morphine is omitted (opioid intolerance, severe OSA, or shortage). It dovetails with the SOAP respiratory monitoring guidance for intrathecal morphine doses of 150 µg or less.

posts.headline: STS database: off-pump CABG in experienced hands cut early complications, long-term survival matched on-pump
posts.summary: Late-breaking analysis at STS 2026 of more than 1.5 million isolated CABG records (2008-2023) with over 184,000 propensity-matched off-pump/on-pump pairs, restricted to surgeons meeting volume and experience criteria.
takeHome: Lower operative mortality, stroke, AF, renal failure, reoperation, prolonged ventilation and transfusion with OPCAB.
More incomplete revascularization and slightly fewer grafts off-pump; early survival edge faded by 5 years.
Supports OPCAB as a tool for high-volume off-pump surgeons, not a mandate for everyone.
posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters.** ROOBY and CORONARY left off-pump CABG with a reputation for fewer grafts and no survival benefit, and US use has been declining for years. This analysis asks what happens when only surgeons who actually do a lot of it are counted.

**What they did.** John Puskas presented a late-breaking STS Adult Cardiac Surgery Database analysis at STS 2026 in New Orleans (31 January 2026). Nonemergency isolated CABG from 2008 to 2023 was linked to the National Death Index and CMS data through 2024. Surgeons had to meet strict experience and volume criteria. About 184,000 off-pump and 1.34 million on-pump cases yielded more than 184,000 propensity-matched pairs on 64 preoperative variables, analyzed by intention to treat.

**What they found.**
- Off-pump had lower operative mortality and lower rates of stroke, atrial fibrillation, renal failure, reoperation, prolonged ventilation and blood transfusion.
- Off-pump had more incomplete revascularization and a slightly lower graft count, though more multiple arterial grafting.
- The early survival advantage shrank over five years. At 15 years a small edge persisted only in single-vessel disease; in multivessel disease long-term survival was the same.

**Caveats.** Observational, with selection by surgeon and by patient that matching cannot fully remove; not yet published in a journal; results cannot be extrapolated to occasional off-pump operators.

**For the anesthesiologist.** If your surgeons are committed off-pump operators, this is the best modern evidence that the early morbidity benefit is real, including less transfusion and less stroke. Expect to keep managing hemodynamic instability during positioning, and keep the perfusionist in the room.

posts.headline: Bilateral ITA and ITA plus radial give similar 15-year survival; a third arterial graft adds benefit (STS data)
posts.summary: Late-breaking STS 2026 analysis of over 172,000 multi-arterial CABG patients in the STS database (2008-2023), comparing bilateral internal thoracic artery grafting with single ITA plus radial artery.
takeHome: Overall 15-year survival comparable between BITA and SITA plus radial after propensity matching.
BITA favored under age 60; SITA plus radial favored at 70 and older; third arterial conduit helped regardless.
Multi-arterial CABG still only about 16% of US cases, mostly driven by radial use.
posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters.** With ROMA still unreported, the choice of second arterial conduit rests on observational data. This is the largest such comparison, and it comes with 15 years of follow-up.

**What they did.** Thomas Schwann presented a late-breaking analysis of the STS Adult Cardiac Surgery Database at STS 2026 (31 January 2026). More than 2.1 million CABG patients were screened; over 172,000 had multi-arterial grafting with bilateral ITA (BITA), single ITA plus radial artery (SITA+RA), or both. Survival came from the National Death Index and CMS claims, with propensity matching and risk adjustment.

**What they found.**
- Overall 15-year survival was comparable between BITA and SITA+RA.
- Age mattered: BITA was associated with better survival under 60, SITA+RA with lower mortality at 70 and older.
- SITA+RA had an early (0-5 year) edge; BITA trended toward benefit beyond 10 years.
- A third arterial conduit was associated with additional survival benefit in either strategy.
- US multi-arterial use rose from about 9% to more than 16% over a decade, mostly through radial grafting.

**Caveats.** Registry data, not randomized; conduit choice is confounded by surgeon and patient; not yet published in a journal.

**For the anesthesiologist.** Expect more radial harvests, with the attendant Allen testing, arterial line planning away from the harvest arm, and calcium channel blocker or nitrate infusions for spasm prophylaxis. Pair this with the off-pump analysis from the same meeting: the signal is that experienced surgeons using more arterial conduits do well.

posts.headline: Military trauma airway guideline rewritten: resuscitate before intubating, ketamine 2 mg/kg first line, VL preferred
posts.summary: The Joint Trauma System published a fully revised Airway Management in Trauma clinical practice guideline (CPG ID 39, Jan 28, 2026) replacing the 2017 version and merging the prolonged field care airway guidance.
takeHome: Resuscitate before you intubate: volume first, two large-bore lines, BP every 1-2 minutes during RSI.
Ketamine 2 mg/kg first line, etomidate 0.3 mg/kg second; reduce doses in unstable patients.
Video laryngoscopy preferred; confirm every surgical airway with waveform capnography.
posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters.** The Joint Trauma System's airway guideline had not been rewritten since 2017. The January 28, 2026 version (CPG ID 39) merges the prolonged field care airway guideline, reorganizes around the SOAP ME checklist and, most importantly, puts resuscitation ahead of the laryngoscope.

**Key points.**
- Resuscitate before you intubate: in hemorrhagic shock, restore volume before induction; two IV/IO lines of 16 g or larger before drugs; blood pressure every 1-2 minutes during the procedure; be ready with fluids or vasopressors.
- Preoxygenation for about 3 minutes at the highest available flow, plus nasal cannula at 15 L/min left on throughout for apneic oxygenation; head up if possible.
- Induction: ketamine 2 mg/kg IV/IO first line, etomidate 0.3 mg/kg second line, with reduced doses in unstable patients and always sedation before paralysis.
- Paralytics: rocuronium 1.2 mg/kg, succinylcholine 1.5 mg/kg or vecuronium 0.1 mg/kg, only for trained providers or under telemedicine direction.
- Video laryngoscopy is the best option, especially for less experienced operators, with direct laryngoscopy competence maintained for soiled airways.
- Cricothyrotomy confirmed by waveform capnography; no surgical airway under 12 years (needle technique instead); an awake cricothyrotomy pathway using ketamine and local anesthetic is included. Remove the front of the collar for RSI.

**Caveats.** Written for deployed military care with telemedicine support; the ketamine-first choice predates, and does not engage with, the December 2025 RSI trial in which ketamine caused more peri-intubation collapse than etomidate in a mostly septic population.

**For the anesthesiologist.** The physiologic sequencing (volume, then drug, then tube) is the transferable lesson for the civilian trauma bay and for the hybrid OR.

posts.headline: FDA grants De Novo clearance to VitaSmart, the first US device for hypothermic oxygenated liver perfusion
posts.summary: Bridge to Life announced FDA De Novo clearance of its VitaSmart HOPE system for hypothermic oxygenated perfusion of DBD and DCD donor livers after cold storage, based on the 219-patient Bridge to HOPE trial. US launch was planned for Q1 2026.
takeHome: First FDA-cleared cold machine perfusion device for liver; indication covers DBD and DCD within defined donor criteria.
No fixed maximum perfusion duration in the labeling, so extended HOPE and daytime transplantation become feasible.
Programs now have a cheaper alternative to normothermic perfusion for marginal grafts.
posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters.** Until this clearance, the only FDA-approved liver perfusion platforms in the US were normothermic (OrganOx metra, TransMedics OCS Liver). HOPE is simpler and less expensive, and European trials had already shown lower biliary complications and graft loss with DCD grafts. The De Novo pathway also creates a new device classification, which eases future entrants.

**What was cleared.** The VitaSmart Hypothermic Oxygenated Perfusion system is indicated for end-ischemic HOPE of donor livers after static cold storage and before transplantation, for both DBD and DCD donors within defined donor criteria. The labeling does not specify a maximum perfusion duration. The supporting evidence came from the Bridge to HOPE pivotal RCT (219 recipients, 15 US centers), which reported a reduction in early allograft dysfunction from 37% to 20%.

**Context.** In September 2025, OrganOx metra separately received FDA approval for operation during air transport, so livers can now be perfused continuously from distant donor hospitals. Together these decisions mean more marginal grafts will arrive viable and more operations will be scheduled rather than done at 3 a.m.

**Caveats.** Clearance was based on a surrogate endpoint. Real-world duration limits, staffing, and reimbursement will be set by each program.

**For the anesthesiologist.** Anticipate a wider donor pool, more DCD grafts, and increasing use of prolonged perfusion to shift cases into daytime. Ask your surgeons which grafts are coming off a pump and what preservation time was; graft quality assessment is shifting from cold-ischemia time to perfusion metrics.

posts.headline: PROSPECT 2025: epidural or paravertebral stays first line after open thoracotomy; ESP and intercostal are second line
posts.summary: The PROSPECT working group reviewed 100 studies from 2015 to 2024 with a modified Delphi process and updated its procedure-specific pain recommendations for open thoracotomy.
takeHome: First line: thoracic epidural or paravertebral block plus paracetamol and NSAID/COX-2 inhibitor for all patients.
Second line when neuraxial or paravertebral is not possible: erector spinae, rhomboid intercostal or intercostal nerve blocks.
Low-level evidence supports acupuncture or cryoanalgesia only when regional techniques cannot be performed.
posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters.** PROSPECT recommendations are the procedure-specific analgesia reference most ERAS protocols cite. Open thoracotomy remains one of the most painful operations and the one where the choice of regional technique is most contested.

**What they did.** The PROSPECT working group searched for randomised trials, systematic reviews and meta-analyses published 2015 to 2024 on pain interventions after open thoracotomy. 100 studies were included. Risk of bias was assessed with RoB 2, certainty with GRADE, and recommendations were agreed through comments from all members and a modified Delphi process.

**Recommendations.**
- Basic analgesia for everyone: paracetamol plus an NSAID or COX-2 selective inhibitor.
- First-line regional analgesia: thoracic epidural analgesia or paravertebral block.
- Second line: erector spinae plane, rhomboid intercostal or intercostal nerve blocks.
- Acupuncture or cryoanalgesia may be considered when regional techniques cannot be performed (low-level evidence).
- Choice of surgical technique, physiotherapy and patient education are also recommended.

**What changed.** The group now lets clinician preference decide between epidural and paravertebral rather than ranking one above the other, and positions the newer fascial plane blocks explicitly as fallbacks rather than equals.

**Caveats.** Many included trials are small and single centre; chronic post-thoracotomy pain outcomes remain thin. VATS has its own PROSPECT document.

**What it means.** If your thoracotomy pathway has drifted to ESP-only, this is the document that says the epidural or paravertebral is still the standard, with fascial plane blocks reserved for patients who cannot have them.

posts.headline: Network meta-analysis of 885 trials: regional anaesthesia, not opioid avoidance, drives postoperative pain control
posts.summary: A systematic review and network meta-analysis compared six strategies combining opioid-free or opioid-inclusive anaesthesia with or without regional anaesthesia across 885 randomised trials in adults.
takeHome: Regional anaesthesia was the key determinant of lower pain; intraoperative opioids added little when a block worked.
Without regional anaesthesia, opioid-free and opioid-inclusive techniques were similar for pain; OFA had less PONV.
Spend effort on a good block rather than on eliminating opioids.
posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters.** The opioid-free anaesthesia debate has generated hundreds of small trials and strong opinions. This network meta-analysis reframes the question: is it the absence of opioid, or the presence of a block, that improves pain?

**What they did.** Systematic review and network meta-analysis of randomised trials in adults comparing six anaesthetic strategies defined by opioid use (opioid-free versus opioid-inclusive) and by the presence or absence of regional anaesthesia. Primary outcome: postoperative pain; secondary outcomes included opioid consumption, recovery times and complications. 885 trials were included.

**What they found.**
- Regional anaesthesia was the key determinant of improved postoperative pain control.
- When regional anaesthesia was effective, intraoperative opioids added little benefit.
- Without regional anaesthesia, neither opioid-free nor opioid-inclusive approaches clearly outperformed the other for pain.
- Opioid-free approaches were associated with fewer cases of postoperative nausea and vomiting.

**Caveats.** Network meta-analyses inherit the heterogeneity of their inputs: surgical procedures, block types, OFA recipes and pain time points varied widely, and many included trials are small. Treat the ranking as directional rather than as effect sizes you can quote to a patient.

**What it means.** For the thoracic and cardiac anaesthesiologist the message is pragmatic: invest in the paravertebral, epidural or fascial plane block and use opioids sparingly on top. Removing opioids entirely mainly buys less nausea. The authors state that regional anaesthesia should be preferred where feasible.

posts.headline: First randomised data: routine VA-ECMO vs off-pump lung transplant shows no PGD difference at interim look
posts.summary: A six-centre US trial (target 228) randomises bilateral lung transplant recipients without significant pulmonary hypertension to planned VA-ECMO or off-pump surgery. At the first pre-specified interim analysis of 75 patients, grade 3 primary graft dysfunction at 48-72 h was 13.6% vs 19.4%, not significant.
takeHome: Grade 3 PGD at 48-72 h: 13.6% (VA-ECMO) vs 19.4% (off-pump), p=0.51; 13% of off-pump patients converted to ECMO.
VA-ECMO arm received more fresh frozen plasma and platelets; no significant safety or secondary-endpoint differences.
Interim only (n=75 of 228): too early to change practice, but the retrospective 'ECMO is worse' signal is not reproduced so far.
posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters.** Planned intraoperative VA-ECMO versus off-pump bilateral lung transplantation is one of the most debated choices in transplant anaesthesia. Retrospective series point both ways, and a 2025 meta-analysis of six retrospective studies suggested worse early outcomes with ECMO. This is the first randomised comparison.

**What they did.** Six US centres randomise adults having bilateral lung transplantation with mean pulmonary artery pressure of 35 mmHg or less, 1:1 to planned VA-ECMO or off-pump surgery (NCT05547698). Exclusions include multiorgan transplant, DCD donors, retransplantation, planned postoperative ECMO, prior lung surgery or pleurodesis, and preoperative ECMO or mechanical ventilation. Conversion to ECMO for instability is allowed. The target of 228 patients is powered to detect a 15-point absolute reduction in grade 3 PGD at 48-72 h. This paper reports the first pre-specified interim analysis, first shown as a late-breaker at AATS in May 2025.

**What they found (n=75).**
- 44 randomised to VA-ECMO, 31 to off-pump; 4 off-pump patients (12.9%) converted.
- Grade 3 PGD at 48-72 h: 6/44 (13.6%) vs 6/31 (19.4%), p=0.51.
- No significant differences in 90-day mortality, the 15 secondary endpoints or serious graft-related adverse events.
- The VA-ECMO arm received significantly more fresh frozen plasma and platelets.

**Caveats.** A third of the planned sample; the authors say so and continue enrolling. Patients with pulmonary hypertension, who most often get ECMO anyway, were excluded, as were DCD and bridged patients.

**What it means.** Nothing to change yet. But the fear that routine ECMO worsens PGD is not supported so far, and the transfusion cost of ECMO is real and measurable. Watch for the final analysis.

posts.headline: Peripartum cardiac arrest under anesthesia care: 11 per 100,000 deliveries, mostly hemorrhage and AFE
posts.summary: MPOG analysis of 778,102 deliveries at 60 US hospitals (2015-2022) with chart-adjudicated cardiac arrests occurring during anesthetic care.
takeHome: 87 arrests (11.2 per 100,000); hemorrhage 40%, amniotic fluid embolism 31%, anesthesia-related 11.5%.
Two-thirds happened during cesarean; ROSC 77%, 30-day survival 68%.
Possible guideline deviations in 18%: drill high-block, failed-airway and massive-hemorrhage responses.
posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters.** Maternal cardiac arrest is rare enough that no single department sees enough cases to learn from them. This is the largest US dataset with chart-level adjudication of what actually happened while an anesthesiologist was in the room.

**What they did.** Using the Multicenter Perioperative Outcomes Group database, the authors screened 778,102 deliveries at 60 institutions (2015-2022) with an algorithm combining billing codes, medications, EHR concepts and free text, then had two reviewers adjudicate every flagged chart. Arrests were counted if they occurred during anesthetic care from delivery through 7 days postpartum.

**What they found.** 87 arrests, or 11.2 per 100,000 deliveries (95% CI 9.1-13.8). Hemorrhage caused 40.2% and amniotic fluid embolism 31.0%; anesthesia-related events such as high neuraxial block accounted for 11.5%. Two-thirds (67.8%) occurred during cesarean delivery. ROSC was achieved in 77% and 67.8% survived to 30 days; median post-anesthetic stay was 6 days. Strong clinical associations included pulmonary hypertension, placenta accreta spectrum, ischemic heart disease and stillbirth; demographic associations included age 40 or older, BMI 40 or higher, and Black, Asian or Pacific Islander race. Reviewers flagged potential deviations from society guidelines in 18.4% of arrests.

**Caveats.** Retrospective, limited to MPOG (largely academic) sites, and dependent on documentation quality; arrests outside anesthetic care were not captured.

**For the anesthesiologist.** Hemorrhage and AFE dominate, so massive transfusion readiness and an AFE/ECMO activation pathway matter more than any drug choice. One in nine arrests was ours: high-block recognition, aspiration prevention and failed-airway drills still save lives. The 18% guideline-deviation figure is the quality-improvement target.

posts.headline: New 2025 ACC/AHA ACHD guideline replaces the 2018 document for adults with congenital heart disease
posts.summary: ACC/AHA/HRS/ISACHD/SCAI joint guideline published simultaneously in JACC and Circulation, built on a 2017-2024 evidence review and replacing the 2018 AHA/ACC ACHD guideline.
takeHome: Lesion-by-lesion recommendations updated; this is now the reference when an ACHD patient reaches your OR.
Moderate and complex lesions still belong with ACHD programs, including before elective surgery or delivery.
Re-read the sections on your common referrals: Fontan, tetralogy, systemic right ventricle, Eisenmenger.
posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters.** More adults than children now live with congenital heart disease, and they turn up for non-cardiac surgery, pregnancy, arrhythmia procedures and reoperations in ordinary hospitals. The 2018 ACC/AHA ACHD guideline was the document most of us quoted; it has now been retired.

**What it is.** A full guideline from the ACC/AHA Joint Committee on Clinical Practice Guidelines, written with the Heart Rhythm Society, the International Society for Adult Congenital Heart Disease and SCAI, published simultaneously in JACC (87:822-976) and Circulation on 18 December 2025. The writing committee, led by Michelle Gurvitz and Eric Krieger, reviewed literature from 2017 to 2024 across MEDLINE, Embase, Cochrane, AHRQ and CINAHL and updated recommendations throughout.

**What is inside.** The document builds on the 2018 anatomic-and-physiologic classification and carries lesion-specific recommendations across the common diagnoses (shunt lesions, tetralogy of Fallot, transposition with a systemic right ventricle, Fontan circulation, Eisenmenger physiology, coarctation and valve disease) alongside cross-cutting sections on heart failure and transplant, arrhythmia, pulmonary hypertension and reproductive care. JACC also published a Guideline-at-a-Glance and commentaries on adapting it to low-resource settings.

**Caveats.** As with most ACHD evidence, many recommendations rest on observational data and expert consensus; a correction notice followed in Circulation in April 2026. Anesthesia-specific guidance is necessarily brief.

**For the anesthesiologist.** The durable message is unchanged: moderate and complex ACHD patients should be managed in or with an ACHD program, and that includes planning non-cardiac surgery and delivery. For the cardiothoracic anesthesiologist, the Fontan, systemic RV and pulmonary hypertension sections are the ones to re-read before the next adult redo or TEE-guided intervention.

posts.headline: FDA clears first AI that measures Impella inlet-to-annulus distance on TTE, plus AI scan guidance for non-experts
posts.summary: In mid-December 2025 FDA cleared UltraSight's PVAD IQ, machine-learning software that finds the aortic annulus and the pump inlet on transthoracic clips and reports the distance, one day after clearing the company's real-time acquisition guidance for ten standard TTE views.
takeHome: PVAD IQ: 963 clips from 186 patients; distance mean absolute error 0.42 cm; it also flags clips too poor to measure.
UltraSight Guidance steers non-sonographers to parasternal, apical and subcostal views; now runs from handheld to cart systems.
Decision support for a qualified physician only; TEE stays the arbiter for Impella position in the OR.
posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters.** Impella position is checked by echo many times a day in the CVICU and OR, often by whoever happens to be at the bedside. An objective inlet-to-annulus number from a TTE clip is the first AI tool aimed squarely at mechanical support imaging.

**What was cleared.** On December 18, 2025 FDA cleared UltraSight's PVAD IQ Software (K252235; Class II, product code QIH). It is indicated for patients 18 and older with a percutaneous ventricular assist device: machine learning locates the aortic annulus and the pump inlet on transthoracic clips, reports the mean distance between them, and labels each clip acceptable or not for quantitative imaging. Testing on 963 clips from 186 patients, graded against US board-certified sonographers experienced in PVAD echo, gave a distance mean absolute error of 0.42 cm (95% CI 0.38-0.47), acceptability kappa 0.71, and landmark detection AUC 0.92 for the inlet and 0.98 for the annulus.

The day before, FDA cleared UltraSight Guidance (K251416): real-time acquisition guidance for ten standard 2D TTE views (parasternal long and short axis at three levels, apical 2/3/4/5, subcostal four-chamber and IVC) for medical professionals who are not expert sonographers, with a Predetermined Change Control Plan. In January 2026 UltraSight said the platform now runs on handheld, laptop and cart-based systems. Clarius followed on March 2, 2026 with a handheld ejection-fraction AI (K253593; ICC 0.78 against expert readers on 279 exams).

**Caveats.** Bench and retrospective validation only, no outcome data, and labeled as decision support for a qualified physician. Performance through post-sternotomy windows is unknown.

**For us.** Expect ICU nurses and APPs to arrive with a number. Learn exactly what it measures, and keep TEE as the referee when the number and the hemodynamics disagree.

posts.headline: AASLD/AST 2025 guideline sets cardiac work-up and portopulmonary hypertension limits for liver transplant candidates
posts.summary: The first AASLD/AST practice guideline on adult liver transplant candidate evaluation (69 statements, with a companion Liver Transplantation guideline on non-graft complications) formalizes ECG plus comprehensive echo for all, risk-factor-triggered advanced coronary testing, RHC thresholds, and a mPAP/PVR contraindication threshold.
takeHome: Every candidate: ECG plus comprehensive TTE; RVSP over 45 mmHg or abnormal RV triggers right heart catheterization.
On optimized PH therapy, mPAP 45 mmHg with PVR over 3 WU is a contraindication to transplant.
Any MASLD risk factor, CKD, LVH, tobacco, family history, or CAC above zero should prompt advanced CAD testing.
posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters.** Cardiac evaluation before liver transplant has been governed by a 2012 AHA/ACC statement, local algorithms, and a 2022 AHA scientific statement on coronary screening. Anesthesiologists sit on selection committees and need a citable standard. AASLD and AST released two linked practice guidelines on December 17, 2025: candidate evaluation (Hepatology; Dove, Chadha, Lai et al.) and post-transplant non-graft complications (Liver Transplantation; Sharma, Izzy, Ghabril et al.).

**What it says for the perioperative team.**
- ECG and comprehensive transthoracic echocardiography for every candidate.
- Risk-factor-based CAD assessment: a single MASLD risk factor, CKD, LVH, family history of premature CAD, any tobacco history, or coronary calcium above zero should prompt advanced testing (stress echo, coronary CT, or catheterization per a center algorithm built with cardiology). Asymptomatic significant CAD goes to a multidisciplinary team.
- Portopulmonary hypertension: RVSP above 45 mmHg or abnormal RV structure or function on echo mandates right heart catheterization. In patients on optimized therapy directed by a PH specialist, mPAP of 45 mmHg with PVR above 3 Wood units should be considered a contraindication; sustained responders may be transplanted.
- Hepatopulmonary syndrome: agitated-saline contrast echo is the preferred screen, with oximetry and arterial blood gas to grade severity.
- Frailty, sarcopenia and nutrition assessed in all; BMI alone should not exclude; BMI above 40 or below 18.5 triggers muscle mass and nutrition screening.

**Caveats.** Many statements are graded on low-quality evidence (Grade 2-4). The guideline names coronary CT as an option but does not mandate it. No intraoperative TEE recommendation.

**For the anesthesiologist.** Use these thresholds in selection meetings and in preoperative clinic notes. The PH numbers in particular give you a defensible line when a borderline portopulmonary patient is pushed toward listing.

posts.headline: RSI trial: ketamine no better than etomidate for survival, and causes more peri-intubation collapse
posts.summary: A 2,365-patient pragmatic trial in 14 US EDs and ICUs randomized critically ill adults needing emergency intubation to ketamine 1-2 mg/kg or etomidate 0.2-0.3 mg/kg.
takeHome: In-hospital death by day 28: 28.1% ketamine vs 29.1% etomidate; no difference.
Cardiovascular collapse during intubation 22.1% vs 17.0%; worse with sepsis (30.6% vs 20.9%).
Etomidate is back as a reasonable default for the sick, hypotensive patient.
posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters.** The etomidate-versus-ketamine argument has run for two decades: etomidate blunts cortisol, ketamine supposedly protects blood pressure. The RSI trial (Randomized Trial of Sedative Choice for Intubation), published in NEJM online 9 December 2025, is by far the largest head-to-head comparison.

**What they did.** Casey, Semler and the Pragmatic Critical Care Research Group randomized 2,367 critically ill adults (2,365 analyzed) undergoing emergency tracheal intubation at 14 sites to ketamine (1-2 mg/kg actual body weight) or etomidate (0.2-0.3 mg/kg). Trauma patients were excluded. The primary outcome was in-hospital death by day 28.

**What they found.** Mortality was 28.1% (330/1,173) with ketamine vs 29.1% (345/1,186) with etomidate; difference -0.8 points (95% CI -4.5 to 2.9). The sepsis subgroup was similar (38.8% vs 38.2%). The secondary safety outcome of cardiovascular collapse (SBP under 65, new or increased vasopressors, or cardiac arrest) was more frequent with ketamine: 22.1% vs 17.0% (difference 5.1 points, 95% CI 1.9 to 8.3), and the gap widened in sepsis (30.6% vs 20.9%) and in APACHE II of 20 or more (31.4% vs 20.7%). Median time to intubation was 112 vs 103 seconds.

**Caveats.** Open label, no trauma or hemorrhagic shock, and the ketamine doses were full induction doses; many clinicians use far less in shocked patients. Adrenal suppression with etomidate did not translate into mortality harm here.

**For anesthesiologists.** The claim that ketamine is the hemodynamically safe induction agent for the crashing patient does not hold at 1-2 mg/kg. Etomidate at 0.2-0.3 mg/kg remains a sound choice, and reduced-dose induction with a vasopressor in hand matters more than the drug name.

posts.headline: GA-CARES: propofol TIVA does not improve survival after cancer surgery; per-protocol analysis trends the other way
posts.summary: Pragmatic multicenter RCT at five US centers randomized adults undergoing resection of poor-prognosis cancers to exclusive propofol or exclusive volatile anesthesia. In 1,763 intent-to-treat patients, all-cause mortality was 26.1% with propofol versus 22.9% with volatile (HR 1.16, 95% CI 0.96-1.41), with disease-free survival similar.
takeHome: No survival benefit from propofol; ITT HR 1.16 and per-protocol HR 1.31 (P=0.017) pointed toward harm.
Protocol adherence 95.9%; results consistent across subgroups and for disease-free survival.
Together with earlier trials, this should end routine 'TIVA for cancer' practice based on recurrence claims.
posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters.** For 15 years, preclinical and retrospective data suggested propofol preserved anti-tumor immunity and volatile agents promoted recurrence, prompting some centers to adopt TIVA for all cancer resections. Earlier randomized data (breast cancer, 2019) were negative but limited to one tumor type. GA-CARES is the largest randomized test with a mortality endpoint.

**What they did.** Bennett-Guerrero and colleagues randomized adults undergoing resection of cancers with poor outcomes at five US centers 1:1 to exclusive propofol or exclusive volatile anesthesia in a pragmatic, partially blinded design. The primary endpoint was all-cause mortality with at least two years of follow-up; disease-free survival was secondary. Results were published online in Anesthesiology on December 9, 2025 (print January 2026).

**What they found.** Adherence was 95.9%. In the intent-to-treat population (n=1,763) propofol did not improve survival: deaths 26.1% versus 22.9% (HR 1.16, 95% CI 0.96-1.41; P=0.115). In the per-protocol population (n=1,411) more propofol-assigned patients died (25.5% vs 20.0%; HR 1.31, 95% CI 1.05-1.64; P=0.017). Disease-free survival followed the same pattern and subgroups were consistent.

**Caveats.** Mixed tumor types dilute any tumor-specific effect; partial blinding; the per-protocol signal of harm may reflect selection and should not be over-read. The trial cannot speak to regional anesthesia or opioid-sparing strategies.

**For the anesthesiologist.** Choose the anesthetic for the patient (PONV, airway, hemodynamics, emergence), not for presumed oncologic benefit. If your institution has a TIVA-for-cancer policy, this trial is the evidence to revisit it. The result also matters for the environmental-sustainability debate, where some had hoped the cancer data would align with reducing volatile use.

posts.headline: ASA 2026 guideline: fascial plane blocks recommended for cardiothoracic, breast and abdominal surgery pain
posts.summary: The ASA Task Force on Perioperative Pain Management graded the evidence for local and regional analgesia after cardiothoracic surgery, mastectomy and abdominal surgery in adults and children, and issued strong and conditional recommendations for fascial plane blocks.
takeHome: Strong: fascial plane blocks after open abdominal, retroperitoneal, pelvic and mastectomy surgery in adults.
Conditional in adults for cardiothoracic surgery and open hernia repair; strong for open cardiac/thoracic surgery in children.
Authors flag low methodologic quality, inconsistent outcomes and small single-centre trials behind most recommendations.
posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters.** ASA's new procedure-specific guideline on regional analgesia covers the operations cardiothoracic anaesthesiologists do every day: sternotomy, thoracotomy and VATS, mastectomy, and open or minimally invasive abdominal surgery, in adults and children. It is the document administrators, ERAS committees and credentialing bodies will cite.

**What they did.** The ASA Task Force on Perioperative Pain Management reviewed the evidence on whether local and regional techniques reduce pain and opioid requirements in the first 24 hours after these procedures and graded the strength of each recommendation.

**Key recommendations.**
- Adults: strong recommendation for fascial plane blocks to reduce pain and/or opioid use after open abdominal, retroperitoneal, pelvic and mastectomy surgery; also recommended after minimally invasive abdominal procedures.
- Adults: conditional recommendation for fascial plane blocks after cardiothoracic surgery and after open hernia repair.
- Children: strong recommendation for fascial plane blocks after open cardiac or thoracic surgery; conditional for the first 24 hours after open hernia repair.

**Caveats.** The Task Force is blunt that the evidence base is weak: low methodologic quality, inconsistent outcome measurement and small single-centre samples. The conditional grade for adult cardiothoracic surgery reflects that, and several 2025-2026 cardiac block trials (EPOCH CardioLink-10, the BJA paravertebral-versus-ESP noninferiority trial) were published around or after the guideline's evidence cut-off. The guideline does not settle which block, what dose, or single shot versus catheter.

**What it means.** A block after sternotomy, thoracotomy or laparotomy is now guideline-endorsed rather than enthusiast practice. Expect it in ERAS protocols and quality metrics, and expect to be asked why a patient did not get one.

posts.headline: Cryopreserved platelets fail noninferiority for cardiac surgical bleeding and drive more transfusion (CLIP-II)
posts.summary: Double-blind noninferiority RCT at 11 Australian hospitals: 202 transfused cardiac surgical patients received cryopreserved (DMSO-frozen) or standard liquid-stored platelets.
takeHome: Cryopreserved platelets missed noninferiority: 24-h drain output ratio 1.13 (95% CI 0.96-1.34) vs 1.20 margin.
More red cells, plasma, cryo and rescue platelets after cryopreserved units.
Keep them as a contingency product, not a routine substitute.
posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters.** Cryopreserved (DMSO-frozen) platelets keep for years and have been positioned as a solution for remote, military and supply-disrupted settings. CLIP-II is the definitive test in a bleeding population.

**What they did.** Double-blind noninferiority RCT at 11 Australian tertiary hospitals, August 2021 to April 2024. Adults at high risk of platelet transfusion after cardiac surgery were randomized to cryopreserved group O apheresis platelets or standard liquid-stored platelets (up to 3 units), with open-label rescue platelets allowed. 388 were randomized; 202 were transfused and formed the primary analysis (104 vs 98).

**What they found.**
- 24-h ICU chest drain output: 605 vs 535 mL (geometric means); ratio 1.13 (95% CI 0.96-1.34) against a 1.20 margin, so noninferiority was not shown.
- Total drain output 1,273 vs 972 mL (adjusted ratio 1.29, 95% CI 1.06-1.56).
- More red cells in 24 h (52.9 vs 38.8%), more FFP (75.0 vs 50.0%), more cryoprecipitate (71.2 vs 54.1%) and far more rescue liquid platelets (42.3 vs 12.2%).
- Lowest platelet count 103 vs 140 x10^9/L. Day-90 mortality 12.5% vs 5.1%, not powered and not formally compared.

**Caveats.** Transfused-only primary analysis; rescue platelet use probably unblinded clinicians; a companion economic analysis found the product not cost-effective.

**For the anesthesiologist.** Cryopreserved platelets are not a drop-in substitute where liquid platelets exist; if they are all you have, expect more bleeding and more product. The strategic answer for supply, per CHIPS eight months later, is cold storage rather than deep freezing.

posts.headline: JTS REBOA update: partial occlusion preferred, Zone 1 partial up to 2 h, trained non-surgeons may deploy it
posts.summary: The Joint Trauma System revised its REBOA for Hemorrhagic Shock clinical practice guideline (CPG ID 38, Dec 3, 2025, rapid update Apr 22, 2026), shifting from short complete occlusion to prolonged partial occlusion for long evacuations.
takeHome: Partial REBOA now conditionally preferred: proximal SBP 90-110, distal SBP 20-50 mm Hg.
Time limits: complete Zone 1 <=60 min; partial Zone 1 up to 2 h, Zone 3 up to 4 h.
Trained non-surgical teams may deploy partial REBOA when surgery is hours away and blood is failing.
posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters.** Civilian REBOA has been in retreat since UK-REBOA (2023) suggested harm and EAST (March 2025) conditionally recommended against it for unstable subdiaphragmatic bleeding. The US military has gone the other way, rewriting its REBOA guideline (CPG ID 38, December 3, 2025, rapid update April 22, 2026) around partial occlusion for prolonged casualty care.

**What the CPG says.**
- Indications: traumatic arrest without thoracic, neck or upper-extremity bleeding (with concurrent compressions); severe shock or impending arrest from non-compressible truncal hemorrhage below the diaphragm; high thigh amputations where tourniquets fail.
