- Contraindicated in penetrating chest trauma, major thoracic hemorrhage or tamponade; rule out chest bleeding first with tubes, X-ray or ultrasound.
- Zone 1 for most shock, Zone 3 only when intra-abdominal bleeding is excluded; Zone 2 not recommended.
- Occlusion limits: complete Zone 1 up to 60 minutes (ideally under 30); partial Zone 1 ideally up to 2 hours, partial Zone 3 up to 4 hours.
- Partial REBOA is conditionally preferred, requires the pREBOA-PRO catheter and pressure monitoring above and below the balloon, targeting proximal SBP 90-110 and distal SBP 20-50 mm Hg.
- Trained non-surgical teams may deploy partial REBOA only when the casualty would otherwise die before surgery, blood is failing, and surgical handoff is expected within 2 hours (Zone 1) or 4 hours (Zone 3). A fully inflated Zone 1 balloon must never fly.

**Caveats.** Expert consensus for combat casualty care with long evacuation times; none of the partial-occlusion time limits come from randomized data.

**For the anesthesiologist.** If you cover a hybrid OR or a level I centre that receives military or long-transport patients, expect partial REBOA with distal-pressure targets, and plan for the reperfusion hit at deflation.

posts.headline: LEVOECMO: levosimendan does not speed VA-ECMO weaning and doubles ventricular arrhythmias
posts.summary: A French double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in 205 patients on VA-ECMO for cardiogenic shock found that a 24-hour levosimendan infusion did not improve successful weaning at 30 days.
takeHome: Successful weaning was 68.3% in both arms; ECMO duration and 60-day mortality were unchanged.
Ventricular arrhythmias 17.8% versus 8.7%; drug stopped for suspected adverse effects 11.9% versus 3.8%.
No reason to add levosimendan routinely to help wean; weaning still rests on hemodynamics and echo.
posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters.** Levosimendan is given in many European ECMO units to help the heart come off VA-ECMO, on the strength of observational data. LEVOECMO is the first multicenter, double-blind, placebo-controlled test (Combes and the ECMONet group; JAMA, online 1 December 2025).

**What they did.** 205 adults with cardiogenic shock on VA-ECMO for under 48 hours at 11 French ICUs were randomized to a 24-hour infusion of levosimendan (0.15 then 0.20 micrograms/kg/min, no bolus) or placebo. The primary endpoint was successful weaning within 30 days, counted only if the patient was alive, off ECMO and free of other mechanical support or transplant 30 days after decannulation.

**What they found.**
- Successful weaning: 68.3% in both arms (69 of 101 versus 71 of 104); subdistribution hazard ratio 1.02, P = 0.92.
- Median ECMO duration 5 versus 6 days.
- 60-day mortality 27.7% versus 25.0%.
- Ventricular arrhythmias 17.8% versus 8.7%, and the drug was stopped for suspected adverse effects in 11.9% versus 3.8%.

**Caveats.** A weaning endpoint rather than mortality, a mixed shock population, and levosimendan is not available in the US. A second trial, WEANILEVO, stopped early for lack of funding after 82 patients, so this is likely the definitive answer for some time.

**For us.** There is no longer a reason to add levosimendan 'to help wean' as routine; it did nothing for weaning and doubled ventricular arrhythmias. Weaning decisions still rest on hemodynamics and echo during flow reduction, with inodilators reserved for a specific indication.

posts.headline: CLEVELAND trial: pre-incision TAP blocks with liposomal or plain bupivacaine no better than saline
posts.summary: 261 adults having major abdominal surgery were randomised to four-quadrant TAP blocks with liposomal bupivacaine, plain bupivacaine or saline before incision. Opioid use and pain scores at 24, 48 and 72 hours did not differ.
takeHome: 24-h opioid use: 26 vs 33 vs 31 MME; geometric-mean ratio vs placebo 0.86 (liposomal) and 0.91 (plain), both non-significant.
No late benefit from liposomal bupivacaine at 24-72 h, and no difference in time to return of sensation.
Routine single-shot TAP blocks in ERAS pathways for mixed major abdominal surgery add little.
posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters.** TAP blocks are written into most abdominal ERAS pathways, and liposomal bupivacaine is marketed as the way to extend them to 72 hours. The Cleveland Clinic group ran the three-arm trial that tests both assumptions against saline.

**What they did.** Adults having major abdominal surgery (colorectal, gynaecological, hernia repair and others) were randomised 1:1:1 to bilateral four-quadrant TAP blocks before incision with liposomal bupivacaine, plain bupivacaine or saline. Most participants and assessors were blinded; IV patient-controlled opioids were available. Primary question: is 24-hour opioid use higher with saline than with either bupivacaine? Secondary: is 24-48 hour use higher with saline or plain bupivacaine than with liposomal?

**What they found (modified intention to treat, n=261).**
- Median 24-hour opioid use: 26 MME (liposomal, n=89), 33 (plain, n=84), 31 (saline, n=88).
- Ratio of geometric means vs placebo: 0.86 (97.7% CI 0.60-1.24, p=0.36) for liposomal; 0.91 (0.63-1.32, p=0.58) for plain.
- No differences at 24-48 or 48-72 hours, in pain scores, or in time to return of sensation.

**Caveats.** Single institution. A mixed surgical population may hide benefit in a specific operation, and the blocks were single-shot and pre-incision, so the result says nothing about surgeon-placed, catheter or rescue techniques.

**What it means.** For general abdominal surgery under multimodal analgesia, the routine pre-incision TAP block, with or without the expensive drug, adds little. Save the time and the liposomal bupivacaine for settings where the evidence is better.

posts.headline: One-hour clear-fluid fasting in children: no extra aspiration risk, same gastric volume and pH, less thirst and PONV
posts.summary: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 8 RCTs (1,234 children) comparing shorter with longer preoperative fasting before elective paediatric procedures.
takeHome: Gastric residual volume (SMD -0.05) and pH (SMD -0.11) unchanged with shorter fasting.
Shorter fasting groups had equal or fewer PONV, thirst and hunger; no aspiration signal at 1 hour or less.
Evidence now backs one-hour clear-fluid policies; the limiting factor is implementation.
posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters.** APAGBI, ESAIC and many children's hospitals have moved to 1-hour clear fluids, while the 2023 ASA update stopped at carbohydrate drinks 2 hours before, but the randomised evidence for liberal paediatric fasting had never been pooled.

**What they did.** Systematic review of MEDLINE, Embase, Web of Science, CINAHL and CENTRAL to August 2024 for RCTs comparing shorter with longer preoperative fasting in children having elective procedures, with pooled standardised mean differences and Cochrane risk-of-bias assessment. Eight trials with 1,234 children were included.

**What they found.** Shorter fasting did not increase gastric residual volume (SMD -0.05, 95% CI -0.17 to 0.07) or lower gastric pH (SMD -0.11, -0.31 to 0.09), the two surrogate markers for aspiration risk. Children fasted for shorter periods had equal or lower rates of postoperative nausea and vomiting, thirst and hunger. Clear-fluid fasting of 1 hour or less was not associated with pulmonary aspiration.

**Caveats.** Aspiration is too rare for 1,234 children to detect a true difference; the conclusion rests on surrogates plus the large observational experience (EUROFAST and others). Trials were heterogeneous in what counted as a clear fluid and in the volumes allowed.

**For the anesthesiologist.** The evidence now runs in one direction: a 1-hour clear-fluid rule is physiologically safe and leaves children less miserable, less dehydrated at induction and less nauseated afterwards. The remaining problem is operational, as the companion BJA piece on implementation (Sip, don't skip) argues. If your unit still writes nil by mouth after midnight for children, this is the paper to bring to the next committee.

posts.headline: APSF and ISMP: remove tranexamic acid vials from perioperative areas to stop fatal intrathecal injections
posts.summary: A joint APSF/ISMP announcement (November 26, 2025) responded to recurring wrong-drug, wrong-route errors in which IV tranexamic acid was injected intrathecally instead of bupivacaine or ropivacaine, with mortality up to 50%. It calls for premixed IV bags only, barcode verification and NRFit connectors.
takeHome: Intrathecal TXA is a never event: seizures, paraplegia, cardiovascular collapse, death; most cases in arthroplasty.
Remove TXA vials and ampules from perioperative areas; stock only premixed 1 g/100 mL IV bags.
Education and double checks are judged insufficient; use barcode scanning and NRFit forcing functions.
posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters.** Look-alike vials of tranexamic acid and local anesthetic, stored side by side in ORs and labor units, keep producing catastrophic intrathecal TXA injections. The FDA had already added a boxed warning and neuraxial contraindication to TXA labeling. In August 2026 the issue returned to national headlines when SOAP, APSF and ASA issued a joint statement after reported neuraxial medication errors harmed patients in Nashville, Tennessee, and reaffirmed that spinal anesthesia itself is safe when given with the correct drug.

**What the alert says.** On November 26, 2025, APSF and the Institute for Safe Medication Practices jointly identified the risk factors: similar vials or ampules, shared storage locations, use in the same operations (most catastrophic errors in orthopedic arthroplasty), and stocking in areas without routine barcode scanning (perioperative units, labor and delivery, emergency departments). Reported mortality is up to 50%, with permanent neurologic injury in survivors.

**Recommendations.**
- Remove TXA vials and ampules from perioperative areas; stock only ready-to-administer premixed IV bags (1,000 mg/100 mL); standardize on one concentration.
- Add high-leverage safeguards: barcode or machine-readable verification at the point of care, NRFit connectors for neuraxial drugs, fewer practitioner-prepared syringes.
- Institutional and regulatory support for safer packaging and distribution.
- Non-punitive reporting to internal systems, FDA MedWatch and ISMP, with peer support for involved clinicians.

**Caveats.** A consensus safety alert, not a study; premixed bags raise cost and waste questions for topical and low-dose uses, which the alert suggests handling by failure mode and effects analysis.

**For the anesthesiologist.** Audit where TXA lives in your ORs and block rooms today. This alert, the FDA labeling, the October 2025 revision of the ASA neuraxial medication-error statement and the Nashville events together make a TXA vial on a spinal tray indefensible.

posts.headline: 1 in 13 patients feels pain during cesarean under neuraxial; epidural top-ups are the worst offenders
posts.summary: Prospective 8-week snapshot at 15 US and Canadian centers: 3,693 cesarean patients were asked on postpartum day 1 whether they felt pain during surgery.
takeHome: Overall 7.6% reported intraoperative pain; median score 6/10 among those who did.
Spinal lowest (3.7% elective); epidural top-up highest (12-13%); CSE and DPE in between.
Ask every patient about pain on day 1 and audit your own top-up and conversion practice.
posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters.** Pain during cesarean under neuraxial anesthesia is the leading cause of successful litigation against obstetric anesthesiologists and a major driver of birth trauma, yet almost all prior incidence data were retrospective or single-center.

**What they did.** The MID-CD collaborators ran an 8-week prospective cohort at 15 centers in the United States and Canada. Every patient who had a cesarean under neuraxial anesthesia was interviewed on postpartum day 1: did you feel pain during surgery, how bad on a 0-10 scale, how was it treated, and were you satisfied?

**What they found.** Of 3,693 patients, 282 (7.6%; 95% CI 6.8-8.5%) reported intraoperative pain, with a median score of 6/10 (IQR 4-8). Technique mattered a lot. In elective cases pain was reported after 3.7% of spinals, 9.2% of CSEs and 12.2% of epidural top-ups. In non-elective cases: spinal 5.7%, CSE 7.1%, dural puncture epidural 8.0%, epidural top-up 13.2%.

**Caveats.** Day-1 recall is subjective and the study could not separate pressure from pain or adjudicate block adequacy. Centers were academic North American units, so your numbers may differ.

**For the anesthesiologist.** Treat 7.6% as the benchmark and measure your own rate. The top-up data are the actionable part: a labor epidural that needed frequent rescue is a poor candidate for conversion, and a low threshold for a fresh spinal, or for honest counselling about general anesthesia, is justified. Two accompanying editorials in Anesthesiology (Landau; Cheruku) argue this should become a tracked quality metric.

posts.headline: OPTN safety notice: transect and vent each arch vessel before NRP, no single clamp, no paralytics, report reperfusion
posts.summary: After verified reports of unintended brain reperfusion during normothermic regional perfusion, the OPTN and HRSA issued national technique requirements for DCD recovery, followed by a 2026 update and Board-approved DCD policy changes.
takeHome: TA-NRP: individually occlude, transect and drain the brachiocephalic, left carotid and left subclavian arteries before perfusion.
No neuromuscular blockers during NRP; any sign of life returns the donor to the primary team.
Document vessel transection times, rehearse clamp-failure contingencies at the time-out, report cerebral reperfusion to OPTN.
posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters.** Thoraco-abdominal normothermic regional perfusion (TA-NRP) is how a growing share of DCD hearts are recovered, and the ethics hinge on no blood reaching the brain. The OPTN has received verified reports of unintended brain and brainstem reperfusion after NRP began, blamed on collateral flow, aberrant anatomy or clamp failure. The 21 November 2025 notice from OPTN President John Magee, issued with HRSA, is the first national instruction on technique.

**What it requires or recommends.**
- TA-NRP: individually occlude the brachiocephalic, left common carotid and left subclavian arteries near their origins, then transect each and let it drain to atmosphere before perfusion begins. 'Occlusion of multiple vessels with a single clamp is not appropriate.' Document each transected vessel and the time of the last one.
- Abdominal NRP: occlude the aorta above the celiac origin and transect the proximal aorta above it so it drains before perfusion; document method and time.
- Review the vessel-securing plan at the pre-recovery time-out, with contingencies for failed occlusion or clamp dislodgement.
- Report every observed cerebral reperfusion through the OPTN Patient Safety Reporting Portal.

**Follow-ups.** A 13 May 2026 update added that paralytic agents should not be used during NRP because they can mask signs of life, and that any sign of life returns the donor to the primary team. On 20 August 2026 the OPTN Board approved DCD policy changes including a standardized five-minute minimum wait after circulatory cessation and a formal process to pause a case.

**Caveats.** The technique recommendations are not yet formal OPTN policy; an NRP Workgroup is drafting policy for public comment.

**For us.** Anesthesiologists who manage DCD donors or attend recoveries are inside this. No neuromuscular blockers during NRP, insist on the time-out, and know the contingency plan before the knife goes down.

posts.headline: DOCS: 12 hours of dexmedetomidine did not reduce death or major complications after on-pump cardiac surgery
posts.summary: Multicenter, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of 1,073 adults in China given dexmedetomidine 0.4 mcg/kg/h or saline for 12 hours from induction, published in BJA.
takeHome: Major complications 30% vs 32% (RR 0.93); in-hospital death 1.9% vs 2.8%; no significant difference.
Only heart block differed between groups; stroke, MI, cardiac arrest and safety measures were the same.
Use dexmedetomidine for sedation or delirium if you like it, not as an organ-protection drug.
posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters.** Dexmedetomidine has been sold for a decade as cardioprotective, renoprotective and delirium-sparing in cardiac surgery, largely on small trials and observational data. DECADE already dented the delirium claim. DOCS asked the bigger question: does it change hard outcomes?

**What they did.** Nine hospitals in China randomized adults having cardiac surgery with cardiopulmonary bypass (mean age 54, 46% women) to dexmedetomidine 0.4 mcg/kg/h or saline for 12 hours starting at induction; 1,073 completed the study. Co-primary outcomes were in-hospital mortality and major complications (stroke, MI, heart block, cardiac arrest), analyzed by intention to treat.

**What they found.**
- Major complications: 161/536 (30%) vs 169/537 (32%), RR 0.93 (95% CI 0.72-1.21), P=0.66.
- In-hospital death: 10 (1.9%) vs 15 (2.8%), OR 0.66 (0.29-1.49), P=0.32.
- Individual complications did not differ except heart block; safety outcomes and process measures were similar.

**Caveats.** A relatively young population (mean age 54); a single dosing regimen; the one component that differed was heart block, and the abstract does not say in which direction, though bradyarrhythmia is a known dexmedetomidine effect. Delirium was not the primary target.

**For the anesthesiologist.** An editorial in Anaesthesia asked whether the case is now closed, and for organ protection it probably is. If you run dexmedetomidine for a smoother emergence or less agitation in the ICU, that is a reasonable preference; expect bradycardia and conduction slowing, and do not expect fewer strokes, infarcts or deaths.

posts.headline: ESICM 2025 shock guideline: echo first for shock type, capillary refill and dynamic indices before more fluid
posts.summary: ESICM's first circulatory shock and hemodynamic monitoring guideline since 2014 issues 50 statements that make echocardiography the first-line test for shock type and set expectations for perfusion and fluid-responsiveness monitoring.
takeHome: Echocardiography is the first-line imaging modality to determine the type of shock.
Follow capillary refill time, skin temperature and mottling; assess fluid responsiveness with dynamic indices before more fluid.
Arterial line for vasopressor-dependent or non-responding shock; monitor cardiac output in non-responders.
posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters.** This is the first ESICM guideline on circulatory shock and hemodynamic monitoring since 2014 (Monnet and colleagues, Intensive Care Med, online 14 November 2025). It defines what standard monitoring means in a European ICU and it leans heavily on echocardiography.

**What they did.** A panel produced 50 statements, most of them ungraded good-practice statements, with a smaller set of graded recommendations.

**What it says.**
- Echocardiography is the first-line imaging tool to establish the type of shock (a graded recommendation). LV and RV dysfunction phenotypes may carry prognostic value.
- Skin perfusion should be followed with capillary refill time, supplemented by skin temperature and mottling.
- In persistent shock after initial fluids, fluid responsiveness should be assessed before giving more, and dynamic indices are preferred over static preload markers.
- An arterial catheter is recommended for shock not responding to initial therapy or needing vasopressors; cardiac output and/or stroke volume should be monitored in non-responders.
- With a central line, follow serial ScvO2 and the veno-arterial CO2 gap, and record CVP.

**Caveats.** A general shock guideline, not a cardiogenic shock or MCS document. Specific positions on pulmonary artery catheters, inotrope choice and device escalation sit with the cardiology and surgical guidelines, and the accessible abstract did not detail vasopressor recommendations.

**For us.** It formalizes point-of-care echo as the entry test for undifferentiated shock and treats capillary refill and dynamic indices as expected practice. For a TEE-trained anesthesiologist covering the ICU, this is the document that says the probe comes first.

posts.headline: PROTHOR: high PEEP plus recruitment does not cut pulmonary complications after thoracic surgery
posts.summary: 2,200 adults having open or thoracoscopic lung surgery with one-lung ventilation at 74 sites in 28 countries were randomised to PEEP 10 cmH2O with recruitment manoeuvres or PEEP 5 without. Postoperative pulmonary complications were the same; intraoperative hypotension more than doubled with high PEEP.
takeHome: PEEP 10 + recruitment vs PEEP 5 during OLV: pulmonary complications 53.6% vs 56.4%, not different.
High PEEP: more hypotension (37% vs 14%) and new arrhythmias; low PEEP: more hypoxaemia rescue (8.8% vs 3.3%).
Pick PEEP by the patient's gas exchange and haemodynamics, not by a fixed 'open lung' rule.
posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters.** Whether to run high PEEP with recruitment during one-lung ventilation has been argued for 20 years, mostly on physiology and small trials. PROTHOR is the first adequately powered answer.

**What they did.** ESAIC Clinical Trials Network trial at 74 sites in 28 countries (January 2017 to February 2024). 2,200 adults with BMI under 35 having open or video-assisted thoracic surgery requiring OLV were randomised to PEEP 10 cmH2O plus periodic recruitment manoeuvres or PEEP 5 cmH2O without routine recruitment. Both arms used protective tidal volumes. Primary outcome: a composite of postoperative pulmonary complications over the first 5 days, assessed by masked observers.

**What they found.**
- PPCs 555/1,036 (53.6%) with high PEEP vs 592/1,049 (56.4%) with low PEEP; absolute difference -2.7 points (95% CI -6.4 to 1.0), p=0.155.
- Intraoperative complications 49.8% vs 31.3%: hypotension 37.3% vs 14.3%, new arrhythmias 9.9% vs 3.9%.
- Hypoxaemia needing rescue manoeuvres 8.8% with low PEEP vs 3.3% with high PEEP.
- Extrapulmonary complications (10.6% vs 10.2%) and adverse events similar.

**Caveats.** The event rate is high because the composite is broad. BMI over 35 was excluded, so the obese thoracic patient remains unstudied. PEEP was fixed rather than individualised, a point raised in a Lancet Respir Med correspondence in February 2026.

**Bottom line.** Neither strategy wins on complications. High PEEP buys oxygenation at the price of hypotension and arrhythmia; low PEEP buys stability at the price of more desaturation. The authors' own interpretation: choose lung expansion or permissive atelectasis according to each patient's gas exchange and haemodynamics, which can change during the case. Keep the pressor and the recruitment manoeuvre both within reach.

posts.headline: EchoPrime: an echo foundation model trained on 12 million clips reads whole studies and beats single-task AI
posts.summary: Cedars-Sinai and UCLA trained a video-based vision-language model on more than 12 million echocardiogram video-report pairs; it interprets entire studies and matched or beat cardiologists on paired reads in retrospective testing.
takeHome: Mean AUCs 0.85-0.92 across 23 benchmarks and five health systems; LVEF mean absolute error 4.79 points.
Balanced accuracy 0.89 versus 0.82 for cardiologists on paired studies, but every dataset was retrospective.
Not FDA cleared and not validated for TEE; wait for prospective trials before trusting it near the OR.
posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters.** Most cleared echo AI does one thing: EF, strain, a single valve. EchoPrime is the first study-level model in a top-tier journal that looks at every clip of an exam and produces the interpretation, which is what a human reader actually does.

**What they did.** Milos Vukadinovic, David Ouyang and colleagues at Cedars-Sinai and UCLA trained a video-based vision-language model on more than 12 million echo video-report pairs with contrastive learning, added a view classifier (one-versus-rest AUC 0.997 across 58 standard views) and an anatomical attention module that weights each clip by its relevance to each cardiac structure, then generates study-level interpretations by retrieval-augmented interpretation. Published online in Nature on November 11, 2025 (650:970-977; DOI 10.1038/s41586-025-09850-x).

**What they found.** Across five health systems it reached mean AUCs of 0.85 to 0.92 on classification tasks over 23 benchmarks and outperformed the earlier foundation models BioMedCLIP and EchoCLIP; LVEF mean absolute error was 4.79 versus 26.93 and 7.00. It matched or exceeded task-specific models on several tasks, including mitral and tricuspid regurgitation detection. Against cardiologists on paired studies, balanced accuracy was 0.89 versus 0.82.

**Caveats.** All data were collected retrospectively; the authors themselves say prospective, real-world studies of human-computer interaction and clinical acceptability are needed. Nothing here is validated for intraoperative TEE, and there is no regulatory clearance.

**For us.** This is the direction of travel: a model that sees the whole study and drafts the report. It will reach the preop echo report long before it reaches the OR, so start thinking now about how you will verify an AI-drafted read you are about to act on.

posts.headline: Liberal transfusion after major surgery did not cut death or ischemic events in high-cardiac-risk veterans (TOP)
posts.summary: JAMA randomized trial of 1,424 veterans at high cardiac risk with anemia after major vascular or general surgery, transfused at hemoglobin below 10 g/dL (liberal) or below 7 g/dL (restrictive), presented at AHA 2025.
takeHome: 90-day death, MI, revascularization, AKI or stroke: 9.1% liberal vs 10.1% restrictive, RR 0.90, not significant.
Secondary cardiac complications (arrhythmia, heart failure, arrest) lower with liberal strategy: 5.9% vs 9.9%.
A trigger of 7 g/dL remains defensible after noncardiac surgery even with coronary disease; watch for heart failure.
posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters.** Restrictive triggers are standard, but patients with coronary disease were always the exception people argued about. TOP is the largest trial to test the question in the postoperative period specifically.

**What they did.** At 16 VA medical centers, 1,424 veterans at high cardiac risk who became anemic after major vascular or general surgery were randomized to transfusion for hemoglobin below 10 g/dL or below 7 g/dL, with 90-day follow-up. Hemoglobin separated by about 2 g/dL at day 5. Panos Kougias presented it at AHA 2025 with simultaneous JAMA publication.

**What they found.**
- Primary composite (death, MI, coronary revascularization, acute kidney failure, ischemic stroke at 90 days): 9.1% liberal vs 10.1% restrictive, RR 0.90 (95% CI 0.65-1.24).
- Secondary cardiac complications other than MI (arrhythmia, heart failure, cardiac arrest): 5.9% vs 9.9%, RR 0.59 (99% CI 0.36-0.98). The authors call this hypothesis-generating.

**Caveats.** Single-blind, so clinicians knew the arm; protocol violations were more common in the liberal group (8.7% vs 3.8%); a US veteran population that may not generalize; the confidence interval does not exclude a modest benefit.

**For the anesthesiologist.** This is noncardiac surgery, but it is the population cardiac anesthesiologists get consulted about. A 7 g/dL trigger did not cost ischemic events. The heart failure and arrhythmia signal is the one to keep an eye on in older patients with reduced ejection fraction, and it echoes the TRICS III cardiac surgery data where a restrictive strategy was noninferior. It does not change cardiac surgery triggers.

posts.headline: DAS 2025 intubation guidelines: 65 recommendations, Plan A to D kept, and a new focus on first-attempt success
posts.summary: The Difficult Airway Society replaced its 2015 unanticipated difficult intubation guideline with a 2025 version in BJA (online 7 November 2025), built on a systematic review of 1,241 papers and a three-round Delphi process.
takeHome: Plan A to D stays: tracheal intubation, supraglottic airway ventilation, facemask ventilation, emergency front-of-neck airway.
65 recommendations now cover peroxygenation, RSI, the physiologically difficult airway, obesity, human factors, POCUS, documentation and training.
The emphasis moves from managing failure to maximizing success: first-attempt intubation and continuous oxygen delivery.
posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters.** The 2015 DAS guidelines were the most-cited airway algorithm in the world and shaped Plan A to D thinking, the emphasis on limiting attempts, and front-of-neck access training. Since then, large trials have favored videolaryngoscopy for first-pass success, apneic oxygenation has spread, and human-factors science has matured. A decade on, DAS has issued a full replacement.

**What they did.** Ahmad, El-Boghdadly, Iliff, Dua, Higgs and colleagues, on behalf of the Difficult Airway Society, ran a systematic review of 1,241 papers and a three-round Delphi process with a multidisciplinary expert panel. The result is 65 recommendations, published open access in the British Journal of Anaesthesia (online 7 November 2025; print January 2026, volume 136, pages 283-307).

**What is in it.**
- The four-step algorithm survives: Plan A tracheal intubation, Plan B supraglottic airway ventilation, Plan C facemask ventilation, Plan D emergency front-of-neck airway.
- New or expanded sections cover airway assessment, peroxygenation, rapid sequence induction, the physiologically difficult airway, obesity, human factors, point-of-care ultrasound, documentation and training.
- The central message is to maximize the chance of success, meaning first-attempt intubation and continuous oxygen delivery, rather than mainly managing failure once it happens.
- DAS has released a full education package (table-top drills, simulation scenarios, slide deck, trolley set-up guidance) to support implementation.

**Caveats.** The guideline addresses unanticipated difficulty in adults; obstetric, pediatric, critical-care and cervical-spine guidance remain separate DAS documents. As with all consensus airway algorithms, many recommendations rest on moderate-quality evidence plus expert consensus.

**For the anesthesiologist.** Read the full open-access document, compare it with your institution's airway algorithm and difficult-airway cart, and refresh simulation curricula. If your department still teaches the 2015 algorithm verbatim, it is now out of date.

posts.headline: ARIES-HM3 follow-on: poor INR control nearly doubles LVAD bleeding; aspirin withdrawal benefit holds at any TTR
posts.summary: A pre-specified secondary analysis of the ARIES-HM3 trial shows HeartMate 3 patients spend almost half their time outside the INR range, and that low time in therapeutic range tracks closely with non-surgical bleeding.
takeHome: Median time in therapeutic range was only 56.7%.
Bleeding was 49.2 versus 26.4 events per 100 patient-years with TTR below versus above 56%; stroke did not differ.
Dropping aspirin stayed safe regardless of INR control; women and Black patients had lower TTR.
posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters.** ARIES-HM3 (JAMA 2023) showed HeartMate 3 patients do fine without aspirin and the FDA label dropped aspirin in 2024. The remaining lever is how well the warfarin is run. This pre-specified secondary analysis (Connors and colleagues, Eur Heart J, online 7 November 2025) looks at time in therapeutic range (TTR).

**What they did.** Of 628 randomized patients, 554 had analyzable INR data; they were split at the median TTR of 56%.

**What they found.**
- Median TTR was 56.7%, so patients were out of range almost half the time.
- Success on the primary endpoint was 77% with TTR at or above 56% versus 66.9% below it.
- Non-surgical bleeding at 12 months: 26.4 versus 49.2 events per 100 patient-years, a rate ratio of 1.84 for low TTR.
- Stroke rates did not differ (3.2 versus 2.8 per 100 patient-years).
- The benefit of withdrawing aspirin held regardless of TTR, with no interaction.
- Female sex and Black race independently predicted lower TTR. Predictors of non-surgical bleeding were age 65 or older, aspirin use, TTR under 56% and BUN 30 mg/dL or higher.

**Caveats.** TTR reflects management quality and patient factors; this is association, not a randomized intervention, and it comes from a trial population with protocolized follow-up.

**For us.** When an LVAD patient presents with GI bleeding or for an urgent procedure, their recent INR control is a real risk variable worth asking about. It also strengthens the case for dedicated anticoagulation clinics and for not restarting aspirin after procedures unless there is a specific indication.

posts.headline: EAST conditionally recommends routine TXA for injured patients at risk of bleeding, prehospital and in hospital
posts.summary: Systematic review, meta-analysis and GRADE practice management guideline from the Eastern Association for the Surgery of Trauma on tranexamic acid in injured patients at risk of hemorrhage (online Sept 15, 2025; print November 2025 issue).
takeHome: Conditional recommendation for routine TXA prehospital and in hospital for injured patients at risk of bleeding.
Conditional recommendation for routine TXA in severe hypotension.
No position on a 3-4 g bolus versus 1-2 g; a 2 g single dose remains permissible.
posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters.** After CRASH-2, PATCH-Trauma and the US prehospital trials, trauma services still vary widely on whether TXA is routine, who gets it and at what dose. This is EAST's first dedicated practice management guideline on the question.

**What they did.** A systematic review and meta-analysis using GRADE methodology, addressing four PICO questions on TXA in injured patients at risk of hemorrhage. Published online in the Journal of Trauma and Acute Care Surgery on September 15, 2025 and in the November 2025 print issue (99(5):785-794), first author Ryan Dumas.

**Recommendations.**
- Conditionally recommend routine TXA in the prehospital setting.
- Conditionally recommend routine TXA in the in-hospital setting.
- Conditionally recommend routine TXA in patients with severe hypotension.
- No recommendation for or against a higher initial bolus (3-4 g) versus a standard 1-2 g bolus; the evidence is sparse and heterogeneous.

**Context.** A 2025 NAEMSP/ACEP/ACS-COT joint position statement similarly supports either 1 g IV/IO with a 1 g in-hospital infusion or a single 2 g dose, started within 3 hours of injury in patients with signs of hemorrhagic shock. Six months after EAST, the 24-month PATCH-Trauma follow-up (May 2026) again showed no functional benefit, which is consistent with the conditional (weak) strength of these recommendations.

**For the anesthesiologist.** If your trauma bay gives TXA to everyone who triggers the massive transfusion protocol, EAST now backs you. If you were waiting for permission to give 2 g as a single push to simplify the handoff, the guideline neither endorses nor forbids it; the joint position statement does allow it.

posts.headline: ACS trauma quality programs issue chest wall injury guideline: blocks on par with epidurals, catheters preferred
posts.summary: The American College of Surgeons Trauma Quality Programs released a Best Practices Guideline on management of chest wall injuries (November 2025) covering analgesia, regional anesthesia, respiratory care, ICU triage and rib fixation.
takeHome: Epidural and paravertebral are both endorsed; paravertebral preferred when bleeding risk or anticoagulation is an issue.
Serratus anterior, erector spinae and PECS-2 blocks are acceptable alternatives and do not require holding DVT prophylaxis.
Catheters over single shots; ICU if two of: age >65, >=4 fractures, lung disease, IS <50%, poor pain control.
posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters.** Rib fractures are the commonest reason an anesthesiologist is called to a trauma ward, and practice ranges from oral opioids to thoracic epidurals. The ACS Trauma Quality Programs released a dedicated Best Practices Guideline on chest wall injury in November 2025.

**Analgesia recommendations.**
- Multimodal, opioid-sparing regimens, reassessed at least three times a day, with early acute pain service involvement where available.
- Acetaminophen first (max 4 g/day), NSAIDs or COX-2 inhibitors as adjuncts (ketorolac may be associated with less pneumonia), plus ketamine, dexmedetomidine, lidocaine or muscle relaxants with dosing cautions.
- Regional anesthesia improves respiratory function and pain and reduces opioid need. Epidural and paravertebral blocks are both effective; choose by age, anticoagulation and spine or positioning limits. Paravertebral carries lower bleeding risk.
- Fascial plane blocks are the alternative when neuraxial is unsuitable: serratus anterior block for anterolateral fractures performs comparably to paravertebral or epidural; erector spinae and PECS-2 are described. These blocks generally do not require holding pharmacologic DVT prophylaxis.
- Continuous catheter infusion is preferred over a single bolus.

**Respiratory care and triage.** Incentive spirometry under 1 L or FVC under 1 L flags respiratory failure risk. A suggested ICU pathway admits patients with two or more of: age over 65, four or more fractures, significant pulmonary comorbidity, spirometry below 50% predicted, or poor pain control. Surgical stabilization is discussed with renewed support.

**Caveats.** Best-practice consensus, not a GRADE guideline; single-shot versus catheter data remain thin.

**For the anesthesiologist.** A citable, trauma-society document that puts paravertebral and fascial plane catheters on equal footing with epidurals and tells the trauma team to call you early.

posts.headline: Lidocaine (IV or paravertebral) instead of remifentanil halved pulmonary complications after VATS lung resection
posts.summary: 154 patients having video-assisted thoracoscopic lung resection were randomised to intravenous lidocaine, paravertebral lidocaine or remifentanil infusions during surgery. Pulmonary complications occurred in 22% of lidocaine patients vs 45% with remifentanil, with lower lavage and plasma cytokines.
takeHome: Pulmonary complications 22.3% (lidocaine, either route) vs 45.1% (remifentanil); OR 0.35, 95% CI 0.17-0.72.
Major (Clavien-Dindo III or higher) complications 4% vs 12%; cytokines after one-lung ventilation lower with lidocaine.
Single-centre and modest size: a strong signal for an opioid-sparing, anti-inflammatory strategy, not yet definitive.
posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters.** Remifentanil is the default intraoperative analgesic for VATS in many centres. Lidocaine has anti-inflammatory and analgesic properties and can be given intravenously or through the paravertebral catheter many of us already place. This trial pits them against each other on complications, not just pain.

**What they did.** Single-centre RCT (NCT03905837). 154 patients (mean age 65, 42% women) having video-assisted thoracoscopic lung resection were randomised to one of three intraoperative infusions: intravenous lidocaine with paravertebral saline, paravertebral lidocaine with intravenous saline, or remifentanil with paravertebral saline. Primary outcome: all-cause complications graded by Clavien-Dindo. Cytokines were measured in bronchoalveolar lavage fluid before and after one-lung ventilation and in plasma over the first 24 hours.

**What they found.**
- Major (Clavien-Dindo III or higher) complications: 4.1% paravertebral lidocaine, 3.7% IV lidocaine, 11.8% remifentanil (p=0.037); OR for severe complications with lidocaine 0.44 (95% CI 0.22-0.88).
- Pulmonary complications: 23/103 (22.3%) with pooled lidocaine vs 23/51 (45.1%) with remifentanil; OR 0.35, 95% CI 0.17-0.72, p=0.004.
- Lavage and plasma cytokine levels after OLV were lower in the lidocaine groups.

**Caveats.** Single centre, 154 patients, and an unusually high complication rate in the remifentanil arm. The comparator carries remifentanil's own possible harms, so this is 'lidocaine instead of remifentanil', not 'lidocaine on top'. Published online in September 2025 and in the November 2025 print issue.

**What it means.** A cheap, available change in intraoperative technique with a large effect on an outcome thoracic patients care about. It needs multicentre replication, but running lidocaine rather than remifentanil for VATS is a reasonable choice today.

posts.headline: Intermacs 2025: HeartMate 3-era survival 86% at 1 year and 60% at 5 years, yet US implant volumes have stalled
posts.summary: The 16th STS Intermacs annual report covers 28,029 continuous-flow LVADs implanted 2015 to 2024, focuses on older adults, and argues that transplant-eligible older patients should be offered an individualized LVAD-versus-listing choice.
takeHome: Magnetically levitated LVAD survival: 85.9% at 1 year, 60.2% at 5 years.
Freedom from GI bleeding at 5 years is 73.5%; bleeding remains the dominant late problem.
Patients 65 and older do well, but national implant numbers are flat; authors call for revised eligibility.
posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters.** Intermacs is the US national LVAD registry and its annual report is the benchmark every program is judged against. The 16th report (Nayak and colleagues, Ann Thorac Surg, online 31 October 2025) focuses on outcomes in older adults.

**What they did.** Analysis of 28,029 continuous-flow LVADs implanted from 2015 through 2024, with recent years dominated by fully magnetically levitated pumps.

**What they found.**
- With magnetically levitated devices, 1-year survival is 85.9% and 5-year survival 60.2%.
- Freedom from gastrointestinal bleeding at 5 years is 73.5%; adverse event rates overall are described as low.
- Survival in patients aged 65 and older is also strong, which is the report's central argument.
- National implant volumes have stagnated despite these results.

**The authors' message.** In transplant-eligible older adults, the choice between listing and durable LVAD should be individualized and value-based rather than defaulting to transplant, and eligibility criteria should be revisited to close what they call an implementation gap.

**Caveats.** Registry data, no randomized comparison of LVAD against transplant, and a survival headline does not capture readmissions, driveline infection or quality of life. The older-adult argument assumes centers can select well.

**For us.** The 60% five-year figure is the number to carry into preoperative conversations and consent. The push toward older recipients means more 70-year-olds with a HeartMate 3 presenting for non-cardiac surgery, endoscopy for bleeding, and eventually transplant.

posts.headline: ANDROMEDA-SHOCK-2: capillary refill-guided resuscitation wins on composite, no mortality difference in septic shock
posts.summary: A 1,501-patient trial in 86 ICUs across 19 countries compared a personalized protocol targeting capillary refill time normalization, using pulse pressure, diastolic pressure, fluid responsiveness and bedside echo, against usual care in early septic shock.
takeHome: Win ratio 1.16 (95% CI 1.02-1.33) for the hierarchical composite, driven by shorter organ support.
28-day mortality identical: 26.5% vs 26.6%.
Supports CRT plus echo to decide fluids vs pressors vs inotropes, rather than fixed fluid volumes.
posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters.** The first ANDROMEDA-SHOCK trial (2019) narrowly missed on mortality but suggested capillary refill time (CRT) might be a better resuscitation target than lactate. ANDROMEDA-SHOCK-2 is the much larger follow-up, published in JAMA on 29 October 2025 to coincide with ESICM LIVES.

**What they did.** 1,501 adults with early septic shock were randomized 1:1 to a CRT-targeted personalized hemodynamic resuscitation protocol or usual care. The protocol reassessed CRT every 30 minutes over 6 hours and used pulse pressure, diastolic arterial pressure, dynamic fluid-responsiveness tests and bedside echocardiography to choose between fluid boluses, vasopressor titration and inotropes. The primary outcome was a hierarchical composite of mortality, duration of vital support and hospital length of stay at 28 days, analyzed as a win ratio.

**What they found.** Win ratio 1.16 (95% CI 1.02-1.33; P = .04): 48.9% wins vs 42.1%. The advantage came almost entirely from shorter duration of vital support (26.4% vs 21.1% of wins), not from death (19.1% vs 17.8%). 28-day mortality was 26.5% vs 26.6% (HR 0.99).

**Caveats.** Open label, composite endpoint, and a modest effect that rests on organ-support days. Protocol adherence and the skill required for serial echo assessments will vary outside trial sites.

**For anesthesiologists.** The protocol is essentially what a perioperative echo-trained clinician already does: look at the patient, check perfusion, use dynamic indices and a quick TTE to decide the next move. It is the strongest evidence yet that this individualized approach shortens organ support, even if it does not save lives on its own.

posts.headline: EVERDAC: skipping the routine arterial line in shock is noninferior, with fewer hematomas and line infections
posts.summary: A French 1,010-patient noninferiority trial randomized ICU patients with shock to deferred arterial catheterization (placed only for predefined triggers) or an arterial line within 4 hours.
takeHome: 28-day mortality 34.3% deferred vs 36.9% early; noninferiority met.
Catheter hematoma or bleeding 1% vs 8.2%; 85% of the deferred group never got a line.
Deferral needs a trigger protocol (high-dose pressors, unreliable cuff, frequent sampling).
posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters.** An arterial line on arrival is reflexive in shock, yet the evidence that it changes outcome is thin. EVERDAC, published in NEJM online 29 October 2025 (print 13 November), is the first large randomized test of that reflex.

**What they did.** Nine French ICUs randomized 1,010 adults admitted with shock within 24 hours to early arterial catheterization (within 4 hours) or a deferred strategy: noninvasive cuff monitoring, with a catheter placed only if predefined criteria were met, such as high-dose vasopressors, unreliable noninvasive readings or repeated failed punctures. The primary outcome was 28-day mortality with a 5-percentage-point noninferiority margin.

**What they found.** 28-day mortality was 34.3% (173/504) with deferral vs 36.9% (185/502) with early lines; adjusted difference -3.2 points (95% CI -8.9 to 2.5), noninferiority P = .006. 90-day mortality was 42.7% vs 44%. Organ-support-free days and SOFA trajectories were similar. Catheter-site hematoma or hemorrhage fell from 8.2% to about 1%, and arterial catheter bloodstream infections from 2.7 to 0.6 per 1,000 ICU days. The price was more arterial punctures for blood gases (742 vs 269 per 1,000 ICU days) and more cuff-related discomfort (13.1% vs 9%). About 85% of deferred patients never received a catheter.

**Caveats.** Open label, heterogeneous shock population, and the margin is debatable. The 2026 Surviving Sepsis Campaign still advises invasive monitoring for patients on high or escalating pressor doses, which is exactly the trigger set EVERDAC used.

**For anesthesiologists.** Postoperative or septic patients on low-dose norepinephrine with a reliable cuff do not automatically need a line. Patients on high-dose or multiple pressors, or needing frequent gases, still do.

posts.headline: BICARICU-2: bicarbonate for severe acidemia with AKI cuts dialysis use but not mortality
posts.summary: A 640-patient open-label trial in 43 French ICUs randomized patients with arterial pH 7.20 or below and KDIGO stage 2-3 AKI to IV 4.2% sodium bicarbonate targeting pH 7.30 or no bicarbonate.
takeHome: Day-90 mortality 62.1% vs 61.7%; no difference.
Kidney replacement therapy by day 28: 35% vs 50%, and later when needed.
Reasonable to use bicarbonate to delay or avoid dialysis in severe acidemia with AKI, not to save lives.
posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters.** BICARICU-1 (2018) hinted that bicarbonate helped the subgroup with severe acidemia and AKI. BICARICU-2, published in JAMA on 29 October 2025, was designed to test exactly that subgroup with mortality as the primary endpoint.

**What they did.** 640 adults (627 analyzed) with arterial pH 7.20 or lower and moderate-to-severe AKI were randomized to IV 4.2% sodium bicarbonate titrated to a pH of at least 7.30, or to no bicarbonate. The trial ran in 43 French ICUs from 2019 to 2023 with 90-day follow-up.

**What they found.** Day-90 mortality was 62.1% (195/314) with bicarbonate vs 61.7% (193/313) without; difference 0.4 points (95% CI -7.2 to 8.0). Kidney replacement therapy by day 28 fell from 50% to 35% (difference -15.5 points, 95% CI -23.1 to -7.8), and median time to KRT doubled (30.9 vs 15.5 hours). Day-28 and day-180 mortality and most other secondary outcomes did not differ.

**Caveats.** Open label, and a very sick cohort with 60% mortality in both arms. Whether avoiding dialysis in a patient who dies anyway is meaningful is debatable, but avoiding a dialysis catheter and circuit in a survivor is not trivial. Read it with SODa-BIC (NEJM, June 2026), which found no MAKE30 benefit from short-course bicarbonate in a less acidemic vasopressor-dependent population.

**For anesthesiologists.** In the cardiac or surgical ICU, bicarbonate for pH 7.20 or less with AKI is a defensible tool to buy time and reduce dialysis, with no evidence it changes survival. For milder acidemia the two trials together argue against reflex bicarbonate.

posts.headline: PARTNER 3 at 7 years: TAVR and SAVR still even in low-risk AS; more valve thrombosis after TAVR
posts.summary: Seven-year follow-up of 1,000 low-surgical-risk patients randomized to SAPIEN 3 TAVR or surgical AVR, published in NEJM and presented at TCT 2025.
takeHome: Death, stroke or rehospitalization: 34.6% TAVR vs 37.2% SAVR at 7 years, no significant difference.
Clinically significant valve thrombosis 2.8% vs 0.5% after TAVR; new pacemaker 17.3% vs 12.8%.
Bioprosthetic valve failure similar (6.9% vs 7.3%); durability question stays open past 7 years.
posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters.** Low-risk patients in their 60s and early 70s now routinely ask for TAVR. The honest answer depends on what happens after year five, and PARTNER 3 is the first balloon-expandable low-risk trial to report that far.

**What they did.** 1,000 patients (mean age 73, STS-PROM about 1.9%) were randomized to transfemoral SAPIEN 3 TAVR or surgical AVR. Follow-up at 7 years was available in about 90%. Michael Mack and Martin Leon presented at TCT 2025 on 27 October with simultaneous NEJM publication.

**What they found.**
- Primary composite of death, stroke or valve/procedure/heart-failure rehospitalization: 34.6% TAVR vs 37.2% SAVR (HR 0.87, 95% CI 0.70-1.08). Hierarchical win ratio 1.04, so a wash.
- Death 19.5% vs 16.8%, stroke 8.5% vs 8.1%, rehospitalization 20.6% vs 23.5%, reintervention 6.7% vs 6.0%: none significantly different.
- Clinically significant valve thrombosis 2.8% vs 0.5% (HR 5.7); about half the TAVR cases resolved with anticoagulation.
- New pacemaker 17.3% vs 12.8%. Bioprosthetic valve failure 6.9% vs 7.3%.

**Caveats.** The early TAVR advantage seen at 1-2 years has gone, the mortality curves have drifted numerically toward surgery, and 7 years is still short for a 70-year-old. The trial was not powered for mortality.

**For the anesthesiologist.** Expect the heart team to keep offering both options to low-risk patients; the discussion is now about thrombosis surveillance, pacing and lifetime valve strategy rather than early safety. Evolut Low Risk (self-expanding) reported a similar picture at 6 years, with a reintervention signal after TAVR.

posts.headline: ENCIRCLE: transseptal SAPIEN M3 mitral replacement clears its 1-year bar in 299 patients with no surgical or TEER option
posts.summary: The single-arm pivotal study of Edwards' fully transseptal transcatheter mitral valve replacement system met its one-year performance goal at TCT 2025, with death or heart failure hospitalization in 25.2% against a 45% target.
takeHome: Death 13.9% and HF hospitalization 16.7% at one year in patients unsuitable for surgery or M-TEER.
72% of screened patients were excluded, about 35% for anatomy; valve thrombosis was 6.7% at one year.
A fully transseptal TMVR means TEE-dependent cases under general anesthesia are coming to your hybrid room.
posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters.** Transcatheter mitral replacement has been the therapy that never quite arrived: anchoring, LVOT obstruction and transapical access sank earlier devices. ENCIRCLE is the first large pivotal dataset for a purely transseptal system.

**What they did.** A prospective, single-arm, multicenter study enrolled 299 patients with MR of 3+ or greater who were unsuitable for surgery or M-TEER. The SAPIEN M3 is a two-component system: a dock that encircles the subvalvular apparatus and a balloon-expandable valve, both delivered transseptally. David Daniels presented one-year results at TCT 2025 in San Francisco (PCRonline coverage October 27, 2025); follow-up is planned annually to five years.

**What they found.** The primary composite of all-cause death or HF hospitalization at one year was 25.2%, against a prespecified 45% performance goal (p<0.0001), with death 13.9% and HF hospitalization 16.7%. Valve thrombosis at one year was 6.7%. Screen failure was 72%, roughly 35% for purely anatomic reasons.

**Caveats.** No control arm; the performance goal is a historical benchmark rather than a comparator; 6.7% thrombosis is a real concern in the mitral position; durability beyond one year is unknown; and the treated population is narrow by design. The commentator notes that M-TEER outcomes have improved with device iterations, so head-to-head comparisons with TEER and with optimized medical therapy are still needed.

**For us.** These are TEE-dependent cases from transseptal puncture through dock and valve deployment, in frail patients with primary or secondary MR, and the device is largely indifferent to MR mechanism. If your center is an ENCIRCLE site or plans to be, anesthesia and imaging should be in the planning meetings from the first case, with LVOT obstruction and transseptal bleeding on the checklist.

posts.headline: AHA 2025 CPR guidelines: 200 J first shock for unstable AF, 32-37.5 C for 36 h, no routine mechanical CPR
posts.summary: The AHA published its full 2025 Guidelines for CPR and Emergency Cardiovascular Care in Circulation on 22 October 2025, the first complete rewrite since 2020, covering BLS, ALS, post-arrest care, ECPR systems, special circumstances and pediatrics.
takeHome: Unstable AF or flutter: cardiovert starting at 200 J; sustained polymorphic VT gets immediate defibrillation.
After ROSC in patients not following commands: 32-37.5 C for at least 36 hours; MAP at least 65 mmHg, no preferred pressor.
Routine mechanical CPR not recommended; ECPR is a regionalized system-of-care decision; compress unresponsive, poorly perfused LVAD patients.
posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters.** Every anesthesiologist runs codes, and the AHA guidelines set the algorithms, teaching and documentation standards in US hospitals. The 2025 edition is the first full rewrite since 2020 and the first written after the ECPR trials of the last five years.

**Adult BLS and ALS.** The separate adult, pediatric, in-hospital and out-of-hospital chains collapse into a single chain of survival. Real-time feedback devices are endorsed. Routine mechanical CPR is not recommended because repeated trials found no survival advantage; it may be used during transport or when manual compressions are unsafe. Prone CPR may be considered when turning supine would delay care. Unstable atrial fibrillation or flutter gets synchronized cardioversion starting at 200 J rather than escalating from low energy; sustained polymorphic VT gets immediate defibrillation; double sequential defibrillation stays 2b; head-up CPR is not recommended outside trials.

**ECPR, mechanical support and special circumstances.** ECPR is framed as a system-of-care intervention: a regionalized approach is reasonable, rapid intra-arrest transport for ECPR may be considered only in limited, highly selected adults, cannulators should be experienced in percutaneous technique, and programs should re-audit selection criteria for survival, equity and futility. VA-ECMO is supported for reversible causes including local anesthetic systemic toxicity, beta-blocker and calcium channel blocker poisoning, pulmonary embolism, anaphylaxis and post-cardiac surgery arrest. An unresponsive patient with a durable LVAD and poor perfusion should receive chest compressions. In pregnancy: manual left uterine displacement when the fundus is at or above the umbilicus, airway prioritized, delivery by five minutes.

**Post-arrest care.** A 12-lead ECG after ROSC is Class 1. For adults who do not follow commands, keep temperature between 32 and 37.5 C (Class 1) for at least 36 hours of total temperature control; keep MAP at least 65 mmHg with no preferred vasopressor; temporary mechanical circulatory support may be considered for refractory shock after ROSC (2b); obtain an EEG promptly when myoclonus is present. Prognostication guidance now also addresses prediction of a favorable outcome.

**Caveats.** Most new recommendations are Class 2a or 2b on limited evidence, and intraoperative arrest is not specifically addressed.

**For the anesthesiologist.** Update defibrillator presets (200 J for AF), code carts, ECMO activation criteria and ACLS teaching. The temperature range is wide and permissive: avoid fever, do not chase 33 C. The explicit endorsement of ECMO for local anesthetic toxicity and the instruction to compress LVAD patients are the OR-relevant lines.

posts.headline: ERC 2025: new traumatic cardiac arrest algorithm, REBOA de-emphasised, treat the most urgent reversible cause first
posts.summary: The European Resuscitation Council Guidelines 2025 Special Circumstances chapter (Resuscitation 2025;215:110753, first author Lott) rebuilds the traumatic cardiac arrest pathway and drops REBOA from the algorithm.
takeHome: New traumatic cardiac arrest algorithm: treat the most urgent reversible cause first, not a fixed sequence.
REBOA de-emphasised and dropped from the algorithm; POCUS may be considered to find the cause.
Hemorrhage control, chest decompression or pelvic binder can rightly come before the airway.
posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters.** Traumatic cardiac arrest is the one arrest where standard ALS can actively get in the way. The ERC's 2025 guidelines (approved June 2025, published in Resuscitation volume 215, October 2025) rebuild the traumatic cardiac arrest pathway inside the Special Circumstances chapter.

**What changed from 2021.**
- A new traumatic cardiac arrest algorithm, explicitly framed as a framework for context-sensitive decisions rather than a fixed sequence: treat the most urgent reversible cause first.
- Invasive procedures (chest decompression, thoracotomy for tamponade) are now built into the algorithm, and the role of chest compressions is specified rather than assumed.
- REBOA is de-emphasised: mentioned, but no longer part of the management algorithm.
- Point-of-care ultrasound may be considered to identify reversible causes and guide interventions.

**Worked example from the guideline.** A patient with a stable airway and a pelvic fracture in hemorrhagic shock may benefit more from immediate pelvic binder and rapid transfer than from airway intervention.

**Caveats.** This is European consensus; the AHA's 2025 guidelines, published the same month, handle trauma in their own special-circumstances part and should be read alongside. The sections we verified do not spell out blood-product or termination rules, so check the full text before changing local policy.

**For the anesthesiologist.** You are often the person managing the airway while the surgeon opens the chest. The 2025 framing supports delaying intubation and positive-pressure ventilation when hemorrhage control or decompression is the more urgent reversible cause, and it removes REBOA from the default pathway, consistent with the UK-REBOA trial and the March 2025 EAST guideline.

posts.headline: ISHLT completes its three-part consensus on ECLS in lung transplantation with 50 preoperative recommendations
posts.summary: A 28-author multidisciplinary ISHLT panel used literature review and two Delphi rounds to agree 50 recommendations on when and how to use extracorporeal life support before lung transplantation. With Part II (intraoperative) and Part III (postoperative) it forms the first complete perioperative ECLS consensus, collected in the January 2026 issue.
takeHome: First society consensus covering ECLS indications and management before, during and after lung transplantation.
Part I: 50 preoperative recommendations on bridging indications and management of the bridged candidate reached Delphi consensus.
Open access; a JCVA 'highlights' paper (Feb 2026) summarises the anaesthesia-relevant points.
posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters.** ECLS is used in some form in a large share of bilateral lung transplants, yet until this series there was no society guidance on who should be cannulated, when, how, and how to come off. For the transplant anaesthesiologist this is now the reference document for the multidisciplinary board and the operating room.

**What they did.** The ISHLT Standards and Guidelines Committee commissioned the statement. Experts from surgery, anaesthesiology, critical care, pulmonology, pharmacy, psychology, physiotherapy, nursing and perfusion were split into preoperative, intraoperative and postoperative subgroups. After a literature review, draft recommendations were refined through two Delphi consensus rounds.

**What is in Part I.** Fifty preoperative recommendations met consensus criteria, covering when ECLS is indicated before transplantation (bridging) and the key management issues in a bridged candidate. Published open access (CC BY) online in October 2025 (Reed et al., 28 authors).

**The full set.** Part II (intraoperative considerations, Martin et al., online October 2024) and Part III (postoperative considerations, online June 2025) complete the trilogy; all three sit together in volume 45, issue 1 (January 2026), pages e1 to e81. An 'Author insights' piece (December 2025) and a JCVA 'highlights and perioperative implications' summary (February 2026) distil the content for anaesthesiologists.

**Caveats.** Consensus, not trial evidence: most recommendations rest on observational data and expert opinion. The randomised VA-ECMO versus off-pump trial now reporting in JTCVS will test some of the intraoperative assumptions.

**What it means.** Use Parts I to III as the standard your programme's ECLS pathway is measured against, and as the citation when arguing for or against planned VA-ECMO in a given recipient.

posts.headline: Only a third of real-world Impella AMI-shock patients meet DanGer Shock criteria; 30-day mortality 39% (J-PVAD)
posts.summary: Japan's nationwide J-PVAD registry sorted 3,975 Impella-supported AMI cardiogenic shock patients by DanGer Shock eligibility; most fell outside the trial phenotype and outcomes varied widely, worst after cardiac arrest.
takeHome: 35.6% of real-world Impella AMI-shock patients matched the trial that showed benefit.
30-day mortality: 37.6% in trial-eligible patients, 51.3% after out-of-hospital arrest, 63.4% without ROSC.
Age, renal dysfunction, VA-ECMO, ventricular arrhythmia and sepsis drove mortality in non-eligible STEMI patients.
posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters.** DanGer Shock gave Impella CP its first mortality benefit, but in a narrow STEMI phenotype. The question since has been how much real-world use looks like that trial. Japan's mandatory J-PVAD registry answers it at national scale (Arai and colleagues, Eur Heart J, online 13 October 2025).

**What they did.** Post hoc analysis of 3,975 patients with AMI-related cardiogenic shock supported with Impella between February 2020 and December 2023, sorted by whether they would have met DanGer Shock criteria.

**What they found.**
- Only 35.6% met the trial's STEMI-shock criteria. The rest were non-eligible STEMI (20.6%), out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (25.0%), mechanical complications (5.4%) or NSTEMI (13.4%).
- 30-day mortality was 38.7% overall: 37.6% in the eligible group, 27.6% in non-eligible STEMI, 51.3% in OHCA (63.4% without ROSC), 39.8% with mechanical complications and 33.3% in NSTEMI.
- In the non-eligible STEMI group, mortality climbed with older age, renal dysfunction, VA-ECMO use, ventricular arrhythmia and sepsis.

**Caveats.** Registry, no control arm, and Japanese practice patterns where Impella is used widely. It cannot say the device helped or hurt any subgroup. The accompanying editorial by Thiele is titled 'DanGerous real-world practice of percutaneous ventricular assist devices', which tells you where the European trialists stand.

**For us.** Two-thirds of pumps go into patients outside the evidence. When a patient arrives in the OR or ICU on an Impella after an arrest without ROSC, the realistic survival figure is about one in three. That belongs in family conversations and in decisions about escalating to ECMO or ECPELLA.

posts.headline: First joint EACTS/STS/AATS guideline on temporary MCS in cardiac surgery: escalate early, full-flow, with a shock team
posts.summary: The three major cardiac surgical societies published their first joint guideline on temporary mechanical circulatory support in adult cardiac surgery, covering post-cardiotomy shock, device choice, LV unloading and team structure.
takeHome: If the patient will not wean from bypass, run the TOE and hemodynamic checklist, then move to temporary MCS without delay.
VA-ECLS for profound failure; full-support microaxial pumps over partial support; IABP is modest and declining.
Interdisciplinary Shock Team input is strongly recommended; VA-ECLS plus microaxial unloading is first-line in overt biventricular failure.
posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters.** Post-cardiotomy cardiogenic shock is the scenario we face at the end of bypass, and until now there was no joint surgical-society guideline telling teams when and how to escalate. EACTS, STS and AATS published one together on 9 October 2025 (co-chairs Potapov, Whitman and John).

**What it says.**
- Post-cardiotomy shock is persistent low cardiac output: failure to wean from CPB or shock in the immediate postoperative period. Survival with timely support is quoted at 25 to 42%.
- Before escalating, reassess the fixable causes: rhythm, PA catheter or equivalent hemodynamics, TOE for valves, ventricular function and wall motion, ventilation and compliance, gases, hemostasis and reperfusion. If low output persists after correction, move to temporary MCS; delays should be avoided.
- VA-ECLS is called the most effective support for profound cardiopulmonary failure. When a microaxial pump is used for post-cardiotomy low output, full-support pumps are prioritized over partial support. IABP gives about 0.5 to 1 L/min, depends on native contractility, and its use has declined.
- Timely LV unloading on VA-ECLS is associated with lower early mortality and better weaning; VA-ECLS plus a microaxial pump is first-line in overt biventricular failure. Right-sided options (tRVAD, OxyRVAD) are mapped for tricuspid surgery with pre-existing RV dysfunction.
- An interdisciplinary Shock Team is strongly recommended, and prophylactic support should be a Heart Team decision.

**Caveats.** Much of the evidence base is observational, and the open-access tables do not display class and level labels. Sections on monitoring and anesthetic management, weaning and anticoagulation are in the full text.

**For us.** This is a citable standard for the pre-escalation TOE and hemodynamic checklist, and for pushing early, full-flow support instead of a prolonged inotrope-and-balloon drift. Expect surgeons and intensivists to quote it.

posts.headline: EACTS consensus defines 'protected cardiac surgery': pre-emptive MCS triggered by VIS >30, CI <=2.2, TAPSE <14 mm
posts.summary: An EACTS expert consensus proposes putting temporary MCS in before high-risk cardiac surgery patients develop low cardiac output syndrome, with explicit hemodynamic and echo triggers and Heart Team device selection.
takeHome: VIS above 30 is a strong indication for early support; VIS 20 to 30 with instability means close monitoring.
CI 2.2 or lower, CPI under 0.6, lactate 8 or higher, SvO2 under 50% should prompt MCS consideration.
RV triggers: TAPSE under 14 mm, RVFAC 30% or less, CVP 20 or higher, PAPi under 1.85; LV: LVEF under 30%.
posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters.** 'Protected cardiac surgery' means placing temporary MCS before the patient fails, not after. This EACTS consensus (chair Lorusso), published on 9 October 2025 alongside the joint EACTS/STS/AATS temporary MCS guideline, is the first society document to say who should get pre-emptive support and when.

**What it proposes.**
- A shift from rescuing low cardiac output syndrome to preventing it, using structured risk stratification, early initiation and Heart Team device selection.
- Three types by timing: Type 1 preoperative, Types 2 and 3 intraoperative and postoperative initiation.
- Explicit triggers: VIS above 30 is a strong indication for early support, VIS 20 to 30 with instability means close monitoring. Cardiac index at or below 2.2 L/min/m2 or cardiac power index below 0.6 W/m2, especially with MAP under 60 mmHg or high-dose vasoactives, should prompt consideration. Lactate 8 mmol/L or higher or SvO2 under 50% signal inadequate oxygen delivery.
- Ventricular phenotyping with numbers we generate: TAPSE under 14 mm, RV free-wall strain above minus 20%, RVFAC 30% or less, CVP 20 mmHg or higher, CVP/PCWP ratio 0.8 or higher and PAPi under 1.85 for the right side; LVEF under 30% and LVOT VTI under 13 cm for the left. Combined markers mean biventricular failure.
- Device options run from IABP through microaxial pumps, VA-ECLS, transseptal LV assist and RV configurations, chosen by phenotype.

**Caveats.** Expert consensus, not trial evidence. The only prospective data for planned Impella 5.5 in high-risk surgery (IMPACT, 100 patients, AATS 2026) is a single-arm pilot; there is no randomized trial of pre-emptive support.

**For us.** The TOE and PA catheter values in that trigger table are ours to measure and report. Expect surgeons to quote these thresholds when arguing for a pre-bypass device, and be ready to say whether the RV numbers support it.

posts.headline: Regional beats general for the baby at cesarean, but only modestly: fewer need respiratory support, NICU unchanged
posts.summary: Meta-analysis of 36 randomised trials (3,456 neonates, 1994-2023) comparing regional with general anesthesia for cesarean delivery.
takeHome: Apgar higher with regional by 0.58 (1 min) and 0.09 (5 min): statistically real, clinically small.
Neonatal respiratory support less likely (RR 0.62); intensive care admission not different (RR 0.75).
Every trial high or unclear risk of bias; use for counselling, not for refusing a needed GA.
posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters.** Neuraxial anesthesia is preferred for cesarean largely on maternal safety grounds; whether it also benefits the neonate has been asserted more than demonstrated. This is the first RCT-only meta-analysis to quantify it.

**What they did.** Random-effects meta-analysis of 36 randomised trials (3,456 neonates, published 1994 to November 2023) comparing spinal, epidural or CSE with general anesthesia for cesarean delivery. Risk of bias was assessed with RoB 2.

**What they found.** Apgar scores were higher with regional anesthesia at 1 minute (mean difference 0.58 points, 95% CI 0.36-0.79) and 5 minutes (0.09, 0.05-0.13). Neonates were less likely to need respiratory support after regional anesthesia (RR 0.62, 95% CI 0.40-0.94), but intensive care admission did not differ (RR 0.75, 0.46-1.21). Every included trial was at high or unclear risk of bias.

**Caveats.** Trials were small, heterogeneous and often from settings where GA technique differs from current practice; the 5-minute Apgar difference is numerically trivial. Long-term outcomes were not assessable.

**For the anesthesiologist.** The neonatal advantage of neuraxial is real but small and mostly about transient respiratory support, not NICU admission. That matters for counselling: a mother who needs or chooses GA should not be told her baby is being put at serious risk. It also sets expectations for the trials now being planned to compare anesthesia options directly, including the willingness-to-enrol survey published in Anesthesiology this year.

posts.headline: Kids with congenital heart disease having non-cardiac procedures: 1 in 20 has an intraoperative cardiac event
posts.summary: Multicenter registry of 6,455 non-cardiac procedures in 4,343 patients (age 21 or younger) with CHD at 7 centers during 2021, tracking hemodynamic instability, arrest and pulmonary hypertensive crisis.
takeHome: Composite cardiac event in 5.2% of procedures; hypotension 4.9%; cardiac arrest 0.2% (12 cases).
Severe CHD (OR 3.5), preoperative ventilatory support (OR 3.9) and respiratory illness (OR 2.2) drive risk.
Respiratory and GI procedures carry higher risk; plan staffing, monitoring and location accordingly.
posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters.** Children with congenital heart disease increasingly come to the non-cardiac OR, endoscopy suite and MRI. Mortality data from NSQIP and PHIS are familiar, but they say little about what happens minute to minute under anaesthesia.

**What they did.** Seven pediatric centers contributed every non-cardiac procedure performed under anesthesia in a patient with CHD (age 21 or younger) during 2021 to a multicenter registry: 4,343 patients and 6,455 procedures. The outcome was a composite of hemodynamic instability, cardiac arrest and pulmonary hypertensive crisis.

**What they found.** An intraoperative cardiac event occurred in 335 procedures (5.2%), affecting 296 patients. Hypotension accounted for most (315 procedures, 4.9%); cardiac arrest occurred in 12 procedures (0.2%). On univariate analysis, risk rose with CHD severity (major CHD OR 2.09; severe CHD OR 3.48), preoperative ventilatory support (OR 3.88), concurrent respiratory illness (OR 2.18), prematurity (OR 1.34), and with respiratory (OR 2.12) or gastrointestinal (OR 1.51) procedures.

**Caveats.** Observational, one calendar year, large academic centers, and hypotension definitions depend on local thresholds; events were not linked to longer-term outcomes in this paper.

**For the anesthesiologist.** One in 20 of these cases will test you, and the risk factors are knowable in advance: severe or single-ventricle physiology, a ventilator or a cold, and an airway or endoscopy procedure. That argues for cardiac-anesthesia involvement or at least a senior second pair of hands, invasive monitoring thresholds set in advance, and doing these cases where ECMO can be deployed. Pair it with the 2025 ACC/AHA ACHD guideline for the older end of the age range.

posts.headline: One in three GLP-1 users has a full stomach at induction; holding under 8 days or fasting under 21h predicts it
posts.summary: The Mayo MAGIC collaborative performed point-of-care gastric ultrasound on 316 adults taking GLP-1 receptor agonists before anesthesia at three hospitals and asked which preoperative factors predicted high residual gastric content.
takeHome: 35.8% had solids or more than 1.5 mL/kg of clear fluid despite standard fasting.
Weekly injectors who held the drug 7.5 days or less, or fasted solids 21 hours or less, were more often full.
Gastric POCUS before induction is the practical answer; a one-week hold or a long fast does not make it safe.
posts.deepDive:
**Why it matters.** The GLP-1 aspiration question has been argued on case series and society statements; this is a prospective, multi-site gastric-ultrasound dataset that puts numbers on who is actually full.

**What they did.** Adults taking GLP-1 receptor agonists and scheduled for anesthesia at three Mayo Clinic hospitals (June 30, 2023 to August 15, 2024) had preoperative point-of-care gastric ultrasound. High residual gastric content was defined as any solid, or more than 1.5 mL/kg of clear liquid. First author Sher-Lu Pai for the Mayo Anesthesia Gastric Imaging Collaborative; Anesthesia & Analgesia, online October 1, 2025, April 2026 issue (142:640-649; DOI 10.1213/ANE.0000000000007764).

**What they found.** Of 316 patients (median age 60.9; 52.8% women), 113 (35.8%) had high residual content. Among the 294 on weekly injections, the high-content group had held the drug a median 6 days (IQR 3-9) versus 8 days (IQR 5-10) in the low-content group (p=0.003), with an ROC cutoff of 7.5 days or less. Solid-food fasting was a median 15.0 hours versus 20.0 hours (p<0.001), with a cutoff of 21.3 hours or less. A recent opioid prescription was also more common with high content (5.3% vs 1.0%, p=0.027).

**Caveats.** Observational; cutoffs came from ROC analysis and were not tested prospectively; no aspiration outcomes; three hospitals in one system; the 1.5 mL/kg threshold is a surrogate for risk, not an event.

**For us.** Skipping one weekly dose does not reliably empty the stomach, and even very long solid fasts do not guarantee it. A two-minute antral scan in the preop bay answers the question for the patient in front of you and decides between a routine induction and a rapid sequence one.
